#3558. How To Rob A Bank Director David Leitch Reveals His Favorite Scene In The Movie [Exclusive]

Warning: This article contains light spoilers for "How to Rob a Bank."

David Leitch doesn't make things easy, and that's entirely by design. Of course, it's little surprise that the director behind punchy, stunt-centric movies like "The Fall Guy" or "Atomic Blonde" would opt for a more deliberate approach rather than the simplest one. His latest, "How to Rob a Bank," is just the latest in that trend. The unconventional, genre-redefining heist flick almost immediately makes a choice to embrace its own way of doing things — in this case, using a content creator aesthetic as star Nicholas Hoult's main protagonist Ryan (aka The Wolf) and his criminal crew go viral with their DIY social media channel. But how do you take that over-the-top stylistic direction and make it work alongside a much more grounded, emotional, and politically relevant storyline?

Fortunately, I had the chance to ask Leitch about how he pulled this off in "How to Rob a Bank" during a recent press junket. As it turns out, balancing two such divergent tones presented its own unique problem that had to be solved creatively. For Leitch, it was a matter of delineating between both aspects of writer Mark Bianculli's script and having form follow function:

"There were two very different visual stories we were telling. We were telling the grounded story of these characters and their very relatable plights that are happening, that are a snapshot of our times. And we shot that on 35 millimeter and there was a very traditional visual style we chose intentionally for that. Then you had these bombastic episodes of this charismatic content creator. And then the challenge was bringing those two worlds together. Actually, the challenge opportunity was exciting to bring them together."

In fact, Leitch pinpoints the moment where these worlds finally collide.

As much as "How to Rob a Bank" presents itself as a rollicking, thrill-a-minute roller coaster ride, things take an abrupt turn an hour in. Our gang of bank-robbing Robin Hoods make a key mistake, their dogged pursuers (led by Zoë Kravitz's tech-wiz Reagan and John C. Reilly's FBI Agent John West) track down their identities, and they soon land on opposite sides of an interrogation room. But, as the leader of this pack, Ryan has never found a setback he can't turn into a teachable moment — or, more cynically, a piece of content.

That's exactly what happens here, when both halves of the movie come into focus. "I think where we do it really well, and it's my favorite scene in the movie," David Leitch explains to me, "is during the interrogation sequence, where we're blurring the lines between the Wolf's show — basically [explaining] how to survive an interrogation — and the actual footage, being in the real interrogation." Here, Leitch and his creative team splice together straightforward imagery from the interrogation (which is mostly our defiant characters sitting silently, demanding their lawyer) and imagery where Ryan uses (or imagines?) this as his latest YouTube video: How to Survive an Interrogation.

According to Leitch, this allowed him to play with what we're seeing versus what's really happening:

"Even the characters in the movie breaking the fourth wall or texts coming up on the screen when we're in the film, now it's like [the] content creator visual style is changing the way that I'm telling you the narrative aspect of the film. And I'm actually using the narrative aspect of the film to influence the way that I composed the content creator footage."

Despite the complexity in putting this sequence together, all of this is seamlessly cut and presented in a way where it hardly even registers to moviegoers. At the moment, we're too concerned with the fate of Ryan, his lover Emi (Anna Sawai), and the rest of their friends as all their best-laid plans come crashing down. Adding to the tension is the delicate balance of power suddenly shifting away from these honorable thieves trying to make a societal point and towards the man representing all the structural ills they're fighting against: FBI Agent John West.

During our conversation, "How to Rob a Bank" producer and 87North production company founder Kelly McCormick chimes in and adds, "That's exactly where the power is shifting and where the worlds are colliding. So, in a masterful way, [David Leitch is] toying with you there, manipulating you with both ways of storytelling." Intriguingly, none of this is meant to register to viewers who are (hopefully) absorbed by the storytelling in the moment. According to Leitch, this is something that he only conveyed through the subtext and through the visuals in how he and director of photography Jonathan Sela shot the scene:

"It's not necessary for the audience to really understand it, but that's the uneasy feeling I'm trying to give, is the power switching."

We won't give away anything that happens next, but it's safe to say this is the turning point where things kick into another gear. From that point on, the film's stakes are firmly set and nobody feels safe. "How to Rob a Bank" is now playing in theaters.

#3557. Blood of Dawnwalker Finally Gets Its Most Requested Feature Next Week

Rebel Wolves is giving fans what they’ve been asking for in update 1.2

It's been just over two months since The Blood of Dawnwalker was released and fans have been clamoring for one missing feature for basically that long. Now developer Rebel Wolves is set to appease that demand with the upcoming update 1.2. Yes, New Game Plus is going to be a reality for the vampire RPG.

Rebel Wolves has already pushed several post-release updates to The Blood of Dawnwalker to address fan feedback. The game's first big patch, update 1.1, added a new difficulty mode, tweaked combat, and introduced the all-important ability to pet animals. It crucially lacked New Game Plus. Back in September, director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz revealed that the studio was exploring the possibility but didn't want to speak about it yet. Staying tight-lipped was likely meant to not overexcite fans if the feature couldn't actually be delivered. Well, now it seems like Rebel Wolves has figured it out. As revealed on the game's social media accounts, New Game Plus will be added as part of update 1.2. The big patch will be released next week. A specific date was not shared, but update 1.1 was dropped on a Thursday.

As detailed by the announcement, New Game Plus will be available once players have completed the game's epilogue. Your level, skills, and inventory will all carry over. Additionally, the level cap will be raised to 100 and enemies will be balanced and scaled across all regions. Items will be given New Game Plus versions with updated stats. Enjoy sinking your teeth back into Vale Sangora.

New Game Plus isn't the only new feature coming to the game in update 1.2, though it is the biggest addition. If you purchased The Blood of Dawnwalker — Eclipse Edition, you'll notice that the in-game soundtrack will be extended with new songs. Streaming services will also get the new soundtrack material soon.

As for general tweaks to The Blood of Dawnwalker, update 1.2 will make some balance changes to enemy health pools and how often they use their abilities during combat. Some terrain geometry has also been adjusted to allow for smoother movement during combat and exploration. The Blood of Dawnwalker has been one of 2026's great surprises, but it is unclear whether it will be able to shine through a crowded field as awards season kicks into full gear.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for Season 35, Episode 10 of Dancing With the Stars, “Grammy Night,” streaming now with a Hulu subscription and Disney+ subscription.

Season 35 of Dancing With the Stars is in full swing on the 2026 TV schedule, with the series officially in its semi-finals era once again. The competition is as tense as ever, with surprising eliminations practically every week. And every week, fans give their thoughts on just about everything. This includes the continuing discourse of whether celebrities with dance training should be allowed to compete.

DWTS always has a wide range of celebrities each season, from actors to musicians to athletes to comedians to influencers and yes, even politicians. This means that everyone has different backgrounds, and naturally, there will be some people who have dance training, whether it was a long time ago or very recently. For Season 35 specifically, a lot of people have been calling out Jenna Dewan, whose experience in dance includes being a backup dancer for artists such as Janet Jackson and in the Step Up films. X user swifferwins shared their opinion on the situation, pointing out just how much of an advantage Dewan has over some of her competitors:

ok at the risk of getting hate for opening my mouth - i am not deep into dwts and haven’t ever really minded when someone w dance experience is on dancing with the stars but someone who was danced in movies, award shows, and major artist TOURS being a star is WILD to me

I personally couldn’t care less if a celebrity on Dancing With the Stars has prior dance experience, since ballroom dancing is so different. Dewan has even opened up about having to unlearn some of the stuff she’s picked up over the years because of the stark differences. That being said, she still has the skills, but X user n1taydefender makes a good point:

Ballroom and Latin is different than most modern dance styles, ballroom has so many rules! But I agree to a certain degree, it’s just really hard to find stars with no dance background at all, since most of them have some kind of theatrical training

On average, DWTS’ celebrity roster each season usually consists of around 16, so it might be hard to find that many celebrities, all in different careers, with next to no dancing background. However, it’s understandable that a lot of people wouldn’t like it since DWTS is all about teaching celebrities the art of dance and seeing them improve. Glee alum Harry Shum Jr. has also been getting a lot of heat for his own experiences, as kismetdiviner replied in the thread:

i feel this heavy about both harry & jenna this season. coming from someone with competitive ballroom dance experience, their backgrounds both give them an incredibly unfair advantage. it’s truly insane!! and prior to the show, harry’s danced with julianne, & jenna with derek 🫠

Just because you have dance experience doesn’t mean that you’re a shoo-in to win the whole thing. For instance, Dewan was just eliminated in this week’s episode with her partner, Val Chmerkovskiy. While it came as a shock, fans are certainly making their voices heard, and it could mark a shift in the entire competition. It can still be anyone’s game, and with the semis coming up, you never know just what will happen.

A handful of actors with musical theater experience also include Jordan Fisher and Corbin Bleu, with Milo Manheim, Zendaya, Chandler Kinney, and Roshon Fegan also coming from Disney Channel and showing off their extensive dancing skills. Out of those six, Fisher was the only one to win the Mirrorball. Not to mention the few Dance Moms contestants who have also graced the ballroom floor, like JoJo Siwa and Mackenzie Ziegler, with neither winning.

All this to say that there’s never a guarantee that someone with dance experience is going to take home the Mirrorball. Even if a couple has a perfect score, they could still go home, which is what happened with Dewan and Chmerkovskiy. Now that we’re getting down to the final couples, fans will be working harder than ever to make sure that their favorites make it to the top, with or without dance experience. And people will still be divided, regardless. Tune in on Tuesday at 8 p.m. ET on ABC to see who could be making it to the DWTS finals.

#3554. Johnny Depp's Ebenezer Makes An Alarming Change To The Story Of A Christmas Carol

When the ads and pre-release buzz articles began running for "Ebenezer," the new film directed by Ti West and starring Johnny Depp as Scrooge, the campaign promised that the movie would present Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol" as you'd never seen it before. Yet, now that the film has released and folks (including yours truly) have screened it, it turns out "Ebenezer" is unsurprisingly more or less the same "A Christmas Carol" we all know well. The movie liberally copy-and-pastes whole swathes of Dickens' text into the script, with writer Nathaniel Halpern even bothering to include the novella's separation into five staves. However, it seems there's some larger artistic liberty wiggle room in that "more or less the same" than might appear at first glance.

When West spoke to Entertainment Weekly back in August, he detailed what made Depp's Ebenezer different than previous adaptations. Amidst talking up things like Depp's "musicality" as a performer, West also explained how his film would present Scrooge in a more both sides-y manner: "As [Depp's] Scrooge cuts someone down verbally or as he makes a financial point or withdraws, you do understand why he's doing it." That offhand mention of "a financial point" baffled many of us when we first read it, as it certainly did sound like a deviation from Dickens.

Was this Scrooge going to be portrayed as a genius businessman? Instead, the changes "Ebenezer" makes to Scrooge and Dickens' story are of a smaller nature. They involve portraying a couple small supporting characters as outright villains, thereby giving Scrooge a justification for his misanthropy. The changes may be merely tweaks, yet their larger implications are alarming, especially for a film which doesn't feel able to support them.

For the most part, "Ebenezer" is a faithful adaptation of "A Christmas Carol." The largest addition comes in the form of a prologue in which we see Scrooge and his partner, Jacob Marley (Ian McKellen), on their last day together. Marley goes to get some tea while Scrooge observes a beggar outside his window. At the same moment the beggar reveals himself to Scrooge as a fraud conning people out of their donations, Marley drops dead, equating the con artist's crime with harm done to a true earner in Scrooge's mind. That Marley (and Scrooge) are just as heartless and dishonest is something the film hopes Dickens' work gets across, as they don't go out of their way to underline it to support their addition.

This problem is compounded twice. Once is when it's revealed that Scrooge's old benevolent boss Fezziwig was murdered by a street beggar, further teaching Scrooge that charity can be met with violence. Next is when the Ghost of Christmas Future shows Scrooge the vultures who've come to sully his legacy after his death, which adds the wrinkle that the two men who sought a donation for the poor at the beginning of the film are actually also embezzlers.

What's more, they're in league with a man who's plotting with the embezzlers to steal Scrooge's nephew Fred's inheritance with the production of a forged will. The alarming quality about these inclusions lies in how they seem to give Scrooge more moral justification for his odious behavior that he doesn't need. It's a bizarrely tone-deaf addition for a story that's ultimately meant to be about the virtues of charity.

Ultimately (and thankfully), these additions do not derail "Ebenezer," for the heart of Charles Dickens' story and his themes remains intact. Although it's tempting to point fingers at the Skydance corporation for the new ideas, it isn't the changes themselves that are the problem. After all, Ti West comes from a background of indie horror films, many of which utilize thorny, morally ambiguous characterizations and themes as their stock in trade. "Ebenezer" is indeed partially constructed to emphasize the horror in Dickens' tale: the three Christmas ghosts are more ghastly and doomed than they typically are. In the more horror-centric version of "A Christmas Carol" the movie seems to want to be, a somewhat justified Scrooge would be a fascinating layer for an actor to play, as it creates a new obstacle for the character to overcome on his journey to selflessness.

Alas, "Ebenezer" is the Johnny Depp show, and for several reasons, Depp is not up to the task. While it's arguable that he may not be able to tackle such material at all, it seems like he's not even interested in trying in the first place. Instead, "Ebenezer" and Depp are too preoccupied with trying to be as likable as possible, which means that his Scrooge rarely gets nasty. He comes off more like an irritable jerk than a man who's nearly lost his soul, so whatever compelling shadings the changes to the story could've presented never materialize. On paper, the possibilities presented by "Ebenezer" range from exciting to alarming. Yet we needn't fret too much, since the finished film plays things so safely that it's hard to get riled up about it one way or the other.

#3553. Nearly a Decade Ago My Friend’s Private Plane Fell Out of the Sky. Then, in Florida This Month, It Happened to Another Friend.

When I was in my late 20s, I lived in the worst building in the best part of SoHo. My apartment above the French restaurant Raoul’s had been created by merging two units, so it was quite spacious. When I decided to move in with my boyfriend in Los Angeles, I still planned to spend a quarter of my time in New York and wasn’t about to give up this gem. But I figured I could find a roommate who would be psyched I wouldn’t be there a ton, and keep the smaller bedroom for myself.

The writer Deborah Schoeneman introduced me to her best friend from Cornell University, who she said would be the perfect roommate. Jen Blumin was a Sex and the City character come to life: a tall, gorgeous blonde who managed a high-end event space with a private pool a few blocks away, mostly for corporate sponsors. I figured she wouldn’t be home much while I was, and told her if she had $1,800 a month, she had a deal. The day she moved in, she gingerly walked up the four flights of stairs carrying a large wrought-iron cage containing a shrieking bird. “Did I not tell you I had a cockatoo?” she asked with such insouciant camp, such mock innocence, that I just had to laugh.

Schoeneman, Grigoriadis, and Blumin in 2010 at Round Hill Resort.

Thus began one of my life’s great friendships, proceeding through many more ripostes, a decade of shared living space, and the birth of two kids each. Jen became wildly successful by turning vacant institutional buildings into heart-stopping event spaces, and even landed the contract for New York Fashion Week at the old post office across from Pennsylvania Station. The love of her life and father of her children, the architect James Ramsey, conceived of an idea with Dan Barasch, another Cornell chum, to create a “low line” under the old Delancy Street trolley terminal, and for a while it seemed like that was going to happen. But the relationship fell apart, and then things move very fast in my memory: Jen started to say she disliked New York City and wanted to live full time in the North Fork, a new boyfriend showed up, now she was moving to Puerto Rico for the climate and tax breaks, then she and the boyfriend were buying a private plane to fly direct from Puerto Rico to Islip, NY.

When I heard about this new acquisition by my far-more successful friend, I have to admit I thought it sounded rad. Private planes occupy an almost mystical place in our culture. You’re up in the skies, free of seatmates chomping tuna sandwiches or annoyances like last-minute checked bags. You’re watching the clouds drift by, close enough to touch God. So what if her plane wasn’t the fanciest! It was still glamorous. As former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown wrote on her Substack, everyone wants to be your friend when you have a plane: “The late TV legend Barbara Walters used to lament the necessity to vacation every year with the crass termagant CEO of a bra company just because said termagant happened to own her own plane.”

For the wealthy, private planes, which have become increasingly popular as a mode of transportation in recent years, aren’t only the ultimate in seclusion, but also the ultimate in spontaneity. You’re in a power position that’s completely the reverse of commercial flights, which reduce you to helpless nose-boned chattel. If you’re paying the bill, most decisions are controlled by you: You decide when you leave, who to invite, what to eat (certainly not pretzels and ginger ale), and whether there’s space for your three bulldogs.

But the day after Mother’s Day in 2017—which Jen memorialized by sending a group text to myself and the core girlfriends with a snapshot of her two toddlers on a big rock in Puerto Rico—Jen’s private plane fell out of the sky. She was flying with her children about 15 miles east of Eleuthera, an island in the Bahamas, in the Bermuda Triangle. None of them were found.

I think a lot about Jen, but rarely more than now, nearly a decade after her death. That’s because this month, the same set of New York friends—loosely—are mourning another person who died with his family, including two more children under five years old. Adam Robinson, who chartered the Learjet that dove into a Florida road on November 1, leaving hypersurreal audio and video recordings that are now seared into the nation’s collective memory, arrived in New York a little later than Jen. I met him in the mid-2000s, but he seemed to be cut from the same cloth as she was: a tall, gregarious Lehman Brothers trader who had inherited a loft on lower Broadway from our mutual friends, the founders of the website College Humor (there was a lot of apartment swapping in lower Manhattan back then).

Adam was the definition of a “good guy”: smart, kind, and wry at the right moments. He had the open-hearted self-possession of someone who had traveled widely, but now he was in New York City to start his career, which, like so many of us, involved being hyper-social. He was not a close friend, but I was always happy to see him, and would usually spend 10 minutes at a crowded party chatting before moving on (this means a lot if you, like me, ascribe to the Fitzgeraldian notion that large parties provide intimacy, and prefer not to waste your breath in this rarefied milieu on dolts). A few guys in the crowd were into email marketing, and I heard that Adam had started a business in that industry but didn’t know much about his life after he moved to Austin, nor that he, too, had become quite successful.

It’s eerie that Adam’s private plane was headed to Eleuthra, the same area where Jen disappeared. But beyond that coincidence, what I keep returning to is how Jen and Adam’s stage in life had so many similarities: both in their 40s, too early to retire, they had nevertheless entered what you could call the “second phase” of success. They weren’t only trying to make money but to enjoy the money they’d made, and for them, that meant devising a new kind of life. Adam had moved from Austin to Aspen and wanted to pursue more outdoor adventures, some of which involved destinations hard to reach by commercial flights. Jen didn’t need to take her fatal private journey—JetBlue flies direct from San Juan to JFK—but having her own plane definitely came with bragging rights, though neither was the type to post a “flashing a peace sign on a PJ” semi-candid shot on Instagram.

And yet the private plane, so much a symbol of freedom and success for both Jen and Adam, led to their demise. This type of aviation is far less regulated than commercial planes, which hew to “strict government regulations enumerated in hundreds of pages of fine print…everything from the stowing of tray tables to announcements concerning lavatory smoke detectors,” as Jeff Wise wrote in Vanity Fair in 2025. That may be okay when you’re traveling in a $75 million G800, or as a guest of Drake in his $185 million plane, or with Kylie Jenner in her $73 million Bombardier, but when you’re on a small plane, it matters. Wise notes in his story that since 2020, almost half of the private plane crashes in the US have been Citations, which are on the smaller side.

And when traveling in a plane that lacks the sophistication of a commercial jet, whether you’re JFK Jr., Aaliyah, or just two people that everyone in a certain downtown Manhattan set knew in the mid-aughts, weather happens. Bad decisions in the cockpit compound, if the pilots even have time to make them. And then everything you’ve worked so hard for is lost, with the wreckage extending to family members and best friends left behind. “If I was Adam, I would rather be on the plane than on the ground” is the refrain I keep hearing from my friends this week, meaning that they’d rather perish with their families than live without them. Success and its luxuries are wonderful things. But they don’t guarantee you’ll get to come home.

#3552. How To Rob A Bank Director Reveals The Real-Life Inspirations Behind The Movie's Influencers [Exclusive]

Of all the movies in 2026 that can claim to be the timeliest, none may have a better case than "How to Rob a Bank." Even setting aside the obvious social and political commentary behind director David Leitch's newest heist flick, in which a group of Robin Hood-like bank robbers team up to send a message to corporate bigwigs and capitalist vultures, the movie's timeliness is also apparent in the way it's shot and edited. The various trailers have made no secret of the content creator angle behind this crew, led by Nicholas Hoult's Ryan (aka The Wolf). When they're not sticking up banks and making thrilling getaways, they're busy editing their escapades into viral-ready YouTube videos to be consumed by the masses.

It's a novel approach that'll either work or not for audiences, many of whom are well aware of the online ecosystem that is influencer culture. It's a tall task for any mainstream Hollywood movie to tackle, but the creative team behind "How to Rob a Bank" clearly did their homework. During a recent press junket for the film, I spoke to both Leitch and producing partner Kelly McCormick about the deep well of influences they drew from in order to nail this specific element of the film — one that certainly attempts to feel true to our digital lives. According to McCormick:

"We were trying to go for what might be the next push for creators, if you know what I mean. Like, the wish fulfillment aspect from a creator's perspective of just pushing the envelope even more. So it was just really absorbing as much as possible to see what was out there and then using some of the prosumer cameras to make sure that we were just being even more wild."

The content creator footage depicted throughout "How to Rob a Bank" will inevitably leave an impression. No, we don't live in a world where adrenaline-seeking influencers actually put themselves and others in harm's way to pull off successful heists and robberies. (Not yet, at least.) But actually capturing those vibes in an authentic way meant resorting to some very specific filmmaking measures.

One scene shows Ryan and his friends fleeing the scene of the crime on motorcycles through a forest, with GoPros strapped to their helmets capturing footage in every direction. When this is filtered through the lens of the video they upload afterwards, well, that's where things get visually dynamic. As Kelly McCormick explained to me:

"The one [scene] in specific I always remember is when they're biking through the forest and you see it from above and we are pivoting the camera in editorial, because literally it's capturing [360 degrees] around [the action]. And so you can spin it around in editorial to get that vibe of this wild editing that I think would be a creator's dream, if they didn't have to hit deadlines and always be feeding as much as possible to their hungry, hungry followers [laughs]."

David Leitch name-checks "extreme sports" as one section of YouTube they paid particular attention to for sequences like that, while the idea of philanthropy and giving back to communities was taken out of the Mr. Beast playbook. Even podcasters get into the mix, like Scott Galloway or King Bach (both of whom make cameos in the film). Adds Leitch with a laugh, "We had a lot of influences in our influencers."

#3551. NCIS: NY Is Off To A Great Start, But There Are Two Subplots That I NEED To Be Resolved Quickly

I’m very new to the NCIS franchise, but I think NCIS: New York, which debuted last month on the 2026 television schedule, is really fun. I love the characters and the actors playing them, and that is the most important thing for procedurals to work for me. I especially like Scott Caan’s character, even if it’s really similar to his Hawaii Five-0. There are two subplots that I’m really not digging, but they are easy to wrap up, and I hope the show does that quickly.

My first issue involves two special agents on the team: Addy Ross, played by Jacqueline Byers, and Wyatt Sellers, played by Shane Harper. There is a weird “will they/won’t they” thing going on between the two characters, and I don’t like it. It’s not the chemistry between the actors or the characters or anything like that. It’s just unnecessary. There doesn’t have to be a romantic angle in a show like NCIS: New York. It feels shoehorned in, and doesn’t feel organic at all.

They are the “other” two members of the field team, with Caan and LL Cool J making up the “A-team” as the two biggest stars on the show. Addy and Wyatt are great when they are doing their jobs, and I can even get behind the idea that Wyatt is trying to learn more about the personal life of his partner, who is very private about it. Hinting at a potential relationship is not believable. These are professionals! Keep them professional!

My other big issue with the character subplots is between the two “office” members of the team. Jennifer Beals plays Robyn Wells, the leader of the team, and she’s great! It’s so fun watching her in a new show. However, she has a consistent beef with the computer nerd, Sean Sullivan (Devon Druid). It stems from the reason Druid is employed by NCIS. His backstory hasn’t been fully fleshed out on the show yet, but we do know that he is there because he was a hacker who was facing a long prison sentence.

That’s all well and good, but every time Sean says almost anything about the job, Robyn reminds him that he has prison hanging over her head. Like, I get it. He’s there against his will and avoiding jail. Great! Fun concept! But do we really need to be constantly reminded of it? Let it just sit in the background and come up when it makes sense. The character’s backstory doesn’t need to be re-established all the time.

As I said, both of these stories can be wrapped up, or at least pushed way to the back burner without really causing any plot holes or other problems with the show, and I really hope they are soon. Otherwise, I’m looking forward to NCIS: New York's future

Hugh Scott is the Syndication Editor for CinemaBlend. Before CinemaBlend, he was the managing editor for Suggest.com and Gossipcop.com, covering celebrity news and debunking false gossip. He has been in the publishing industry for almost two decades, covering pop culture – movies and TV shows, especially – with a keen interest and love for Gen X culture, the older influences on it, and what it has since inspired. He graduated from Boston University with a degree in Political Science but cured himself of the desire to be a politician almost immediately after graduation.

#3550. 8 New TV Shows to Watch This Weekend on Netflix, Prime Video, and HBO (November 13-15)

From the return of one of the biggest fantasy series, to a new Netflix horror

It’s a big weekend for new TV. VisionQuest has concluded its first season, including a post-credits scene with big implications for Avengers: Doomsday. The Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power is back with a third season, continuing the story of a Middle-earth set thousands of years before Bilbo and Frodo Baggins. The Body is also available on Netflix, delivering a fun and campy high school drama with some religious horror thrown in the mix.

Thriller lovers have some shows to look forward to. The Good Daughter, a 6-episode series based on Karin Slaughter's bestseller, has just been released. It’s adapted by Slaughter herself, making her the rare novelist who’s also the showrunner for her own story. There’s also 12 12 12, starring Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan, as two men involved in a high-stakes cat-and-mouse game that starts with a robbery.

We have a few picks for lovers of documentary and true crime. Murder in Galicia is streaming on Netflix, telling the story of the murder of 66-year-old Isabel Fuente, who was beaten in her sleep, with her husband claiming that some intruders had gotten inside their house.

There’s also HBO’s Silent Night, a series based on the murders that took place on Christmas Eve in 1976 in a small community in Poland. Lastly, if you want something a little breezier, there’s The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, premiering on Hulu and Disney. Happy watching!

The Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power is back with a third season, exploring the tales of Middle-earth thousands of years before the events of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. Season 3 tries to course-correct a series that has never managed to get things right. Set five years after the events of season 2 and billed as a soft reboot to welcome in new watchers, the season finds Sauron establishing his power.

Prequels always have difficulty justifying their existence since it’s a foregone conclusion how the story will end. Last season, Rings of Power leaned into that inevitability in the same way as the Game of Thrones prequel House of the Dragon, building a Shakespearean tragedy from the corruption of the dwarf king Durin III (Peter Mullan) and the elven smith Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards). There’s still some of that in season 3 as the island kingdom of Númenor and the dwarven stronghold of Khazad-dûm inch closer to their dark fates. But the show also spends too much time taking the same approach as Solo: A Star Wars Story, providing unnecessary origins for everything from the construction plans of Lothlorien to the origins Gandalf’s hat.

The Body is set in 2004 and follows a dance team at a Catholic High School located somewhere in the Northeast. After partying too hard and botching a dance initiation ceremony, the girls inspire a mass hysteria in the town, with residents believing they have a saint in their midst.

One of the best parts of The Body is its many references. Shephard borrows archetypes and textures from films like Bring It On, Mean Girls, and White Chicks. Story-wise, there are clear shades of The Crucible and The Exorcist. The show’s cast of characters take these archetypes and complicate them. With dyed eyebrows and a sweet but alienating approach, Lisbeth feels like Needy from Jennifer’s Body with a dash of Brigitte from Ginger Snaps. Anya and Elise are clear successors to Bring It On’s Torrance and Missy, who raised a generation of queer viewers with their ridiculously charged friendship. But the great thing about The Body is that even though it depicts the aughts and the social concerns of the era, it’s made in 2026, allowing the writers to revisit these tropes and probe further.

Set in Georgia, The Good Daughter follows two estranged sisters reunited by a school shooting that may be closely tied to their past. The women have spent years apart due to an incident in their childhoods, when a group of men broke into their home, killing their mother and leaving one of them gravely injured.

Following a massive heist in Europe, 12 12 12 follows three timelines and two main characters: Paul (Jamie Dornan), the skilled criminal who pulled off the heist, and Jack (Anthony Mackie), a disgraced FBI agent with a personal vendetta against Paul.

Based on the real-life crime of Isabel Fuente, “Murder in Galicia” is a scripted series following a seemingly perfect aging couple based in a small town in Spain. After the woman is almost beaten to death after a break-in at their house, a civil guard becomes convinced that the culprit is actually the husband.

Based on a series of notorious crimes that took place on Christmas Eve in a small town in ‘70s Poland, the 6-episode series tells the story of the three murders that were committed on a snowy night in the town, initially staged as a hit-and-run.

The spin-off series trades the internet-famous Salt Lake City moms and swaps them for a new location: Orange County. The new reality series follows a new batch of influencers and features moments captured in famous reality TV destinations like Laguna Beach and Huntington Beach.

Power, the Starz series that ran for six seasons, is now available on Netflix in full. The show follows a wealthy New York City club owner who’s also a drug kingpin and is trying to leave his life of crime behind to protect and focus on his family.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3549. Mississippi Goddam: Scott Colom Is the Answer to Anyone Who Looked Down on the South

“Mississippi is not who you think we are.”

This is what an older Black woman said to MS NOW’s Nnamdi Egwuonwu as he interviewed Scott Colom supporters on the Tougaloo College campus Thursday night. The crowd was waiting for Colom to speak after his historic victory, becoming the first Black Mississippian elected to statewide office since Reconstruction, and its first Democratic senator in nearly a half century. The woman did not give her name, but her simple statement has tattooed itself inside my brain.

“To understand the world, you must first understand a place like Mississippi” is a more famous cautionary quip that scratches at the same sentiment. If you’ve known anyone from Mississippi, you’ve probably heard it. Everyone cites William Faulkner, even though nobody has definitively sourced it. But as the world looks with fresh eyes on my home state, the wisdom checks out.

Onlookers, including longtime national political strategists, seem surprised by Colom’s win. Mississippians are not. The extremes of the moral universe have always been duking it out down there, which makes Mississippi not strange or anomalous, but illustrative.

There’s no avoiding the facts: Human beings have committed the most brutal violence imaginable against their fellow humans in Mississippi, as a matter of law and legacy. One of the consequences of that horror is that it has become prophecy. It is impossible not to feel a sense—from within the state and from without—of frustration and dread that it is taking way too long to emerge from a racism that has raptured the entire culture.

But to people who do not know Mississippians, who do not understand Mississippi—to those who suggest any right-minded or good people simply up and leave, or think the rest of the country should abandon all hope, or worse, look away entirely—you are missing one of the most important threads in the future of American politics and culture. Colom got at this rub when he said that outlets like Cook Political Report, who prognosticate a “solid R” conclusion, are destructive. “They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long,” he wrote. And if you dismiss possibility in Mississippi, you are compounding the neglect. You are part of the destruction.

You think John McCain was a maverick? Scott Colom is a maverick.

During the race, he drew national attention not only for his prospect of flipping the unflippable, but also because he was doing so through one of the most vivid, creatively engaged, and original campaigns in modern politics. He built a coalition virally, with his twin brother, Andrew Robert Colom, as collaborator, offering “Sheeeeit” to the world (yes, that’s how many white Mississippians really talk), along with a Hollywood-worthy Sinners send-up, and Andrew’s searing spoken-word poem set to the strains of Fannie Lou Hamer. Colom even stood in line at a Trump rally to speak earnestly with voters who would otherwise be against him—I guarantee he won some of them over.

His entire strategy was built on making people recognize Mississippi, in all its underdog idiosyncrasies. He asked Kamala Harris to campaign with him, even as his advisers reportedly told him it would be an error, because he knew she would draw media attention to underfunded hospitals. And he took the phone call informing him that he’d won while wearing a Richard Pryor hoodie. Because we like to laugh in Mississippi, okay?

As Kiese Laymon, novelist, memoirist, and modern-day Mississippi bard, told me, “Once I saw the protein ad, I knew he’d win.”

History doesn’t echo in Mississippi; it rhymes. You can draw a straight line from the murders of Medgar Evers, or those of James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, to the killings of Jorge Gomez or Renee Good or Alex Pretti. You can draw a straight line from Theodore Bilbo to Tate Reeves to Donald Trump.

As Kiese wrote in this magazine in 2020, Mississippi politics flow from its culture. (Incidentally, Kiese and Colom both attended Millsaps College, about 10 years apart, and had the same thesis adviser.) In “Mississippi: A Poem, in Days,” Kiese describes how he got into “an altercation with two fraternities on Bid Day”—when the students who want to be in the Greek system receive offers from frat and sorority houses. “Some fraternity members wore Confederate capes, Afro wigs, and others blackened their faces.” They called Kiese and his girlfriend the N-word.

I have never written about the heartbreak of seeing the future governor of Mississippi in that group of white boys, proudly representing the Kappa Alpha fraternity and its confederate commitment to Black suffering. I have never admitted that after playing basketball against Tate all through high school, and knowing that he went to a public school called Florence, not a segregation academy, like so many other white boys we knew, it hurt my feelings to see Tate doing what white boys who pledged their identities to the Old South ideologies were supposed to do.

When I saw Tate in that confederate cacophony of drunken white boyhood, doing what they did, I knew he could one day be governor of Mississippi and president of the United States.

That is still the most damning thing I can ever say about a white boy from Mississippi.

Damning things still happen, and will again. Just days ago, as the votes continued to stack up for Colom, the old ugliness reared its head. White women in my hometown, students at the University of Mississippi, were captured on video making racist gestures—gesturing and making sounds like monkeys—at their Black neighbors’ video doorbell. The school, still embarrassingly insistent on calling itself “Ole Miss,” continues to investigate, while the offenders get so much more grace than they deserve from the victims and their families, as you can see in their CBS interview. I feel deep shame in these moments, because I know this is what so many people think Mississippi is. There is no excuse for it, and no explanation beyond the obvious. The shame should be obvious, too, but a white person from Mississippi is compelled to express it.

The women are not from Mississippi, according to a source familiar; one, Alaina Kunes, is from Wisconsin, where a car dealership that bears her family’s name is now being sued for a separate allegation of racist actions. This is not an excuse, but rather a fear: that Mississippi’s reputation for the worst parts of history continues to attract the worst sorts of people.

But this is partly what Faulkner, or whoever it was, meant by understanding the world through the lens of Mississippi: Everywhere we must hope our better angels prevail.

I was born and raised in Mississippi among a large, politically engaged family who have wanted change for generations. When Sargent Shriver turned up unexpectedly at my grandparents’ house for dinner one night, on a swing through the South in a failed presidential bid, my grandmother whispered the urgent directive of “FHB”—“family holdback”—so her five sons would leave enough food for Shriver. This story, and that guest, was a point of pride her whole life. She was an unforgiving George McGovern campaigner; in our family photo album, among the pool parties and Christmas mornings, are pages of Polaroids she snapped of Richard Nixon’s televised resignation.

Local private schools, as I understood them, were inherently racist. Public school was a choice of one, and I got a world-class education in the Oxford school system. (Hyde-Smith attended Lawrence County Academy and she sent her own child to Brookhaven Academy, both segregation academies.) My class of 2000—I came up with the same kids from kindergarten through high school—was roughly half Black and half white, with the skinniest pie slivers of anything else. I left for college and never moved back, but my parents, brother, and extended family are still there. Today, Mississippi’s public-school students are doing better than most of their peers across the nation; my own children in the New York City school system are getting a more segregated, less excellent education than I did.

My father, a green-energy mayor and a Barack Obama appointee to the Tennessee Valley Authority (fired by Trump amid a Republican board takeover), pushed throughout my childhood to take the Confederate flag off the state flag and to remove the Confederate monument that still mars the Oxford Square. I was about eight years old when someone keyed “LIBERALS” into the trunk of our Honda Civic, probably because of the Ray Mabus for Governor bumper sticker. I recall being worried about it, until I saw that my parents were amused.

As white Southern liberals, we were in a tiny minority. And though the mantle was worn proudly, it was more existential than that—you were proud to be a Democrat not because it was one party over another, but because it was a stand-in for compassion, common good, and humanity. And nowhere could this be truer, or more necessary, than in Mississippi. (By way of disclosure, I see no conflicts in telling you all this. As former Time editor Rick Stengel says, “You should be non-partisan, but not neutral. Journalists must be biased in favor of the truth and facts. Biased in favor of democracy itself.” And this is the truth, in favor of democracy.)

Scott Colom and I were born a year apart in the earliest 1980s, during a sort of second-wave new New South rebranding. More jobs were coming into the state thanks to manufacturing; more national attention was being paid to Black Mississippians’ cultural contributions (the Delta Blues Museum was established in 1979). William Winter was governor the years of our respective births, and he gave us free kindergarten. William Allain, whose moment was virtually destroyed by a racist, homophobic GOP slander campaign, followed. And Allain was succeeded by Mabus—who won on the slogan “Mississippi will never be last again.” Now, with the exception of Ronnie Musgrove, the governor has been a Republican since 1992. We’ve never had a Black person, or a woman for that matter. Have you had many good thoughts about Mississippi in all this time? I don’t think you have.

Heavy, Kiese’s devastating and raw memoir of coming of age as a Black boy in Mississippi, written in address to his activist and educator mother, gives his own view into 1980s and ’90s Mississippi: “You worked on Governor Mabus’s campaign and kept talking about how much was possible politically in Mississippi because it was the blackest state in the nation,” he writes. And his mother says to him: “Do you understand what’s possible if we actually get effective radical politicians in place down here?” Kiese responds, “I’m glad Mabus won but hearing about it every day is just kinda mee-guh.” Meager. It was not enough then, and we have plenty far to go.

Heavy was published in October 2018, just before Stacey Abrams turned Georgia purple, signaling to the rest of the country that it was time to take notice of the deeply disenfranchised Southern states.

When I reached out to Mabus, who went on to become Bill Clinton’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia and then Obama’s Secretary of the Navy, he identified the dominoes that knocked toward Colom’s win: the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act, rampant corruption, a welfare scandal featuring Brett Favre, and “office holders taking constituents for granted” over decades. Mabus was a young man working for Winter when Colom and I were little, and this election, he said, “brings hope for the future.”

It doesn’t really matter which party you’d like to claim. Repulsive policies will eventually push everyone away. Mississippi Republicans are not moderate, are not descended of gentle governance. (See: Bilbo et al.) This is the state that put “personhood” on the ballot as part of a national antiabortion strategy; fortunately for all y’all, Mississippians rejected the idea of life beginning at conception. Lynn Fitch, the current attorney general, not only effortfully attempted to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election, but she is the signed counsel for the petitioners in the Dobbs brief, which ultimately reversed Roe v. Wade. (Because I keep underscoring to you the infinite refractions of Mississippi, Fitch also went after Colom for one of his ads that used AI; he removed it.) Even the affidavit ballots that have taken so long to count are a result of strident, generational attempts by Republicans to disenfranchise Black voters. Which is why Mississippians knew, as the Colom–Hyde-Smith race came down to those affidavits, exactly in whose favor they would tally up. Were it not for the dedication of young Black canvassers—especially Black women—and homegrown mobilization efforts, things would have gone differently.

“There is a radical history of Black academics, activists, lawyers, and judges who have really been working to see a Mississippi where this was possible,” Kiese emailed me over the weekend. “I am thankful that someone like Leslie McLemore, who was a young member of Hamer’s Mississippi Democratic Party, can see what they worked and died for.”

What does Colom’s win mean for Kiese? “It means that the people, not any party, get what they organize and fight for,” he replied. “Our state taught the world that again last week.”

My privileged position occluded my own understanding of Mississippi’s true potential until I was older. Growing up, I mostly just clocked defeat—every presidential election, every midterm, Mississippi was red as red could be, as Mississippi’s poverty levels ratcheted toward a 21st-century high of 24%. In 2008, John McCain beat Barack Obama in the state by a 13% margin (the two staged a debate in Oxford). In 2016, Trump bested Hillary Clinton by almost 18 points.

After Trump won in 2024, an old childhood friend who’d gone MAGA texted me a GIF of a penis ejaculating stars that reconstituted in the shape of a patriotic eagle. Flash forward a year later, he’s angry about gas prices, and, more striking to me, horrified by the war in Gaza. Colom’s protein ad is for him, and that nerve of enthusiasm it struck is going to keep firing.

Colom didn’t run on pronouns or any numerical strain of woke. He has said he is a fan of Trump’s border security, agrees with him on certain tax policies, and supports the Second Amendment. When asked about improving wages for government employees, he has said he wants to take care of teachers—and cops. As Colom told Jen Psaki in a televised interview, “We gotta be a party that represents our whole country, that understands all parts of the country.”

Now that people outside Mississippi are waking up to Colom, leftists may find his centrism irritating or even offensive. You may find a new reason to look down your noses at Mississippi. It all but promises to provide an opportunity.

So I will just leave you with the brothers Colom.

“They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state, but the cotton cow fed the nation. Europe eating off the same plate. They lied about Mississippi. Said the torture was only here, but the banker’s desk in northern mills still dripping blood from hostage tears. They lied to us all. That’s propaganda machine on both sides, running on slander…. Denying the nation condoned it, denying the nation owned it, denying the nation fed off pain…. They lied about Mississippi. Said that evil lived in one state.”

He says, invoking Hamer, “Mississippi Freedom Party began again.”

And the vision of Scott: “There is nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed by what’s right.”

#3548. Doctor Who Star Peter Capaldi Knows How To Save The Struggling Sci-Fi Series

As "Doctor Who" fans (aka Whovians) are no doubt aware, the show is in a bit of a bind. Since its debut way back in 1963, the series has sustained itself with a clever sci-fi concept that has allowed multiple actors to canonically play the title role of the Doctor. The character, you see, is a time-traveling alien known as a Time Lord, and when they die, they're able to regenerate into a new person. Each time the Doctor regenerates, their personality changes a bit, although they still have the same memories, intellect, and enthusiasm

Unfortunately, after running for so long, "Doctor Who" has developed a bad habit of falling back on stale tropes. A Whovian friend of mine has agreed that "Doctor Who" is in a bad place right now, and the franchise's future is uncertain in the wake of Disney ending its partnership with the show due to its relatively low viewership. As my friend put it, the series is, indeed, in a "tepid" place, and no one knows where it will go moving forward.

Peter Capaldi, however, has some suggestions. The actor, who played the Twelfth Doctor from 2014 to 2017, shared his ideas during his recent appearance on the "Half the Picture" podcast, explaining that he thinks the show needs to get back to basics. He added that it would do well to reorient itself by returning to its lower budgeted origins and tapping back into the shoddy charms of its earliest days.

In the same interview, Peter Capaldi clarified that he is fine with no longer being associated with "Doctor Who," as there are other ventures he would like to pursue. "Doctor Who," he noted, is the kind of show that takes over your life, adding, "You can't do it [...] as a part-time role." When it comes to the property's future, though, Capaldi is uncertain, stating:

"What it's got to be, I don't know. I was thinking about this [...] I don't know what people want from it. Because my love for the show was the old show. That's what I grew up with. And that's not going to work. I can't come in and say 'Let's set it in the '60s. Let's make it black-and-white with very wobbly sets. Let's make more cheaply. Or with less ambition.' I mean, 'Doctor Who' has always had ambition, it's just that budgets haven't always met that."

Capaldi then mused out loud if audiences might want "David and Kylie." He was, of course, referring to David Tennant's highly popular iteration of the Doctor appearing with a character played by Kylie Minogue on "Doctor Who" in the 2007 Christmas special "Voyage of the Damned" (which brought in an impressive number of viewers). Or maybe they're more interested in previous "Doctor Who" stars like Christopher Eccleston or Jodie Whitaker. Basically, Capaldi is very unsure what fans really want out of the series.

All he can say is that he enjoys "Doctor Who" the best when it experiences what he calls a "ripple" from the old show. Not a reused monster, necessarily, but a specific tone that sometimes breaks through. Something humble and old-fashioned.

Although "Doctor Who" is a time-travel series that involves aliens, monsters, major historical figures, and ineffable, universe-ending technologies, Peter Capaldi feels that it's actually a "small" show. It's about a small group of characters and their time-traveling TARDIS, which looks like a police box that, via advanced technology, is larger on the inside than on the outside. Capaldi added that if the series could focus on those basics, it could sing once again, explaining:

"It's the Doctor and the assistant-slash-assistants in the TARDIS. Quite contained. Kind of balming. And like in 'The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe,' they step out the door to this drama. And those dramas change shape, and they've got monsters in them. Magical, strange, weird, sad. It's that central core of that small group of people with the Doctor at the center of it."

I have personally watched enough of the show to know that most of the best "Doctor Who" episodes embody what Capaldi talked about. The problem, then, is that many of the series' seasonal storylines climax with some sort of supervillain threatening to destroy the universe, unwrite history, or commit some other kind of massive sci-fi cataclysm. And if those types of cataclysms are regularly happening, then it's no surprise that fans are experiencing a sense of fatigue (or that the show's creatives may be running low on ideas).

Time will tell if the minds currently behind "Doctor Who" take Capaldi's advice and scale the series back into a cheaper, more humble form. It certainly wouldn't hurt, what with the series being adrift following its short-lived Disney era and the planned 2026 Christmas special being canceled. Capaldi might just be onto something.

The Odyssey, one of the highest-grossing films of the 2026 movie schedule, is a serious movie that blends mythological themes and modern storytelling as it explores the journey of Odysseus as he faces a dangerous voyage through fantastical realms on his way back to his family. And its director, Christopher Nolan, is a revered filmmaker known for paying attention to little details as he brings his signature narrative and visual style to life on the big screen. That doesn’t mean hilarious behind-the-scenes moments and shenanigans don’t still happen during production, and one in particular involves Tom Holland requesting skirt alterations.

The fantasy epic marked Tom Holland’s first time working with the filmmaker, and boy does he have some memorable stories to share from the experience. For example, according to Variety, who was at the November 10 FYC event, the current Spider-Man decided to take matters of his skirt into his own hands with costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, asking her to hem it to help give him some height on screen.

In the 75-minute documentary Behind the Scenes of The Odyssey, chronicling the making of the three-hour blockbuster, Holland revealed that his reasoning for the change didn’t matter because you can’t sneak anything by Christopher Nolan. He said:

I asked Ellen, the costume designer, I said, ‘Could you just make the skirt a little shorter?’ It’ll make me look a little taller.

Estimated to fall somewhere between 5’6” and 5’8”, I can absolutely understand wanting to appear as tall as possible while starring in such a big movie.

I also appreciate that the Peter Parker actor has enough self-awareness to make such a request. Apparently, he even got the request fulfilled when the costume designer had his tailored skirt ready six weeks later. However, Christopher Nolan noticed that something was amiss and had the following question:

Two seconds into taking in the costume, [Christopher Nolan] was like, ‘How come the skirt is shorter?’

Critics heaped praise on The Odyssey, and the box office numbers reflected that audiences couldn’t get enough, so the length of Tom Holland’s skirt clearly had no effect on the ultimate outcome. But personally, I now wish I knew what the actor’s response was when the Inception director asked what happened. Did he cop to his attempt to look taller on screen? Did he try to play it off in some other way? Did the filmmaker find it as hilarious as I do?

Without a camera turned on them both in that moment, we might never know for sure, but I’m not surprised that someone as meticulous as Christopher Nolan noticed almost immediately and called out the change.

There have already been plenty of memorable stories about the shoot, as Matt Damon talked about being “wet” and “cold” during portions of the production while Charlize Theron acted through massive winds that got up to 30 to 40 miles per hour. Now, I hope we get more silly tales like this one from Tom Holland.

With The Odyssey expected to be a major awards contender this year, I feel like that's very possible. So, here's hoping we get to learn more about Tom Holland trying to shorten his skirt for this Christopher Nolan epic.

#3546. Johnny Depp’s ‘Ebenezer’ Makes a Weak Case for His Post-Trial Comeback

For weeks, Los Angeles has been plastered with posters of a malevolent-looking man in a top hat and gray sideburns. It always takes me a few minutes to process that this elderly curmudgeon is Johnny Depp, doing his Hollywood walk of shame in Ebenezer.

“It’s good to be back,” Depp gurgles in the movie’s trailer. He’s either reveling in his return from infamy or trolling the audience, depending on your point of view.

I adored Johnny Depp back in his Edward Scissorhands/Gilbert Grape/Ed Wood heyday; he probably would’ve been my hall pass if I’d known about the concept back then. Now, though, it feels as if the once chiseled-cheeked heartthrob has found a character that suits him: a monstrous figure seeking redemption.

“Grant me the grace to prove that I am no longer the man that I once was,” Ebenezer Scrooge begs one of the ghosts haunting him in this rather plodding new version of Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol, directed by horror auteur Ti West. Scrooge is trying to make up for a lifetime of stinginess and cruelty, whereas Depp seeks to win back mainstream audiences after the ugly, drawn-out brawl that was his marriage and divorce from Amber Heard.

Heard alleged that he was an abusive addict. Depp denied abusing her and filed two defamation suits. He aimed one at the British tabloid The Sun for calling him a wife-beater (which he lost, since the court found the characterization to be “substantially true”). The other was leveled at Heard for describing herself in a Washington Post op-ed as “a public figure representing domestic abuse.” What started as a defamation trial ended up as a livestreamed referendum on post-#MeToo gender politics.

The saga spawned organized smear campaigns soaked in misogyny. Social media erupted with vile memes, hashtags, and videos targeting Heard, bearing hashtags like #AmberHeardIsAPsychopath and #DontBelieveAllWomen. One men’s group launched a “Ditch the Witch” protest in support of Depp. It seemed to echo one of Depp’s texts about Heard, released during the trial, in which he proposed to a friend: “Let’s drown her before we burn her!!!…I will fuck her burnt corpse afterwards to make sure she is dead.” And it wasn’t just ordinary guys taking up arms for Depp. Moments after the verdict was announced, the GOP’s House Judiciary tweeted a GIF of Depp in Pirates of the Caribbean from its official account, showing support for him.

“The craziness [aimed at Heard] was a kind of pent-up anger at women,” a film producer suggested to me back in 2022. “I think it really stirred up a lot of deep-seated resentment that hasn’t been allowed expression since #MeToo.”

Depp didn’t come out of the crucible with his career intact. He was asked to resign from the Fantastic Beasts franchise—though Warner Bros. still paid Depp his full $16 million salary—and his former agent claimed Disney dropped him from the next Pirates of the Caribbean movie. Still, he never really went away. In fact, like so many guys who have been supposedly “canceled,” he wormed his way back in quite easily. In 2023, he got a standing ovation at Cannes for his role as Louis XV in the French film Jeanne du Barry. The next year, he directed the movie Modì, Three Days on the Wing of Madness. Meanwhile, producer Jerry Bruckheimer confirmed in 2025 that he’s been talking to Depp about a sixth Pirates film after all. All the while, Depp has also kept his massive brand deal as the face of Dior’s Sauvage.

“I don’t feel boycotted by Hollywood because I don’t think about Hollywood,” Depp announced imperiously a few years back. “I don’t have much further need for Hollywood.” Enter Ebenezer, his official return to…Hollywood. Which he doesn’t need or think about. At all.

Call it Christmas-washing: What could be more wholesome and uncontroversial than A Christmas Carol? According to Variety, Paramount paid Depp just $5 million—a big drop-off from the days when he could reportedly command $50 million for a single film—and only spent $38 million to produce the movie, hedging its bets. Still, this film is a pretty warm welcome back to American movie screens, major marketing campaign and all.

Unfortunately, Depp’s mediocre performance in Ebenezer doesn’t dispel the sour scent of desperation that hangs over his career. Scrooge is one of the most unlovable characters in all of literature, and Depp’s charm does not shine through the gnarled facial prosthetics. He plays the archetypal miser in the broadest of ways, spending much of the nearly two-hour movie alternating between exaggerated expressions of cantankerousness and horror. Depp’s inspiration for the role might as well have been Oscar the Grouch, though one with less educational value who’s hollow at his core. At various points, the actor campily throws himself into physical comedy that is at odds with the horror-soaked vibe of West’s production.

Knowing this is a test run for Depp’s uncanceling, viewers will find it hard not to see Ebenezer as a wink-filled plea for absolution. “I’m not the man I was!” his character screams over and over. “Allow me my redemption.” To which the answer—or my answer, at least—is simple: Bah, humbug.

Netflix put out a ton of content in 2026, and it's not showing any signs of slowing down. Case in point: those with a Netflix subscription can watch Jessica Chastain's new thriller movie Heartland this weekend. The movie is set in Nashville, and filmed some scenes right in the heart of Broadway. Director Shana Feste spoke to CinemaBlend about this experience, and one problem they kept having during production in the country music destination.

In Heartland Jessica Chastain was deep into character playing Misty Jones, a washed up (Grammy-winning) country singer. After living in seclusion for years she returns to Nashville in search of her missing niece Charlie Heart, played by real-life country singer Carter Faith. As you can see in the video above, I spoke to director Shana Feste about shooting on location, where she told me:

We were a big movie, but we weren't that big. So it's not like we could really shut anything down. So we just went on to Lower Broadway right in the middle of like chaos. And we got our truck and we just, I think we didn't even have really any camera equipment. So we used the like, what is that? The lever from the, one of the big trucks, whatever it's called. We just put our camera on that and we like pressed down and he like went, so we had this big top shot and then it like went into the audience.

Nashville is a big vacation destination, and most of the action happens on Broadway. As such, there are ton of people there at any given day, going to the various bars, restaurants, and music venues throughout the strip. Feste wanted to make sure Heartland captured that energy, which is why there were a number of scenes shot in Nashville itself. Although it was a bit of a logistical challenge.

Chastain crushed it in the movie's 114-minute runtime, with the Oscar-winner transforming her body and voice into Misty. Still, filming in Nashville had challenges, including one common issue with the background actors. As Feste went on to say:

I mean, the hardest thing was getting people to like stop looking at the camera and just like walk naturally because you're, it's like shooting a Las Vegas strip, you know? It's like pure chaos. But that is what I wanted to include in the movie.

Between the busy street traffic and folks looking directly into camera, those days in Nashville were not without roadblocks. Although having seen Heartland before it arrived on Netflix this weekend, I think it was totally worth it. The energy was electric, and helped to make the new streaming film all the more immersive.

When speaking with Feste about shooting on location, there was one other factor that I couldn't stop thinking about. Namely all the Bachelorette Parties that are happening in Nashville on any given day. The Run Sweetheart Run director confirmed they were part of the equation, offering:

Oh total bachelorette parties. So funny that you say that. A lot of the actual background players that we got to choose like and dress that we threw into the world were... I had like six bachelorette parties. So we provided all those costumes.

It sounds like shooting in Nashville isn't for the faint of heart, but the cast and crew of Heartland were ultimately able to pull it off. It helps give the new movie a tactile and real time and place, especially as Misty searches the town in search of her niece Charlie.

Folks can see it all for themselves, as Heartland is on Netflix as part of the 2026 movie release list. Jessica Chastain crushes her role as the film's protagonist, including belting out a few country musical numbers. After all, this is Nashville we're talking about.

#3544. Ryan Phillippe's Two-Part Action Thrillers Have Been A Paramount+ Streaming Hit For Weeks

All you really need to know to understand what you're getting with the "One Mile" movies is a single line from Phillipe: "These guys don't know it yet, but they messed with the wrong dad." That's it. The movie is a guy unleashing his dad rage on a bunch of bad guys who took his daughter. The films are basically "Taken" in a forest.

But clearly there's something more to "One Mile" than your average B-movie actioner. After receiving a digital release back in February 2026, the films hit Paramount+ on October 1, 2026 and have been holding strong in the most-watched charts ever since. In fact, this has to be one of the strongest streaming runs of any release this year. Per viewership tracker FlixPatrol, "One Mile: Chapter One" and its sequel have now been in the Paramount+ movie rankings in the United States for 42 days apiece.

Before he rose to fame with roles in the 1997 slasher craze cash-in "I Know What You Did Last Summer" and 1998's "Cruel Intentions," Ryan Phillipe made his film debut in the submarine action thriller that pit Denzel Washington against Gene Hackman, "Crimson Tide." Three decades later, he's leading his own action thrillers that draw heavily on the tone and style of their '80s and '90s predecessors. The "One Mile" movies most obviously bear a striking resemblance to 1982's "First Blood" in terms of their one-man-army outnumbered in a forest story. Unlike in that seminal Sly Stallone outing, however, Phillipe's ex-soldier isn't opposed to racking up the kills.

The actor plays former special forces operative Danny Beckett, who has had very little time to connect with his teenage daughter Alex (Amélie Hoeferle). To make up for lost time, he takes Alex on a road trip to visit colleges ahead of her high school graduation. On their way, they make an impromptu stop in a remote area where they set up camp, only for a violent off-grid community to descend.

At first Danny uses his special forces skills to evade the group, but they eventually get their hands on Alex. Cue a violent rampage in which Danny runs through the survivalists one by one in a desperate attempt to get his daughter back. If you're wondering why such a straightforward action premise requires two movies, it's because Alex manages to get kidnapped twice. Yes, twice. Look, these movies might not measure up to the Denzel and Hackman effort that gave Phillipe his start, but they're a solid way to waste away a weekend and come with a ringing endorsement from Paramount+ users.

The "One Mile" movies are directed by Adam Davidson, who has a prolific career stretching back to the late-'80s when he made his directorial debut with the short "The Lunch Date." His filmography otherwise includes dozens of directing jobs on shows such as "Bosch" and Ryan Phillipe's former USA series "Shooter." "One Mile" chapters one and two represent a rare feature film project for the director, and thus far it's proven a worthy departure for him.

Per FlixPatrol, not only have both chapters been in the Paramount+ charts for over a month, until November 13, 2026, "Chapter One" was sitting at the very top of the U.S. movie charts, with "Chapter Two" occupying the second spot. At the time of writing, both have slipped to the second and third position respectively, but that's an impressive run for the duology. What's more, the films are clearly sticking around for some time to come, having thus far only succumbed to the might of "PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie," which only just batted Phillipe's thrillers down a slot to take number one.

The runtime for "One Mile: Chapter One" is 89 minutes while "Chapter Two" runs for 83 minutes. That means you're essentially getting an almost three-hour action epic, if you watch the films back to back. Why couldn't they just be one movie? Who knows, but Paramount+ viewers, who previously turned Aaron Eckhart's neo-Western "Thieves Highway" into a Paramount+ hit, don't seem to mind at all.

#3543. Cities: Skylines' Best Replacement Is Finally Here and Better than Expected

Transport Fever 3 turned me into a logistics nerd

Transport Fever 3 turned me into a logistics nerd

2026 is the year I got massively into city builders, and by massively I mean I played Cities: Skylines more than anything else for the first half of the year. I started dabbling with city builder-slash-logistics games in the second half of the year, like Anno 117, and turned my attention to Transport Fever 3 soon after. When I first learned about Transport Fever 3, I called it "like" Cities: Skylines. It looked a lot like a traditional city builder, albeit one where you focus on roads more than zoning. After playing it over the last month or so, though, I realize the difference between city builder and logistics planner is a lot more distinct than I initially gave it credit for — and I've irreversibly become a logistics sicko.

The first thing you do in Cities: Skylines is build a road, and then you start earmarking plots of land for residential and commercial zoning. The biggest logistics puzzles you end up solving involve road improvements, or more accurately, managing traffic as your city gets bigger. It's a design and aesthetics challenge more than anything, though. In the struggle to make roads big enough to handle the needs of a growing city, keeping things from looking like a dystopian hellscape is more important than optimizing traffic flow. Well, for me it is anyway, but the game's comparatively lax management requirements let personal preference prevail over logistical needs.

Not so with Transport Fever 3. Here, you start with a small town and a burgeoning transport company. The first task is creating a small network of transport lines to support consumer travel and industrial growth. Then you encourage new industry by making more lines that connect resource deposits with processing facilities in, or near, the town. This small-but-important difference captured me instantly. Planning industries in Cities usually takes little foresight. Once you have the money, you just construct the necessary buildings as close to the resource as possible and make sure there's a road that can link them back to the main city for deliveries. Most resource nodes exist on map tiles outside your main metro area anyway, so you can just position any old road how you’d like and go on about your business. Or you can just ignore industry entirely and turn your town into a strip mall paradise.

But the goal in Transport Fever 3 is to grow the existing town, and it won't grow without industry. More people need more food, more places to work, and more ways to get to work, ideally on time and without being crammed on a tiny coach ill-adapted for the purpose. You find places suitable for residential building and industry like in Cities, but it all builds up based on roads and road types, which gives you more control over how everything develops and more challenges to solve. Opting for a country road influences the kind of residential areas that will populate along it and makes it easier to create neighborhood-like areas, for example, as opposed to having homes just pop up inconveniently on a standard road. Country roads aren't suitable for all types of travel, though, so you have to find alternative solutions to ensure the people living there have access to all the goods and transportation methods they need. Multiply those considerations for every new residential and commercial area, imagine designing a functional and aesthetically pleasing infrastructure network to accommodate them, and you've got an idea of how this game works.

There are a slew of other considerations to deal with, too. Terrain gradient determines the type of road you need — and now much it'll cost to maintain — so freight vehicles don't get stuck. Trains are wonderful for moving goods and people, but require special production chains in place to operate, which puts another burden on your local infrastructure. That's true for pretty much every transport improvement. It makes one area easier, but requires a lot more planning and work to keep others from spiraling out of control.

It's all comparatively easy to maintain when settlements are smaller, and in sandbox mode, the game doesn't punish you for keeping things small. Heck, you can have a bunch of mid-sized towns connected via water transport and airports if you want. As long as your business isn't bankrupt, you're winning. But once your town grows into a city with multiple districts, managing everything is a nested stack of challenges that just gets more complex as time passes.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Which, it turns out, is exactly what I want. I frequently find myself speeding up the simulation in Cities until some disaster or other requires my direct intervention. It's very passive once you get to a certain point, where improvements are additive and routine. Make a new district, zone it like the last one — or, how about this for excitement, get a bit wild and invert the zoning swatches — connect the roads, add more power and water, proceed like before. I certainly still enjoy designing a huge city and seeing the results of my planning pay off, but I miss the hands-on requirements of early city building. That hands-off feeling never disappears in Transport Fever 3. It's a never-ending puzzle that captured me and won't let me go, and I couldn't be happier about it.
