#3542. See Bruce Springsteen, Martin Scorsese, and Surprise Guest Tom Cruise Honor Steven Spielberg at MoMA

Bruce Springsteen and Steven Spielberg are good friends. They’ve vacationed together a number of times on the director’s yacht, the Seven Seas. They went to Portofino in 2019, Sicily in 2017, and to Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in 2024—the latter time with Bono and The Edge. But when Springsteen took the stage at MoMA Thursday night to toast Spielberg at the museum’s annual Film Benefit, he had a bone to pick with the director.

“In June of 1975, I went to a small theater directly across from the Atlantic Ocean and I saw Jaws. I was 25 years old,” Springsteen said. “Now, one of the great pleasures on the Jersey Shore in 1975 was night swimming, preferably naked, on one of those 90-degree, 80% humidity August nights, preferably with someone you wanted to have sex with. There was nothing like after the bars closed, you had a few drinks in you—naked night swim.”

“Steven Spielberg fucked that up,” Springsteen continued. “He fucked it up good. Now, many times over the years, I asked myself, Why? Why would a nice man like that—why would he do that?”

Here at MoMA, a guitar slung around his back, Springsteen then attempted a bit of playful psychoanalysis. He recalled his trips on the Spielberg family yacht. Maybe, thought the guy who wrote “Born to Run,” the guy who directed Jaws is scared of swimming.

“I’ve been on that boat many times and I can tell you: Steven Spielberg does not go in that water— ever. Steven’s boat is so fucking big it has water on it. There’s a pool on it. Steven Spielberg does not go in that fucking pool—and I mean ever,” Springsteen said. “I’m not sure I’ve seen him in a bathing suit. So the reason night swimming is fucked—not just on the Jersey Shore, but every fucking place in the world—is because that nice man, Steven Spielberg, is very afraid of the water.”

“The name of that boat is the Seven Seas,” Springsteen finished. “And I guarantee you, Steven Spielberg has not been in any of the water on any of those fucking seven seas.”

Springsteen added, of course, that he loves Spielberg and his wife, the filmmaker and artist Kate Capshaw. And he wanted to sing a song for them. So he broke into “Dancing in the Dark.”Ch

The whole night was like this. I’ve been to the MoMA Film Benefit a number of times, and it’s always a celebrity-stuffed evening at the museum, always sponsored by Chanel, a highlight of the season. But this was on another level. The museum was honoring a director synonymous with the modern era of blockbuster movies: the avatar of American celluloid excellence, the closest thing Hollywood has to a Michael Jordan. What’s more, there’s a true connection between the art institution and the director. His first theatrical feature, The Sugarland Express, had its New York premiere at MoMA, in 1974, as part of a series called New Directors/New Films.

“This is where it all began, here at MoMA,” Spielberg said. “Why did you wait so long to invite me back?”

He went on to praise the institution’s herculean efforts to restore films and add them to the collection. He also thanked Chanel for dressing him in a look way fancier than his usually quite casual (but fawned over) director ’fits, and for supporting the benefit over nearly two decades.

“MoMA’s dedication, since 1935, to curation, preservation, and restoration is what makes this honor so deeply personal for me, for all of us who love film,” Spielberg said.

Earlier in the night, Spielberg caught up with Amy Sherald, showing the artist some pictures on his phone, as Jeff Goldblum, who played Dr. Ian Malcolm in a little movie called Jurassic Park, pulled up to his table. Nearby, Christopher Walken—who had a great turn in Spielberg’s Catch Me If You Can—was wandering toward his seat, looking a bit lost, when another slightly older man came up to say hello. It was Robert De Niro.

The artist Taryn Simon and her husband, Jake Paltrow, were chatting with Christy Turlington Burns at the bar when Stephen Colbert went up to get a drink. Studio Museum director Thelma Golden was chatting with MoMA board president Sarah Arison, and Jennifer Lawrence strolled in with her husband, the art dealer Cooke Maroney. Michael Ovitz, the collector and MoMA board member for nearly four decades, who happens to also have a long history with Spielberg—“Michael Ovitz, my former agent from a long time ago!” Spielberg said onstage—invited the artist Nicolas Party and the novelist Sarah Blakley Cartwright to his table, with Larry Gagosian sitting nearby.

Lorne Michaels was chatting with collector Ray McGuire—though when everyone sat for the opening remarks, the seat across from Michaels remained mysteriously empty. Soon, a montage of iconic Spielberg clips filled the room. As the lights came up, a figure walked across the stage, mouthing the word “wow” over and over. Surprise: It was Tom Cruise. A MoMA rep, sitting near me, confirmed that Spielberg had no idea that the star of Minority Report and War of the Worlds would be attending the event.

“Since I was a young man, you were very generous with me, always on movie sets—and at your home with Kate, the meals that we had together, the hours that you shared talking about your films and what inspired making them,” Cruise said from the stage. “The stories about you as a young boy with that eight-millimeter camera. You were gracious enough to listen to my stories about the jobs that I took, so that I could buy the tickets to go see your movies.”

Cruise later waded into the crowd to hug his director and take that empty seat across from Michaels. MoMA director Christophe Cherix then got up to gush about his favorite Spielberg movies before introducing the next speaker: Martin Scorsese.

“The films he has made have changed the world. So art does matter. It always will,” Scorsese said. “We’re here tonight surrounded by art in the museum, and it’s really the appropriate setting all the more to honor Steven. And so Steve, I don’t want to… Listen, we’ve known each other since 1972, and how do we get to be in our 80s? What happened?”

To introduce Spielberg himself, the museum managed to rope in Steve Martin and Martin Short, who have never been in a Spielberg-directed movie. Actually, they have no obvious connection to the honoree, except for the fact that they’re two of the funniest people alive.

“You know Steven is very proud that he has never used AI in any of his films. By the way, AI is Steven’s nickname for us,” Steve Martin said.

“I’ll never forget the first time I saw Saving Private Ryan,” Martin Short said. “I found the film so mesmerizing that, halfway through, I whispered into my phone, ‘I’m going to have to call you back.’”

Spielberg was dying in his seat, just losing it laughing, and then had to follow up Martin and Short, which he compared to playing after a Taylor Swift concert. “Marty and Steve, I’d happily follow you anywhere, except up here,” the director joked.

Michelle Pfeiffer, Steven Spielberg, and Michelle Williams

He looked even more moved as Springsteen ripped through a no-bullshit, full-throated performance of “Dancing in the Dark,” which is not something you usually get to see at a museum that’s got The Starry Night and Les Demoiselles d’Avignon hanging upstairs. And then it was time to leave the museum, to go back to the reality of a stormy New York where you can’t catch a cab. In the coat check line, Spike Lee turned to Donna Langley, the studio head at Universal, for whom he’s made a number of pictures.

Then Lee bounced outside, giving a fist bump to every single security guard working the door at MoMA, greeting each of them with what’s going to be a lifelong mantra: “Knicks in five.” “Knicks in five.” “Knicks in five.”

For now, though, fans will have to settle for the fall finales of 9-1-1 and 9-1-1: Nashville, airing on Thursday beginning at 8 p.m. ET on ABC, and streaming the next day with a Hulu subscription.

#3540. Marvel Officially Confirms Sam Wilson's Avengers Roster In Doomsday

It hasn't been an easy time for Marvel Studios of late, but if anyone can get the franchise back on track, it's surely the Avengers (well, them and the box office behemoth that was "Spider-Man: Brand New Day"). "Avengers: Doomsday" is almost upon us, but the titular roster looks a lot different in 2026 than it did when "The Avengers" debuted back in 2012. Now, Marvel has officially confirmed who will stand beside Anthony Mackie's Sam Wilson/Captain America in the upcoming team-up movie.

Marvel Studios announced the full "Doomsday" cast some time ago, but there's been some confusion about who counts as an Avenger, ever since the tumultuous events of "Captain America: Civil War." More recently, we've had "Thunderbolts*," which ended with Florence Pugh's Yelena Bolova/Black Widow leading a newly-christened "New Avengers" team. Now, "Doomsday" is bringing together the 20th Century Fox-era X-Men, the aforementioned New Avengers, Wakandans, Fantastic Four, and the Avengers proper to take on Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor Von Doom. So, who is still considered part of the official Avengers roster?

In Empire's issue on the upcoming Marvel blockbuster, we finally get a concrete answer. It seems Sam Wilson will lead an Avengers team made up of himself, Joaquin Torres/Falcon (Danny Ramirez), Scott Lang/Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), Shang-Chi. (Simu Liu), and Thor (Chris Hemsworth). The trailers have sort of confirmed as much, but it's nice to get some official clarification.

Both "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Avengers: Secret Wars" were previously delayed, but it's finally time to get the band back together again. Or at lest they're bringing a few band members out of retirement and pair them up with some relatively fresh faces. At the end of "Captain America: Brave New World," Sam Wilson officially invited Joaquin Torres into the Avengers fold. He'll now join fellow new recruit Shang-Chi alongside Avengers vets Ant-Man and Thor. We also know Chris Evans' Steve Rogers is returning, and he'll surely be considered an Avenger given his prior tenure.

Otherwise, the team is looking much different to the OG lineup, which started out with Steve Rogers/Captain America, Thor, Scarlett Johansson's Natasha Romanoff/Black Widow, Mark Ruffalo's Bruce Banner/Hulk, Robert Downey Jr.'s Tony Stark/Iron Man, and Jeremy Renner's Clint Barton/Hawkeye. Of course, RDJ will be back as Doctor Doom in "Doomsday," but Marvel has seemingly confirmed he won't be playing a Tony Stark variant and will, in fact, portray an entirely separate character in Victor Von Doom. That means the only original member in "Doomsday" will be Thor, and if he's fully welcomed back into the fold, Steve Rogers.

Meanwhile, for Anthony Mackie, this is all a chance to showcase himself as the true leader of the latest Avengers lineup. "In 'Endgame,' Steve gave him the shield and said, 'You need to be the leader of the Avengers,'" he told Empire. "Now you get to see more of him leading the charge with everyone into battle."

Whether the Avengers roster will change by the end of "Doomsday" or its planned follow-up, "Avengers: Secret Wars" remains to be seen (there's bound to be some cameos at least). For now, we know who's heading into battle against Doom alongside the new Cap.

"Avengers: Doomsday" arrives on December 18, 2026.

#3539. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3538. A Look Inside the Scorpion Ball, Princess Grace Kelly’s Scorpio-Themed 40th Birthday Party

Grace Kelly always had a deep passion for astrology. Born on November 12, 1929, she was a Scorpio, and very proud of it. To celebrate her 40th birthday on November 15, 1969, the Princess of Monaco organized a party themed by her astrological sign, resulting in the extravagant Scorpio Ball, held at the Hôtel de l’Hermitage in Monte Carlo. For the occasion, she only invited celebrities who were also Scorpios. Among the 60 or so guests were Swedish actress Hjördis Paulina Genberg, American actor Rock Hudson, and Italian actress Virna Lisi.

Actor Richard Burton was also in attendance, accompanied by his wife Elizabeth Taylor, even though she was born under the sign of Pisces. An exception was made for the actress, who was granted special permission thanks to her husband’s astrological sign—Scorpio, born on November 10. For the occasion, Taylor chose to dazzle, wearing a Cartier diamond necklace with an estimated value of $1 million around her neck—a gift from Burton two weeks earlier. She also wore a spectacular evening cape by Tiziani, made of black velvet and adorned with two rhinestone scorpions on the front and a third on the hood.

Guests were required to adhere to a dress code devised by Kelly, inspired by the colors associated with the sign of Scorpio. Red, black, and white were therefore strongly recommended. The princess, for her part, opted for an off-the-shoulder black velvet dress by Balenciaga from the fall-winter 1967 couture collection. Two ruby brooches set with diamonds—a wedding gift from Prince Rainier III—completed her ensemble.

The decor also reflected the evening’s theme. Red candles, portraits of famous Scorpios, and a lavish cake adorned with golden scorpions set the tone. No detail had been left to chance: The waiters, wearing powdered 18th-century wigs, dressed in velvet suits embroidered with sparkling stars and held silver candelabras adorned with red candles.

Princess Grace was seen on numerous occasions alongside Carroll Righter, an astrologer and Hollywood columnist nicknamed “the astrologer to the stars.” According to People magazine, the princess’s birth chart also revealed a Scorpio ascendant, while her Midheaven was in Leo. In astrology, the Midheaven is associated with career, public image, and reputation. Some attributed her commanding presence and magnetism in the spotlight to this configuration.

Kelly embodied the mysterious aura that her admirers associated with her astrological sign. Unfortunately, that light was extinguished on September 14, 1982, when the Princess of Monaco lost her life in a tragic car accident on the hills above the principality.

1976’s Rocky may be 50 years old now, but the franchise, powered by Sylvester Stallone’s iconic character, has proven to be as durable as the fighter himself. In total, there have been nine entries so far in the Rocky franchise (six Rocky movies and three Creed movies), and that doesn’t include I Am Rocky, the biopic about Stallone making first movie made, which hits the 2026 movie schedule this month.

In a recent interview with Andy Cohen on Cohen’s SiriusXM channel, the host asked Stallone which of the five sequels (not including the original movie) was his favorite, and I have to admit I didn’t expect one of them. Here’s how Stallone answered the original question:

It's II and VI for me. II because that's when he gets married. That's when he really, like, wins. It's very, very potent.

That he loves Rocky II isn’t really a surprise. Though I don’t think it’s quite as good as the original, I do think it’s a really great follow-up. Stallone obviously hones in on how personal it is for the character, a character he certainly feels a kinship with. Getting married to Adrian (Talia Shire) is a big moment in the franchise. Yes, the Rocky movies are boxing movies, but they are just as much about Rocky and Adrian’s relationship from their courtship in the original, through her tragic death before the events of Rocky Balboa (VI).

That makes Stallone’s second choice for a favorite a clear choice. It is the one that surprised me, but it makes perfect sense. The sixth movie in the franchise (and the first not to have an actual number attached) is a movie about aging, loss, and death. It picks up many years after the events of Rocky V. Rocky is retired from boxing and now owns a restaurant in his hometown of Philadelphia. Here’s what makes it special, according to Stallone:

And then Rocky VI, it deals with something that everyone deals with, which is grief and the loss and how he's talking to his child about, 'I held you here, you were the greatest thing, and now.' It's not how hard you hit, you know, it's about life. So, it was very poignant that – I love that movie. That was some of my best writing by far.

I agree with Stallone that Rocky Balboa is some of his best writing (outside of the original). It was such an interesting way to bring the character full circle. It starts with his love for Adrian and ends with him dealing with the loss of his beloved wife. It’s also about family relationships, specifically with their son, Robert Jr. (Milo Ventimiglia), and how they shift and ebb and flow over the years. Rocky Balboa gets the series back to its roots after, let's be honest, so many more cartoonish entries. I LOVE Rocky IV, but it doesn’t have the emotional depth of I, II, or VI, and let’s not even talk about Rocky V.

You can celebrate all the Rocky movies this month, either for the release of I Am Rocky, or for Rocky’s 50th anniversary with a Prime subscription, where they are all available.

#3536. Marvel Officially Confirms New Avengers Team for Doomsday

Avengers, New Avengers, Thunderbolts — it’s a lot to keep track of

The Marvel Cinematic Universe's Avengers lineup has been a bit muddled since the events of Captain America: Civil War, which broke up the team of besties. Things got more confusing when the team of misfits in last year's Thunderbolts* was declared the New Avengers at the end of the film, causing a bit of a kerfuffle between the team and Anthony Mackie's Sam Wilson/Captain America over who gets to call themselves Avengers.

Avengers: Doomsday is the next MCU blockbuster, and will include multiple teams of heroes squaring off against Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom. In an interview with Empire, Marvel confirmed the latest official lineup of Avengers: Sam Wilson/Captain America, Joaquin Torres/Falcon (Danny Ramirez), Scott Lang/Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), Thor (Chris Hemsworth), and Shang-Chi (Simu Liu).

Thor's a longtime Avenger, and Lang essentially joined the team during the time travel shenanigans of Avengers: Endgame. Torres has been working with Wilson for a while now, so it makes sense he'd be considered an official Avenger. Shang-Chi was introduced to Bruce Banner/Hulk (Mark Ruffalo) and Carol Danvers/Captain Marvel (Brie Larson) at the end of his solo 2021 film, so perhaps he either got an invite from Wilson between movies, or he'll be inducted as an official Avenger during the course of Doomsday.

The events of Avengers: Doomsday could not be happening at a worse time for the team. "We’re coming out of years of seemingly no organized Avengers team, and that’s exactly when they face these incursions," Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige told Empire. "That’s always fun, to put your heroes on the back foot."

Mackie is excited to take his Captain America in a new direction. "In Endgame, Steve gave him the shield and says, 'You need to be the leader of the Avengers,'" he said. "Now you get to see more of him leading the charge with everyone into battle."

The first Avengers movie in seven years will unite old MCU favorites like Chris Evans' Steve Rogers, newcomers like the Fantastic Four, and old hats from the Fox movies like Patrick Stewart's Charles Xavier for the explosive film.

Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters Dec. 18.

#3535. Johnny Depp's Ebenezer Features One Character Most Adaptations Usually Cut

At this point in the life of Charles Dickens' 1843 novella "A Christmas Carol," so many stage and screen adaptations have been produced that the process of boiling the story down to its core elements has turned them into veritable tropes unto themselves. This aspect was being parodied as long ago as 1988's "Scrooged," which utilized an adaptation-within-an-adaptation as a bit of meta satire, as well as a commentary on how rote adapting Dickens' tale had become. Everything from a Victorian London setting to the line "God bless us, everyone" became not just quintessential to a new adaptation, but necessary, in much the same manner as the umpteenth cover of a popular song carries its own expectations. In a similar fashion to the elements which began to be regarded as a must-include, there were some other elements seen in Dickens' novella which got treated as unnecessary, and thus became more and more overlooked.

The most notable of these latter elements is the presence of a sister character for Ebenezer Scrooge. It would be erroneous to say that the sister is always cut from "A Christmas Carol" adaptations. After all, Fan Scrooge (as played by Carol Marsh) appears in one of the most revered film versions of the story, Brian Desmond Hurst's "A Christmas Carol" from 1951 starring Alistair Sim. Yet Fan or her equivalent tends to be missing or altered in most modern adaptations. She's nowhere in "Scrooged" or "The Muppet Christmas Carol," and she's heavily changed in the 2019 BBC miniseries starring Guy Pearce. This month's "Ebenezer," then, holds the honor of reinstating a sister character close to Dickens' Fan after a lengthy absence. While this is admirable, the reason for it doing so is due to the film's awkward revisionist take on Scrooge, as played by Johnny Depp.

In "Ebenezer" as in "A Christmas Carol," Scrooge is reunited with his sister during his trip through his earlier years, courtesy of the Ghost of Christmas Past (Andrea Riseborough). As in Dickens' novella, the sister is a fairly beatific figure, a protector of the bullied (and, it's heavily implied, abused by their father) Scrooge. In the film, screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern has renamed the sister from Fan to Molly (for what reason, only he knows), played by Rose Williams.

On the one hand, one wonders why so many adaptations mess around with the character, considering how important she is to Scrooge's nephew, Fred (Sam Claflin). She's literally his mother, and the idea of Scrooge shunning Fred due to his discomfort over the untimely death of his beloved sister is a good source of dramatic tension.

Yet on the other hand, it's likely that most adaptations either reconfigure or leave the sister out because her presence exists to humanize Scrooge in a way that some adaptations would rather not deal with. The sister and her fleshing out of Scrooge's origin story, as it were, forces the character to be more nuanced. Of course, most intelligent audience members should be able to understand that a young victim turned adult monster doesn't mean his misdeeds are automatically forgiven, yet those who think of "A Christmas Carol" primarily as a story for young children might.

In any case, "Ebenezer" corrects this error too far the other way, adding to it some other odd changes which make Scrooge a little too sympathetic. At least director Ti West and company don't let him completely off the hook, either, but it's too bad that the sister is re-included in the film for little more reason than as a character witness.

And there’s all the details from the star-studded MoMA Film Benefit honoring Steven Spielberg. Tom Cruise shocked the crowd with surprise remarks, and Bruce Springsteen roasted the director. It was a whole night.

MENTIONED IN THIS ISSUE: Donald Trump, Jason Calacanis, Brendan Dugan, Siniša Mačković, David Zwirner, Lorenzo Amos, Kate Capshaw, Zohran Mamdani, Jessica Craig-Martin, Dean & DeLuca, Indochine, Stanley Whitney, Marina Adams, Will Whitney, The Beverly Hills Hotel, Elon Musk, Lana Del Rey, Grimes, Travis Scott, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, Tyler, the Creator, Bad Bunny, Julia Wachtel, Todd von Ammon, Frieda Toranzo Jaeger.

The major arts institution named for Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, appears to be—shocker!—very much in jeopardy.

Just months ago, Huang was getting a phone call from President Trump while onstage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles. “I’m here with the besties, Mr. President,” a laughing Huang said, putting his phone up to the mic. “Tell him I say hi!” said All-In cohost Jason Calacanis.

But Huang’s recent weeks have not been marked by good times with the besties. First, the Democrats took over Congress, throttling all the goodwill he built with the administration. Then he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by the US to be a Chinese spy—and then news of another affair, this time allegedly with a subordinate, came via a shocking New York Times bombshell. Amid rumors that yet another affair would soon break, he stepped down as CEO and, according to Forbes, has watched nearly $20 billion of his estimated net worth vaporize since Monday.

What’s unknown is the current state of his relationship with his wife, Lori Huang—and their ambitious plans for an arts organization that was set to bear their name. Earlier this year, the Huangs pledged $75 million to Vanderbilt University in order to help transform the soon-to-be-closed legendary San Francisco art school California College of the Arts into part of Vanderbilt’s SF campus. Vanderbilt announced that it planned to name a portion of its SF campus the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design.

Which is now a bit awkward, given the multiple alleged affairs, and the whole Chinese-spy thing. Plus, Huang is no longer affiliated with Nvidia, which teamed up with CCA in 2025 to form the CCA-Nvidia Incubator for Creative Intelligence. Will Jensen and Lori Huang still put their names together on arts organizations after all that’s happened? And if there is no Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design, what will happen to Vanderbilt’s SF campus when it opens next year?

The CCA was started in 1907, and Huang and his wife were expected to support its transition to a new chapter. It would be a shame if this is how it ends. Reps at Vanderbilt didn’t get back to me.

It’s a new era in Tribeca. Tonight, Karma, a burgeoning mega-gallery with spaces in New York’s Chelsea and LA’s Hollywood, opens its new gallery at 38 White Street. Founder Brendan Dugan and director Siniša Mačković took me on a tour earlier this week, and it’s easily one of the most generous spaces anywhere in the neighborhood. Plus, an outpost of Karma Bookstore—a much needed bookstore for a neighborhood shockingly lacking in one—is coming in right across the street.

This will be the latest big-tent blue chipper to take a space in the Triangle Below Canal, as they used to call this neighborhood. Something to consider: In the last few years, mega-galleries such as David Zwirner and Hauser & Wirth have shut their uptown townhouses and opened downtown.

Also opening tonight is a White Street outpost of Gratin gallery, which has a roster of incredibly exciting young stars, including Lorenzo Amos (whom we wrote about a year ago). I’m hearing about other younger dealers grabbing spaces in the neighborhood. The art market isn’t exactly on fire, but dealers are betting on one thing: the enduring power and capital of New York City.

Speaking of New York, guess who’s lived here full-time for almost a year? Steven Spielberg, that’s who. On New Year’s Day 2026, the GOAT American director—who is married to the artist Kate Capshaw—moved his official residence from California to New York, and has made the apartment in the San Remo his home base. You will not be surprised to hear that, post-move, Spielberg is doing extremely cool stuff in town. He’s walking around with a script and a Tracy Kidder book while slugging down an iced McCafé. He’s getting lunch at Benvenuto Cafe. He’s having Mayor Zohran Mamdani over to the crib.

The only thing left was for one of the city’s great museums to throw a big party for the Hollywood-royalty-gone-Gotham. Last night, Spielberg got just that: He was honored at the MoMA Film Benefit, sponsored by Chanel. I was there. Read the full report—with fun pictures!—here.

Also on VF this week: an exclusive excerpt from an uproarious new memoir by artist Jessica Craig-Martin, I Regret I am Able to Attend. Craig-Martin is a real treasure of the art world, a great photographer—and, as it turns out, a hell of a writer. The whole book is a compulsively readable blast. The chapter where Craig-Martin recalls working as an extremely inexperienced, occasionally larcenous teller at Dean & DeLuca is one of the funniest, most satisfying New York vignettes I’ve read this year. And of course, all the scuttlebutt from the ’80s art scene is fabulous. Read the excerpt, in which our narrator spills all the tea—and, um, stuff stronger than tea—about working as a waitress when Indochine opened.

Happy 80th birthday to the great painter Stanley Whitney. His wife, the artist Marina Adams, and son, dealer Will Whitney, threw Stanley a party to celebrate his octogenarian status on Nine Orchard’s roof, overlooking Dimes Square. Writers, artists, dealers, old heads, everyone was there. A fabulous Wednesday night.

#3533. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, Prime Video, HBO Max, And More (Nov. 13-15)

Can you believe we're halfway through November? Wild. 2026 is passing by alarmingly quickly, and we're about to hit full holiday mode as we approach Thanksgiving ... but you don't need to get your turkey and stuffing recipes out of storage just yet. We've still got some time, and you should consider using that time to watch a whole bunch of stuff.

Yes, it's time to round up the buzziest, best, and biggest streaming releases for the weekend of Friday, November 13 to Sunday, November 15, which does include releases from earlier in the week as well. As always, the list is limited to releases new to major streamers entirely (case in point: though the hit Colleen Hoover movie adaptation "Reminders of Him" only just came to Netflix, it was already available on Peacock, so that's a nonstarter here), but between a killer dinosaur flick, a new thriller starring an Oscar winner, a drama with an innovative structure, a fresh literary adaptation, and the continuation of a massive fantasy series, you've got plenty of options.

If you didn't get enough Jessica Chastain in this year's admittedly silly horror movie "Other Mommy," you're in luck — she has a new film coming to Netflix this weekend. Written and directed by Shana Feste (the filmmaker behind "Country Strong," "Run Sweetheart Run," and "Boundaries," to name a few), "Heartland" stars the Oscar-winning Chastain as Misty Jones, a country singer who's retired from show business but has to come out of her self-imposed solitude to find her niece Charlie Heart (real country singer Carter Faith), who's gone missing. As Misty tries to locate Charlie, other family secrets come to light, and she tangles with a criminal underbelly in Nashville in the process ... and the fact that Misty is notoriously prickly and was nicknamed the "queen of mean" in her days as a country star certainly doesn't help matters.

"Heartland" also stars John Hawkes, Garrett Hedlund, Jennifer Nettles, and Ross Lynch in supporting roles, but Chastain is the real draw here, and whether or not you saw or loved "Other Mommy," you should check this pick out. "Heartland" drops on Netflix on November 13, so stay in this Friday and have a movie night.

If you, like me, love dark and twisted thrillers, you're probably familiar with the name Karin Slaughter. (Incredibly, I'm pretty sure that's her actual name.) Even casual TV fans are aware of her, even if they think they're not. Indeed, ABC's massively successful procedural "Will Trent" is adapted from Slaughter's novel series about an Atlanta detective (though it tones down some of the more depraved stuff found in the books), and in 2022, Netflix released a series adaptation of Slaughter's novel "Pieces of Her" starring Toni Collette and Bella Heathcote in its lead roles. Now, Slaughter's book "The Good Daughter" is getting an adaptation from Peacock, and it stars two of the most talented women acting today: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy.

The premise of "The Good Daughter" is enticing on its own: Decades after a brutal and violent incident in the Quinn family, sisters Samantha and Charlotte (Byrne and Fahy) still reside in their hometown of Pikeville, Georgia, with Charlotte working in law enforcement. Hence, when she starts looking into a particularly violent crime, Charlotte is struck by her own experiences, as is Samantha — and new family secrets come to light. Byrne and Fahy are both excellent on the show, and they're joined by Brendan Gleeson, Harper Steele, and Paula Malcomson, just to name a few. So, whether or not you're already a fan of Slaughter's body of work, you'll definitely want to get acquainted with "The Good Daughter," which dropped all of its episodes on Peacock on Thursday, November 12.

Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" film trilogy was a cinematic triumph when it released over the course of three years in the early 2000s, and it stands the test of time (though, the same can't really be said of his interminably drawn-out three-part "Hobbit" prequel). So, if you've already watched the extended versions of every single "Lord of the Rings" movie thousands of times, I've got great news: Amazon Prime Video has a "Lord of the Rings" TV show, and it's entering its third season.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power," which has been running since 2022, takes its lore from the appendices of J.R.R. Tolkien's massive fantasy tomes (but notably not Tolkien's "The Silmarillion" due to rights issues, so that has yet to be fully adapted). There are some "familiar" faces here from the Jackson movie trilogy, like Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and Elrond (Robert Aramayo), but "The Rings of Power" admirably expands the world of Tolkien during the second age of Middle-earth. This is also, incidentally, when the Rings of Power (that's the title) were forged, which led to the rise of the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers). As such, there's plenty to explore as this series forges ahead.

The first four episodes of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 dropped on Amazon Prime Video on November 11. Two more will arrive on November 18, and the season will wrap up one week later on November 25.

I truly cannot believe a movie as delightfully weird and ambitious as "The End of Oak Street" got made in the first place, but I sure am happy that it did. David Robert Mitchell ("It Follows," "Under the Silver Lake") helmed this ode to dinosaur movies, summer blockbusters, and 1980s Steven Spielberg classics, which stars Ewan McGregor as Greg Platt, Anne Hathaway as his wife and aspiring writer Denise, Maisy Stella as the couple's eldest child Audrey, and Christian Convery as their son and youngest Brian. (There's also a family dog, Starbuck, and don't worry — nothing bad happens to him. That's as close to a spoiler as I'll get.) The Platts are an everyday family with everyday problems — Greg is secretly working as a pizza delivery driver after losing his job, while Denise is growing dissatisfied with their suburban life — but one night, a storm hits and traps them all in a bizarre prehistoric playground full of dinosaurs. This sounds almost magical, but here's the thing: those dinosaurs are starving.

On one level, "The End of Oak Street" is the only movie in existence, as far as I'm aware, where you can watch Anne Hathaway wreak havoc on dinosaurs with a shotgun. On another level, it's a treatise on the importance on family, and on another level, it's an audacious science-fiction story with a little bit of time travel and a lot left unexplained. What "The End of Oak Street" is above all else, though, is fun ... and it's streaming on HBO Max as of November 13.

In the aughts, "24" innovated a new style of episodic television by using a real-time conceit as a spy tries to save the world. Decades later, "The Pitt" used that same structure to great effect for its real-time experience of working a busy 15-hour emergency room shift. Apple TV's new drama series "12 12 12," though, is even stranger. Created by creative partners Jim Keeble and Dudi Appleton, "12 12 12" stars Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan as Jack Strickland and Bobby Galvin, two men involved with a high-risk heist in Zürich.

So, how does "12 12 12" tell its story? As former FBI agent Strickland and master criminal Galvin circle each other in Europe, the heist in Zürich is where they eventually meet ... and Keeble and Appleton use three timelines within each episode. First, you get the 12 months of planning the heist, followed by the 12 hours required for said heist — and finally, the 12 days' worth of heist-related aftermath. "12 12 12" also stars Jack Kesy, Kali Reis, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, and Patrick Fabian in supporting roles, and its first two episodes are streaming on Apple TV as of November 13.

#3532. 6 Most-Anticipated Steam Games You Should Add to Your Wishlist Right Now

Sometimes when we put together a new installment of Wishlister, Polygon’s weekly newsletter that highlights upcoming Steam games, we look to events like Steam Next Fest and the Triple-I Initiative to dig up gems. But the most tried-and-true method we’ve found for finding promising games is simply stumbling into them by accident.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

All of the games in this week’s Wishlister follow that methodology. These are six games that flew onto our radar without looking for them, whether we bumped into their demos at live events or had them recommended to us by friends. We’re paying that energy forward this week, as you’ll see in this grab bag of upcoming PC games that deserve a spot on your Steam wishlist.

With Bub, developer Paperfrog looks well on its way to delivering a jaw-dropping debut. The narrative game takes anxiety around a developer’s real-life Multiple Sclerosis diagnosis and channels it into a personal story about preserving your memory in art. That’s reinforced by an analog art style that looks downright incredible.

False Echo turns wartime cryptography into a life-or-death narrative game. You play as a code cracker aboard a submarine in 1942, and you’re tasked with processing incoming transmissions. There are some clear shades of Papers, Please here, which should make for a brainy political thriller steeped in World War II history.

If you’re looking for your next high-score chasing game after this month’s great Faraway, Strikemania is one to watch. The retro arcade game is basically a reverse Missile Command; you control the missile attacking enemy defenses. With slick 2D art that evokes Geometry Wars, it should be a direct hit for fans of retro games.

Floor Plan: Slap It Out! hinges on a satisfyingly goofy gameplay hook: You can slap the crap out of everything. The latest game from developer Turbo Button is a physical comedy that has you solving puzzles using your noodly arms. It’s also the developer’s first non-VR game, so you’ll be able to enjoy the studio’s quirky brand of humor without a headset.

A perfect compliment to this year’s excellent Over the Hill, Hodka is an open-world driving game that has you fixing up an old RV. You’ll use a metal detector to dig up scrap that can be used to upgrade your van. It also seems to have a spooky undertone to it, making it look like an on-land alternative to Dredge.

For those who love RPGs that give you a lot of freedom, World of Anterra seems poised to become a hidden gem. The retro-inspired game drops you in a pixel art world and sets you loose to discover its non-linear story. It’s all meticulously hand-crafted to give players a retro RPG that’s as rich with secrets as an Elder Scrolls game. (And it will likely be out before Sentinel!)

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3531. Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Woman Unknown,’ May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion Winner, Sells to Cohen Media Group

What will the buyers be snapping up at the fall festivals? With this year’s Toronto International Film Festival already touting a high number of premieres for movies that originally bowed at Cannes or Sundance, there’s fewer world premiere sales titles that aren’t already with distributors than we’re used to. Still, the festival (with its very first market in place), plus Telluride, Venice, and New York are loaded with options, and there’s always the potential for another historic breakout like last year’s “Obsession.”

We’ll be tracking all the sales as they come in here, so check back frequently.

Distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno. Related Stories Jensen Huang’s Biopic Feels Inevitable — The Right One Might Be Impossible Miles Teller Opens Up About ‘Paper Tiger,’ Adam Driver, and Losing His Home Before Filming James Gray’s Movie

Distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

Distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

Distributor: Black BearDirector: Nahnatchka KhanFestival: TIFF MarketBuzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Distributor: 1-2 SpecialDirector: Jacqueline LentzouFestival: Venice OrizzontiBuzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Distributor: Sony PicturesDirector: Roshan SethiFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

Distributor: Universal Pictures and Blumhouse Atomic MonsterDirector: Joshua GiulianoFestival: TIFF Midnight MadnessBuzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Company and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

Distributor: HBO Documentary FilmsDirector: Rebecca HunttFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: “Rapinoe” about US Women’s National Soccer star Megan Rapinoe was the opening night documentary at TIFF. Rapinoe was in attendance at the premiere screening of director Rebecca Huntt’s (“Beba”) film, which grapples more with Rapinoe’s progressive politics, such as her kneeling in solidarity with Colin Kaepernick, and her coming out story, than it does on the stories from her soccer career about how she led the US Women’s team to two World Cup titles, an Olympics Gold, and the Ballon d’Or. HBO Documentary Films has North American TV and streaming rights to the film. THR first reported the news.

Distributor: Roadside Attractions and VerticalDirector: Lauren Miller RogenFestival: TIFF Gala PresentationBuzz: Lauren Miller Rogen directs her husband Seth Rogen alongside Anna Kendrick and Kate Berlant in this comedy about parenthood and prospective parenthood. It follows a childless couple who begin debating the merits of having kids when their divorced friend and her child move in with them. The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

“Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

Distributor: Focus FeaturesDirector: Simon StoneFestival: Telluride and TIFFBuzz: Andrew Scott is said to be fantastic in this performance based on the true story of “Chariots of Fire” and “Gandhi” star and thespian Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS at the age of 40 but managed to raise awareness for the epidemic after his death. Focus has already dated the film for late November, the same time slot it gave “Hamnet” last year.

Distributor: NetflixDirector: Danny BoyleFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: The opening night film for this year’s Biennale, “Ink” is the story of the birth of The Sun tabloid in the ’60s and the collaboration between editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) and Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) that made it the notorious publication it is today. Netflix didn’t acquire worldwide rights to the film, so it could easily be something it sees as both commercial and an awards play.

#3530. After 46 Years, The Strongest Transformer Of All Time Finally Debuts

In 2023, Image Comics/Skybound debuted the Energon Universe in Void Rivals No. 1, starting small with the reveal that the Transformers were part of the project. Over time, it became clear that the war between the Autobots and the Decepticons was one of its biggest storylines. Those tales take place in the crown jewel of the Energon Universe, Transformers.

The everlasting war between the alien machines didn’t just affect them. People on Earth were injured, unhoused, and killed by being caught in the middle of their battle. In Transformers No. 24, the Decepticons took a major loss to their rivals. They tried to fight them again in issue No. 29, but ended up retreating before Optimus Prime and his team could finish them off.

The results of that battle had lasting repercussions on both sides. Optimus relinquished his title of Prime to Elita One. On the villains’ side, Megatron was trapped inside a crystallized cocoon until he submitted to Megatronus. While Optimus has yet to adjust to no longer being as powerful as he once was, Megatron has returned, and he’s stronger and more determined than ever.

During the 2026 New York Comic-Con, it was announced that Megatron would return as something bigger and better, and he’d be called Megatronus Rex. The design showed more weapons, but that was a given. A Transformer doesn’t get an upgrade without getting bigger guns. However, Transformers No. 39 showed that giant guns were only part of the improvement. Megatron was no longer just a laser pistol to be aimed by Starscream. He could turn into a tank that was big enough to destroy the mountain housing the Autobots.

Megatronus Rex and the Decepticons didn’t waste any time attacking their enemies. At first, it seemed like the Megatronus Rex may have changed. Instead, he’s the same ruthless, uncaring evildoer as always. So much so that as Soundwave went to attack Optimus, he backhanded his second-in-command hard enough to send him flying (more on that later).

Megatronus Rex showed readers that he was the new big dog in the yard, but he wasn’t done. He had one more trick to reveal before the final page, and it was huge. He transformed into a railgun big enough for Devestator to hold. He officially became the biggest gun in the game, and there may not be any way to stop him. However, there is a chance of survival.

During Transformers No. 38, Elita Prime understood why Optimus wanted to stay on Earth. This realization made her agree to Jazz’s idea about sending help and Energon to Earth to assist with the former Autobots’ battle. If the timing works out, Jazz and others could return to help save their teammates before Megatronus Rex and the Decepticons end them. It may not be enough to win the battle, but enough for a tactical retreat.

Along with the Autobots, don’t be shocked if Soundwave helps his enemies. He was captured by his rivals, but shown mercy when he wouldn't have. There was also a moment when the former Decepticon, Firecracker, told Soundwave that one day he'll understand why he switched sides. That day may have come.

After being Megatron's most loyal soldier for eons, getting attacked by him in his new form must have been a slap in the face to Soundwave (pun intended). It could be the moment of clarity he needed to see his leader for who he truly is. Megatron has always been selfish, reckless, and willing to hurt his own people if it means survival. Meanwhile, Optimus has given up parts of himself to ensure the safety of the Autobots.

If Soundwave helps, it would be one of the more shocking moments in Image Comics' Transformers lore. Considering that the Energon Universe has continued to shake things up, it wouldn't be surprising to see a classic villain help his enemies in one final and brave act. The word final is used because there's no way Soundwave survives after betraying Megatronus Rex.

#3529. Amazon Prime Members Can Get Two Free E-Books in November

You can get thousands of free e-books over the course of 2026 if you know where—and when—to look. All year long, Amazon is offering free Kindle e-books to readers, with new opportunities popping up every month. In November, Prime members can get two free Kindle e-books from Amazon's First Reads program.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). This will send the e-book directly to the Kindle linked to your Amazon account. You can see what it should look like from the screenshot below.

You’ll know you did it right when you see a “Thanks, [your name]!” order summary indicating the e-book is being auto-delivered to the Kindle Cloud Reader.

This month, you can choose one from nine new Kindle e-books, plus this month's short read. Amazon notes the genre for each of the books above the title, offering a quick way to narrow down your options. (If you hover over the "See Editor Notes" under the "Shop Now" button, you'll be able to read a short description from the First Reads editor who picked the book.)

Here are your options for November 2026. You can get one of these nine e-books, plus this month's short read, Certainty: A Short Story:

Covering tech deals and reviewing TVs, headphones, speakers, and projectors.

#3528. ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters

Peacock‘s latest limited series “The Good Daughter” adds to the streamer’s solid run of women-led thrillers, though it’s best to interpret that label loosely. When stretched to include biographical mysteries, the streak dates back to 2022 with Nancy Oliver’s limited series “Angelyne,” showrun by Allison Miller and starring Emmy Rossum as the enigmatic ’80s era L.A. personality known only by her mononym (until some man decided that’s not good enough).

Then came a slight pivot into pulpy book adaptations with “Apples Never Fall” (2024) an adaptation of Lianne “Big Little Lies” Moriarty’s novel of the same name that was showrun by Melanie Marnich and centered around a wealthy family’s missing mom, played by Annette Bening. Not only did “Apples Never Fall” make the perfect amuse-bouche for Peacock’s next whodunit — “All Her Fault” (2025) the Emmy-nominated yet deeply unserious Sarah Snook showcase — it also teed up Jake Lacy, Hollywood’s leading expert in the field of “entitled douchebags,” for a meta-fun Keyser Söze moment as the devil hiding in plain sight (while his wife took on all of their family’s emotional and physical labor). Related Stories ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

Two less successful entries, by viewership anyway, were this year’s jaunty critical favorite “Ponies,” from co-creator and director Susanna Fogel, which starred Emilia Clarke and Haley Lu Richardson as the CIA’s first female spies operating within the Soviet Union; and the jaundiced “Long Bright River” (2025), a limited series co-created by Liz Moore (who wrote the novel on which it was based) and Nikki Toscano (who served as showrunner), starring Amanda Seyfried as the only cop in a bad/pale part of Philly who cares about neighborhood sex workers and opioid addicts getting killed (one of whom may turn out to be her missing sister).

All of these shows share common tropes, despite disparate tones, topics, and objectives — not the least of which are their glorious feminist underpinnings. Within each of these thrillers lurk so many shady husbands, brothers, bosses, and dads. The patriarchy looms large enough to get name-checked, and the leading ladies are all fighting an uphill battle just to be seen, heard, and understood. “All Her Fault” was so attuned to the ways men routinely let down their families Vulture hailed it as a “misandrist masterpiece.”

But “Long Bright River” carries the most direct parallels with “The Good Daughter,” both by design and on accident. They’re both gritty and dark. They both follow leads whose careers connect back to their personal demons, and they both track working-class women fighting for their impoverished communities (and against the shitty men who run them). Where “All Her Fault” and “Apples Never Fall” could be carelessly devoured as melodramatic amusements, “Long Bright River” and “The Good Daughter” are too brutal and self-serious to constitute anyone’s idea of a “fun” binge, even if there is a morbid bit of fun to be found in the latter’s performances, dialogue, and many, many character quirks.

“The Good Daughter” is set in the fictional town of Pikesville, GA, where Charlie (Meghann Fahy) works as a public defender, adjacent to her sole-surviving parent, town pariah, and private defense attorney, Rusty Quinn (Brendan Gleeson). Her mother, lovingly referred to as Gamma (Olivia Williams), didn’t live long enough to be a grandma; she was murdered in front of her daughters when they were just kids, and the resulting assaults left Charlie’s sister Sam (Rose Byrne) with a lifelong motor speech disorder called dysarthria, as well as impaired vision and a notable limp.

Sam is also a lawyer, but she specializes in patent law (to avoid the anxiety that comes with criminal cases) and moved to New York as soon as she was old enough to get out of Georgia. She only returns to Pikeville when Rusty, for the first time, calls to say her sister needs help. Why now? Well, the list of Charlie’s hardships is nearly as long as her sister’s, but Rusty — who tends to speak in Flannery O’Connor quotes — is likely referring to the most recent trauma: a school shooting she witnessed that left the principal and a 13-year-old student dead.

Once Sam is back in town, the two sisters start mounting a defense for their dad’s client: the school shooter, Kelly Wilson (Shayna Benardo), an 18-year-old student with an intellectual disability. The maniacal powers that be are eager to kill her — first at the scene of a shooting, where a teacher (played by Jake McDorman) saves her from the trigger-happy cops, and then in court, where a self-righteous district attorney argues for the death penalty, competency laws be damned.

They’re all under the Coins’ thumb, a powerful family (with connections throughout the local government) who turned the township against Rusty and his family long ago. Everyone believes Charlie and Sam lied about who killed their mother, and they resent Rusty for defending so many “obviously” guilty parties. The only folks willing to help the Quinns are Rusty’s best friend and legal aide, Lenore (Harper Steele), and Charlie’s husband and assistant district attorney, Ben (Michael Dorman). Otherwise, they’re on their own, standing up for Kelly, standing up to the Coins, and standing against Bad Men™️.

Adapted by Karin Slaughter (from her own book) and directed entirely by Steph Green (“Duster,” “Dare Me”), “The Good Daughter” holds back too many revelations for the finale, creating an exposition-heavy ending that covers its bases but functions like an endless list of answers. It’s not as powerful as it needs to be in order to justify its upsetting subject matter, and it’s trauma-drama plotting skews into overkill well before it’s done doling out distress.

And yet, I have to say, much of it works. Credit goes to the cast, particularly Byrne and Gleeson, for internalizing their showy character quirks to such a degree that Sam’s limp, vision impairment, and sporadic stutter — yes, also a stutter! — never feel like her defining traits. The same goes for Rusty’s folksy banter, poetry quotes, and even his red-nose routine, in which the professional attorney pops on a clown nose whenever he feels the moment calls for a little levity. Such a strange, impractical choice, deployed as often as it is here, could spoil a curious character who’s always viewed from his children’s removed perspective. Maybe he’s unbelievable, maybe he’s too cute for the rest of the story, maybe he’s simply too silly. But Gleeson gathers it all up to form a heartbroken widower who just wants to give his traumatized children the light they need in an ever-darkening world.

Fresh bursts of creative Southern witticisms are similarly rewarding, like hearing Gleeson say, “Never kick a fresh turd on a hot day” or Byrne tell a patronizing windbag “to shit in both hands and start clapping.” The series ultimately rests on Sam and Charlie’s relationship, and their relationship is strong. Their dialogue, particularly when poking fun at one another, rings true, and there’s a buddy-cop dynamic to their investigation that demands to be extended into an ongoing series.

Not this series, mind you. Peacock should limit this limited series to its established, er, limits. But I know a streamer where Byrne and Fahy could pitch another thriller centered around two crusading women looking to crack a case, save their souls, and destroy the patriarchy in one fell swoop.

Just maybe base the next one on a slightly easier read.

“The Good Daughter” premieres Thursday, November 12 on Peacock. All six episodes will be released at once.

#3527. 10 New Movies to Watch This Weekend on Netflix, Prime Video, and HBO Max (November 13 - 15)

A big horror movie, one of the best dinosaur movies of the year, and more

Happy weekend! Several movies are hitting theaters this week, from the action-comedy How to Rob a Bank, starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, and Christian Slater, to Ti West’s take on A Christmas Carol, titled Ebenezer and starring Johnny Depp.

If that’s not enough to get you into theaters, we understand. Thankfully, Polygon has a full slate of new movie recommendations, available on streaming and VOD. The End of Oak Street is available on HBO Max, taking the crown for the best dinosaur movie since Steven Spielberg's Jurassic Park. It also has one of the scariest T-Rexes ever captured on film. Heart of the Beast is now available on VOD, following Brad Pitt and an adorable German Shepherd as they try their best to survive the harsh Alaskan wilderness.

If you’re looking for Netflix dramas, there’s Heartland, a musical-crime-western mashup starring Jessica Chastain and Garrett Hedlund. There’s also Chris Rock’s latest feature, Misty Green, following an out-of-work actress in Los Angeles desperate to make a career comeback. If you're into documentaries, there’s Avedon, exploring the life of career of the life of the beloved photographer whose work left a big imprint on fashion photography.

Lastly, Being Heumann, based on the autobiography of Judy Heumann’s life as an activist, is now streaming on Apple TV. There’s also a new 4K reissue of one of Guillermo del Toro’s most beloved movies, Pan’s Labyrinth.

David Robert Mitchell’s The End of Oak Street is an incredible riff on Spielberg’s Jurassic Park, following a family in the '80s going through some personal challenges. As the parents contemplate a divorce, their neighborhood gets hurled back in time to the dinosaur era, with the outside of their home crawling with all sorts of terrifying pre-historic reptiles.

The dinosaurs themselves are magnificent, rendered with the feathers and fuzzy hair that we now know dinosaurs sported without losing the fearsome nature imbued by Spielberg 30 years ago. This is a movie where dinosaurs repeatedly slaughter and eat random humans, and each kill got an applause from my theater's rowdy audience every time. Mitchell and his team also take some creative swings with the creature designs that largely pay off, including a family of large rocky turtles and a terrifying silent serpent as long as a train with rows of impossibly sharp teeth.

Heartland is one of the strangest movies in Jessica Chastain’s career. The Oscar-winner plays Misty Jones, a former country megastar who returns home to Nashville to investigate the sudden disappearance of her niece, Charlie Hart, who’s following in her footsteps as a country musician.

Being Heumann is based on Judy Heumann's memoir, "Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist," dramatizing the 28-day sit-in protest at the San Francisco Federal Building by disability activists. The demonstration led to the first U.S. federal civil rights protections for people with disabilities.

Ron Howard’s most recent film is a documentary centered on Richard Avedon, one of the most important photographers in fashion history. The film has great access to Avedon’s personal files, showing never-before-seen images and interviews with family members and figures like Twiggy, Isabella Rossellini, and more.

Misty Green follows a once-successful actress and performer whose career has been derailed due to addiction, self-sabotage, and an evolving, challenging industry. After facing challenges from all sides, Misty goes on a desperate job hunt, pursuing a starring role in a remake of the musical Dreamgirls.

Heart of the Beast follows Brad Pitt as a traumatized soldier who gets stranded in the Alaskan wilderness alongside his combat-trained German Shepard. The two band together to survive and return to civilization.

Two isolated middle-aged siblings' lives (Gayle Rankin and Grant O’Rourke) are disrupted when they receive an eviction notice from the government. Raised to view all outsiders as threats, the siblings are shocked by the arrival of a mild-mannered land recovery coordinator (Domhnall Gleeson), who doesn’t know how to communicate with them.

Pan’s Labyrinth is a special film in Guillermo del Toro’s filmography, and his most direct exploration of fairy tales. The series is set in the aftermath of the Spanish Civil War and follows Ofelia (Ivana Baquero), a 12-year-old girl who’s just moved to a military outpost managed by her terrifying stepfather (Sergi Lopez). She uncovers a rich fantasy world after stumbling upon a labyrinth and a faun, who informs her that she’s the reincarnation of a Princess and must complete three tasks to return to her kingdom.

After terrifying everyone with its amazing trailer, Other Mommy is finally available on streaming. The film follows Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark), the daughter of parents who are going through a marital crisis. She starts to form a relationship with a malignant shapeshifting entity that calls itself Other Mommy.

V/H/S Mixtape is the latest entry in the VHS franchise, a found-footage horror anthology that has featured directors like Ti West, Adam Wingard, Scott Derrickson, and more. This year’s version is centered on the music industry and framed in the style of an MTV news show.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3526. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.
