#3490. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3489. Marvel Officially Debuts New Avengers Movie on Disney+ Today

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

After three hours of watching the Avengers try to undo what Thanos did, the last thing Avengers: Endgame gives us is a dance in somebody’s living room. Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) finally gets to be with Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell), and for a few seconds, nobody needs Captain America for anything. The Russo Brothers went back to that scene seven years later and added a knock at the door.

When Marvel brought Endgame back to theaters in September, audiences got to see who was on the other side of that door. There was more waiting in the credits, too, including a sound anyone who’s seen the first Iron Man might recognize before they realize whose face they’re looking at. Fans who saw the re-release in IMAX or an Infinity Vision-certified theater also got a separate sneak peek at Avengers: Doomsday.

Marvel Studios’ Avengers Endgame: Encore is now streaming exclusively on Disney+. The extended cut arrived on the streaming platform today, November 13, with updated color grading and about four minutes of new footage connecting the 2019 movie to Avengers: Doomsday. Disney+ confirms the added scenes are included in the streaming release. The premium-format sneak peek was advertised separately for theaters.

Four villains, and four arguments the films were honest enough to actually let them make. Here is the one you lean towards, the part of it that holds up, and the exact point where it stops holding up.

You align with the one who was right about the problem and wrong about the solution. Killmonger is the most persuasive villain Marvel has produced because the film never pretends his anger came from nowhere.

You align with the protector, which is the most understandable and most dangerous position on this list. Namor is not chasing power or revenge, he is doing whatever keeps his people hidden, and he has been doing it for centuries.

You align with the patient one, the only man on this list with no powers, no army and no hurry. Zemo lost his family in Sokovia and then spent years working out that you do not fight the Avengers, you introduce them to each other's secrets.

You align with the one who decided the answer was arithmetic. Thanos is not angry and not grieving in any way he will admit to, he simply reached a conclusion and never once revisited it, which is precisely what makes him frightening.

Spoilers for the new Encore footage follow.When Peggy answers the door, it’s Tom Hiddleston’s Loki. He tells her he can help both of them, and “both” is the part audiences keep coming back to. Steve spent years trying to get back to Peggy, and the first person to interrupt their dance makes his pitch to her. It’s an especially good use of Loki, whose own second chance came courtesy of the Avengers’ time heist. They gave him an opening to grab the Tesseract and run, setting his Disney+ series in motion. Now he’s on the doorstep of the life Steve went back in time to have.

The first credits scene picks up with Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner after Spider-Man: Brand New Day. He’s recording himself in an underground bunker, explaining how he plans to keep the Hulk under control when the feed glitches. Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom speaks from off-screen. There’s a flash of green, the Hulk roars, and a magical sigil is all that’s left in the cell. At the TVA, Mobius, Casey, and O.B. watch the Fox X-Men universe and another Earth fire missiles at each other as they collide. The alerts keep coming, and the count of lost universes climbs into the thousands.

Then comes the sound of Tony Stark hammering out his first Iron Man mask. That’s a hell of a sound to hear at the end of Endgame, especially with Downey Jr. back in the picture. You know whose face you expect to see, but this time, the last face the movie leaves you with is Doom’s.

Avengers Endgame: Encore is streaming on Disney+. Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters December 18.

#3487. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3486. Amazon Officially Finds The Next Period Romance To Compete With Bridgerton & Outlander

Amazon may be a major player in the streaming landscape, but they've never had a megahit period romance series that can compete with the likes of Bridgerton — though that may be changing with a new project. While Amazon has seen success with Prime Video period shows before, notably the multi-Emmy-winning The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, its biggest attempt to compete with the juggernaut Shondaland series fell flat: My Lady Jane, though a critical hit, was canceled after one season due to disappointing viewership numbers.

However, it looks like they're taking another shot at the genre. Earlier this week, Amazon MGM Studios announced that The American Heiress, a new period series for MGM+, was officially going into production this month. Based on the bestselling Daisy Goodwin novel of the same name, The American Heiress is a "romantic comedy of errors" set in 1893 and starring The Good Wife's Julianna Margulies as Isabella Cash, a wealthy American woman who moves to England with her beautiful "dollar princess" daughter Cora in hopes of marrying her into British aristocracy.

This may sound more like The Gilded Age than Bridgerton, but complicating Isabella's plans is the fact that Cora is head over heels in love with an American artist named Teddy. But things change when a hunting accident results in Cora waking up in Lulworth Castle, home to the 12th Duke of Wareham. A storyline like that could give Benedict and Sophie's "My Cottage" romance a run for its money, and be just what Amazon needs to compete against Bridgerton, Outlander, et al.

Just like contemporary period romance series like Bridgerton and Starz's Outlander, Amazon's The American Heiress comes with a built-in fanbase, as Goodwin's novel was a bestseller. Moreover, Bridgerton and Outlander were both backed by experienced TV professionals in Shonda Rhimes and Ronald D. Moore, respectively. For The American Heiress, Goodwin will not only serve as showrunner and executive producer, but she too has experience in television, having successfully created and written Victoria for PBS and ITV, and later turning it into a novel.

The American Heiress will stream on Amazon's MGM+ platform, not Prime Video.

The American Heiress also looks to do its part in helping dispense with the notion that the period genre is stuffy, promising to find the humor of the "naughty nineties" era. Like Bridgerton, The American Heiress novel has also drawn comparisons to Gossip Girl, with dollar princesses — affluent American women looking to marry cash-strapped European nobility in an exchange of wealth for prestige — serving as the "It girls" of the day. Though dollar princess Cora has yet to be officially cast, veteran actress Julianna Margulies playing her mother is a jewel in the show's tiara.

When Isabella and Cora Cash arrive in England, it will have been many years since the Bridgerton siblings had their romantic adventures, as The American Heiress takes place in the Victorian era (and the Gilded Age in the United States), while Bridgerton is a Regency-era romance.

The American Heiress and Bridgerton also differ in scope and tone. Bridgerton is based on Julia Quinn's novel series, with each season centering on a different Bridgerton's love story, while The American Heiress is a standalone novel that revolves around Cora's romantic future. (Currently, however, The American Heiress is billed an "eight-episode series," not a miniseries).

While viewers of the MGM+ series will surely relish the escapist thrills of The American Heiress's opulent balls and glamorous gowns, the show will be considerably more grounded and realistic than Bridgerton, the ultimate maximalist escapist fantasy. Still, that doesn't mean The American Heiress will be dull. Its "romantic comedy of manners" description suggests there will be plenty of humor to be milked from the Cashes' fish-out-of-water situation. Whether it's enough for the show to find itself in leagues with Bridgerton remains to be seen.

#3485. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.

#3484. 7 Sci-Fi Masterpieces Goodreads Readers Love More Than ‘Dune’

That is an incendiary-sounding headline, so at the risk of getting defensive too quickly, let’s get some things in line and explain it. If you're skimming and scrolling already, then you're a lost cause, and you're already not reading, so whatever. That’s funny. You find an article about books and you don’t read any of it. Anyway… sci-fi books better than Dune? Really? No! Well, probably no. Dune is a fantastic book, and even if you don’t love it for whatever reason, you can likely, at the very least, admire what it’s done for science fiction, as a genre.

If you go on Goodreads, it has an impressive average rating, at 4.29/5, but there are a few well-known sci-fi books that have higher ratings, and some of them are below. That’s the metric. It’s to do with average ratings on Goodreads. It’s not a guarantee, by any means, that everyone on Goodreads feels these sci-fi books are better than the original Dune, but for whatever reason (or reasons, maybe sometimes some potentially understandable ones), they are rated higher. Do with that what you will, and please don’t shoot the messenger.

You're probably better off pretending Ender’s Game is one of those books that hasn’t received some kind of adaptation, since there aren’t a whole heap of positive things that can be said about the movie of the same name that came out in 2013. But hey, the book’s the book, and having the source material feel superior isn't exactly uncommon. The reception on Goodreads reflects that, because it’s got a 4.31/5 on there.

Also, Ender’s Game has more than 1.5 million ratings, and something you find when it comes to books with tons of ratings is that the average rating can be a bit lower than expected. Like, certain heavy-hitters like Nineteen Eighty-Four, Fahrenheit 451, and Slaughterhouse-Five don’t rank as highly as Dune, maybe because some people rating it feel those books are overrated. And sure, maybe some people on Goodreads still find Ender’s Game and Dune overrated, but probably not as many.

Apologies in advance to anyone who’s not a huge Andy Weir fan, but the people of Goodreads are, at least when it comes to two of his books. The first of those two books worth mentioning is Project Hail Mary, which is about an astronaut on a spacecraft on his own, and he doesn’t entirely remember how he got there. But he slowly learns, as does the reader, and his mission out in space turns out to be a high-stakes one, to say the least.

At the time of writing, it has nearly 2 million ratings on Goodreads, and the average rating is at a 4.51/5.

That might make Project Hail Mary sound quite intense, but it’s also very entertaining, since it does some interesting things structurally while ultimately being quite hard to fault as far as pacing is concerned. At the time of writing, it has nearly 2 million ratings on Goodreads, and the average rating is at a 4.51/5. It cannot claim to have the cultural legacy or significance of Dune, by any means, but hey, people who've read it have generally seemed to really love it, so that’s worth something.

The Stand falls a little short of being the highest-rated Stephen King book on Goodreads, but then again, it’s second only to The Green Mile, and that definitely counts for something when you're looking at an author with as many published novels as King. Regarding The Stand specifically, it’s a bit of a blend of genres, though one of them is possibly science fiction, or at least that’s one of the genres it belongs to on Goodreads, so there you go, and here The Stand is.

Maybe it’s easy to define as a dark fantasy book, sure. It’s got the whole end of the world thing going for it, which is post-apocalyptic, and post-apocalyptic books are generally sci-fi, but the conflict here does, before too long, lean into some pretty intense supernatural/horror territory. The Stand is frightening, then, in many ways, but that’s also to be expected with King. Look, it’s a long book (especially the uncut version from 1990). It’s hard to summarize. But it is immense, and it is very much deserving of a 4.35/5 rating, which is what it’s sitting at on Goodreads currently.

This one might seem alarming, and once more, it has to be stressed that the messenger shouldn’t be shot, but the first The Hunger Games book is beloved in general, and particularly so on Goodreads. It sits at 4.36/5 on there, so here it sits at #4 here, within this particular ranking. It struck a chord. People dug it. And it does have a higher rating than some books in long-running young adult series of this rough generation… certainly more than Twilight, though a little shy of the rating for the first Harry Potter book.

Sure, they're works of fantasy, so all that’s a bit of a tangent, but The Hunger Games (2008) is/was iconic. Not perfect, but something that got people more interested in reading, and that’s generally worth celebrating. There are more challenging dystopian and/or sci-fi novels than this one, but if you read this when younger and it got you interested in reading more of the stuff that it might've been influenced by, that’s undeniably a good thing.

Somehow, Andy Weir returned. Returned in this ranking. He didn’t technically return with The Martian, since this one came out before Project Hail Mary and also before the one novel of his that doesn’t have that much love on Goodreads (2017’s Artemis, which sits at a 3.67/5 rating). It’s worth highlighting some of the similarities with Project Hail Mary and The Martian, though, because the latter is also largely about one guy having to do quite a lot on his own.

Sure, that’s not a perfect description of Project Hail Mary, given some of the things that are revealed as it goes along, and The Martian has a bit more going on than just one man trying to stay alive in space, yet the similarities are there. It’s not hard to see how these two novels were written by the same person, but Weir does this kind of science fiction well, and so The Martian sitting at 4.42/5 on Goodreads feels pretty deserved. It is an easy-to-like book, after all.

Okay, when The Stand was mentioned before as having the second-highest rating of a Stephen King book, it’s a little more complicated, since 11/22/63 also sits at a 4.35/5. It’s more of a science fiction novel, for what that’s worth, since the premise involves time travel and the plot concerns someone going back in time to try to prevent the assassination of John F. Kennedy, hoping that getting to the bottom of said event and stopping it will positively impact everything that happens after the titular date.

Complications do ensue, and also, the method of time traveling is far from convenient, since the protagonist can only go back to 1958, and has to navigate life in the past while waiting for the inevitable. Stephen King gets a whole lot of tension out of the high-concept premise here, with the start of 11/22/63 being great, the ending being one of the author’s best, and then everything in between also being amazing. If anything, 4.35/5 could be a tad low for something this good.

There is a lot in Watchmen, both by the standards of a graphic novel and any kind of non-graphic (so normal?) novel, which makes it worth putting here. It’s got a dystopian sort of thing going for it as well, and even if it’s not set in the future like a good many works of science fiction, it’s got an alternate history setting, and that alternate history has developed quite differently, as far as technology and science are concerned.

It makes for something worth rereading and analyzing, and Watchmen is also the kind of thing you can appreciate if you don’t read a lot of superhero-related stuff, but then it becomes more rewarding the more you do know (it helps with appreciating how good it is as a deconstruction). It lives up to the hype, in other words, and so the 4.39/5 rating for the compilation of all 12 volumes on Goodreads definitely makes sense.

#3483. 10 Shows Like 'Phony' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What if you knew your mom wasn't really your mom, but no one believed you? That's the improbable but entertaining premise of Hulu's Phony, which stars Sam Nivola as a teenager who wakes up from a car accident and quickly comes to believe that his mother (Friday Night Lights' Connie Britton) is an imposter. Of course, no one believes him. I'm not sure I believe him, but it'll be pretty boring if it turns out that he just had a really bad concussion the whole time.

It's a coming-of-age drama and a surreal mystery with hints of comedy, and though it borrows elements from other shows, it stands apart for the skill with which it blends everything together. While you wait to see how the story plays out, here are 10 more twisted mysteries to stream now.

A twisty-turny (and well-reviewed) bit of fake identity folderol, Apple Cider Vinegar stars Kaitlyn Dever as Belle Gibson, a real-life Australian cancer survivor (except not really!) With a cheeky sense of humor and a willingness to distort reality, the show follows the wellness influencer as she fakes multiple cancer diagnoses in order to better market her alternative, MAHA-esque app and remedies to the unwitting. As her livelihood comes under threat, her lies grow more elaborate. Stream Apple Cider Vinegar on Netflix.

Alia Shawkat stars here as Dory Sief, an aimless millennial who decides, after seeing a missing-person poster for a college acquaintance, that she's going to make it her purpose to track her down—with the extremely begrudging support of her friends. But neither Chantal nor her disappearance are anything like what Dory expects. The show shifts focus from season to season. Initially a darkly comic take on a Nancy Drew-style mystery, it later finds the gang desperate to cover up a mostly unintentional murder, and getting in deeper each season. It's a funny, smart, and weird and shares talent with Phony in the form of writer/producer Anthony King, who serves as co-showrunner on the new series. Stream Search Party on Netflix.

This one's largely about adults, so it skips the coming-of-age angle central to Phony, but it has a quirky mystery, gaslighting, and a protagonist whose sanity is questioned by just about everyone all the same. This fun and very loose adaptation of the 1989 Tom Hanks film finds Keke Palmer's Samira and Jack Whitehall's Rob moving back to his impossibly safe and tidy hometown. Their house happens to be across the street from a dilapidated Victorian eyesore that may or may not have been the location of a murder a couple of decades before—a murder of a girl who made the mistake of trying to get away. As Samira adjusts to new motherhood and life on the cul-de-sac, she learns that even the nicest of her neighbors have secrets, and comes to suspect that her husband knows more about the missing girl than he's letting on. Stream The 'Burbs on Peacock.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate, working her way into the missing girl's social circle, and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Based on a Harlan Coben novel, Fool Me Once is a bit more of a political thriller than a coming-of-age thing, but we're still in "what the hell is up with my family?" territory: Michelle Keegan plays Maya Stern, a former special ops pilot dealing with the murder of her husband, whom she then impossibly catches playing with their daughter on a nanny cam. The resulting mystery ties into the earlier death of her sister and leads to a web of conspiracy involving her husband's family and a shady pharmaceutical company. Stream Fool Me Once on Netflix.

A vibe match more than anything else, this dark and twisty mystery with a slightly surreal sense of humor also features a single mom who is definitely not what she appears to be. Kim Mo-mi (Lee Han-byeol, initially), the Mask Girl of the title, is a uniquely complicated woman; she always wanted to be a K-Pop idol, but it was always made clear to her that she's not nearly pretty enough for that kind of stardom. So, in order to fill that void, she's got a side hustle. On top of her boring office job, she puts on a blonde wig and a mask to perform as a camgirl for anonymous men. It's a means to express herself creatively and sexually with a level of control—until a mistake causes her to lose that control, a co-worker discovers her secret life, and desperation leads to murder. The show shifts perspectives continually, feeling most like Phony when it focuses on Mo-mi's daughter. Stream Mask Girl on Netflix.

Flipping things around a bit, albeit in a similar "am I just being paranoid?" vein, The Girlfriend deals with a mom who may or may not be freaking out for no reason. Starring Robin Wright as Laura Sanderson, a wealthy art gallery owner in London whose son (Laurie Davidson) brings home a new, working-class girlfriend, Cherry Laine (Olivia Cooke)—immediately strikes Laura as not-our-kind. But is there more to it? Can someone with the name "Cherry Laine" truly be trusted? There's definitely something off, and we're kept guessing as to whether or not this is the story of a dangerous con artist or an overbearing mom—or maybe a little of each. Stream The Girlfriend on Prime Video.

Coming from Irish playwright and Derry Girls creator Lisa McGee, this show eschews the relatively subtle dark comedy of Phony for something much more gloriously surreal. Three high school friends from Belfast reunite after learning that an estranged bestie has died unexpectedly—except that maybe she didn't; a mixed blessing given that they all have secrets that they were hoping would be buried with the maybe departed. Now they're off to investigate the mystery of the murder(?), which turns into a hunt for the friend that they only thought they knew, while inadvertently revealing plenty of secrets of their own. The tone is all over the place in a way that somehow works, with flashes of sincerity balancing out the comedy. Stream How to Get to Heaven From Belfast on Netflix.

Shin Hye-sun offers up a phenomenal performance as Sarah Kim (well: sort of), a wealthy businesswoman who is discovered, at the series' opening, under a sewer grate. The police detective charged to investigate quickly finds inconsistencies in the woman's identity, and after interviewing Sarah's friend and business associate, comes to feel that neither woman is exactly (or anything, like she seems. Though it takes itself more seriously than Phony, it's still an addictively twisty mystery built around a constructed identity. Stream The Art of Sarah on Netflix.

There's a lot going on in this steamy, telenovela-esque drama. Camila Román (Carolina Miranda) finally meets Fernando Castell (Rodolfo Salas), a Tinder match, in Las Vegas, and things get very hot very quickly—he's everything he seemed to be and then some. If anything, she's the sketchy one: a dancer, not a nurse as she said, and with a possessive ex following her around. Still, it's all going great until she decides to surprise Fernando after he flies back to Colombia (which: never do that), and gets a totally different dude when she asks for him at his work. And that's just the beginning! Stream Fake Profile on Netflix.

Apple's new ceramic watch cases are mighty pretty

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Should you upgrade to the new ceramic Apple Watch 12? It’s been quite a while since Apple offered its flagship wearable in a material other than metal. The last ceramic Apple Watch model was 2019’s Series 5.

Long a fan of the ceramic case, I was thrilled to see Apple bring it back for 2026. That excitement only increased after my colleague Jane got her hands on the Series 12 Ceramic at Apple HQ and confirmed its immense beauty.

But is the Apple Watch 12 Ceramic right for you? I can think of three major reasons that justify the upgrade, along with two drawbacks worth considering.

The Apple Watch Series 12 comes in ceramic for the first time since 2019. Compared to Apple's metal case options, ceramic is more durable, with a smooth, pearl-like finish. Choose from Midnight Blue or Pearl White.

Beauty is in the eyes — on the wrist — of the beholder. Let’s be real, though: The primary reason most folks are considering the Apple Watch 12 in a ceramic case is because of its premium and unique look and feel.

The Series 12 is offered in both Pearl White and Night Blue ceramic options; I’m particularly partial to the former, which apparently looks a bit more cream than white IRL with a lovely pearl-like finish.

The Night Blue option, meanwhile, is more of a muted, metallic blue, giving it a less ceramic-like look than the white one. It’s also overall a bit more subtle on the wrist, i.e., less likely to lead to folks "ooing" and "aahing" at parties.

Apple’s ceramic cases are also smoother to the touch than the metal options, adding to the premium vibes.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In addition to a more premium look and feel, the ceramic Apple Watch 12 models are also more durable than their metal counterparts. Apple’s ceramic case combines zirconium dioxide and aluminum oxide, which results in exceptional hardness/scratch resistance, fade resistance, and structural strength.

Ceramic is also more skin-friendly than aluminum or titanium, something worth considering if you have sensitive skin.

For the standard Apple Watch 12 aluminum models, users can choose between a more affordable GPS-only watch or a slightly pricier GPS+cellular model. The Series 12 Ceramic, on the other hand, only comes with both GPS and cellular, saving you the decision.

Better yet, unlike aluminum or titanium, ceramic doesn’t tend to block cellular and WiFi signals. Now, Apple won’t tell you the connectivity of the ceramic models is superior to that of the metal ones thanks to this higher degree of radio transparency, but I suspect it is.

The primary reason to skip the ceramic Apple Watch Series 12 is the cost. The standard aluminum Series 12 starts at $399 for the 42mm GPS option. The titanium Series 12 starts at $699, while the ceramic Series 12 will set you back either a cool $899 for the 42mm or a piggy-bank-smashing $949 for the 46mm.

Those prices make the Ceramic Series 12 even more expensive than the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

The other reason to consider skipping the Apple Watch 12 in ceramic is its comparably larger size and weight versus the aluminum and titanium models. For example, the 46mm Midnight Blue option weighs 52.9 g compared to 38.6 g for the aluminum 46mm.

The ceramic model is also 1 mm taller and 1 mm wider than the aluminum models, making the bezel appear slightly chunkier. Finally, the Series 12 Ceramic is 0.15 mm thicker, though I’m not certain you’ll notice that increase.

What are your thoughts on the new Apple Watch Series 12 in ceramic? Are you pleased to see the case option return? Have you owned a ceramic Apple Watch before? Are you considering the upgrade? Let me know your thoughts below.

#3481. Firefox's New 'Mini Window' Feature Is a Game Changer for Productivity

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

For many of us, web browsing involves juggling dozens of tabs at once, and it's easy for important pages to get lost in the chaos. Now, Firefox has introduced something I think could help us multi-taskers: a "Mini Window." As highlighted by ZDNET's Jack Wallen, this new Firefox feature works like picture-in-picture overlays for videos—only here, that PiP displays a website.

"[Mini Window] lets you move a tab, or a selected section of a page, into a compact window that stays on top of your other windows while you browse," runs Mozilla's official blurb. "It's useful when you're multitasking and need to keep a few sources of information in view at once: Reference docs, a chat, a video call, a form you're filling out." As such, Mini Window doesn't necessarily replace running tabs side-by-side; rather, you can prioritize one tab in a full-size window, while keeping another page in view at all times.

This is a feature that's still in its early stages, and right now you can only get it in the "Nightly" version of Firefox, a very early beta version of the browser. Mozilla says it will push the feature to the full version of the browser later this month.

If you want to try this out as soon as possible, first install Firefox Nightly on your Mac or PC. Once up and running, you can launch Mini Window by right-clicking on a tab header and choosing Move Tab > Move to Mini Window. The tab shrinks and drops down to the lower right corner by default, staying on top of all other windows (not just Firefox). You can then scroll through the page and follow links as normal in the Mini Window—any links set to open in a new tab (manually or automatically) will launch in the main Firefox view, not the window overlay.

By dragging the title bar around, you can put your Mini Window anywhere you want on screen, and you can change its size by dragging the edges of the window too—so it doesn't necessarily have to be all that "mini." Firefox hides all buttons by default—including forward, backward, and refresh buttons, together with the address bar and buttons for closing the window or putting it back as a normal tab—though they appear when you hover over the Mini Window.

I'm finding the feature most useful when writing up articles where I need to refer to something else already on the web (so almost all of them), but there are a host of ways this can be used. It's particularly handy on a small laptop, where you don't necessarily have the screen space to put two tabs side by side, or when running a lower-priority window (like checking a social media site while reading an important document). No doubt, Firefox will continue to refine and improve the feature as it makes its way to the stable version of the browser, and it feels like something other browsers (looking at you, Google Chrome) might adopt as well in the near future. Eventually, using Mini Windows might become as common as opening up a long row of tabs.

#3479. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

Black Friday discounts may not be quite as exciting as they used to be, but it doesn't change the fact that it's the perfect time of year to buy a brand new smartphone. Pulling the trigger at launch often feels like being ripped off, and Black Friday is one of the few times we get to enjoy some serious discounts.

Considering how much phone prices have risen this year, with no sign of stopping, saving some money is more important than ever. But it's not quite as simple as loading up Amazon on November 27 and looking for a new deal. There are plenty of ways to maximize your savings both on Black Friday, and the run up to the day itself.

So, to help you out, here are seven essential tips to save money on your new phone this Black Friday.

The most obvious thing to remember is that you shouldn't stick to a specific retailer or carrier to get your phone. If you want to get the best deal you'll need to shop around, and see where your chosen smartphone is on sale and how much everyone is selling it for. Only then can you actually figure out the best place to actually buy it.

But always remember that you should always look at the full scope of the deals, rather than just the listed price or monthly payment.

If you prefer to buy a phone through a carrier, and pay off the price over two to four years, then you'll likely gravitate towards the mobile carriers' own stores. But you should always remember to check out MVNOs as well.

MVNOs may be virtual operators that piggyback off the infrastructure of the big three, but that doesn't mean they don't sell phones too. In fact some of them have a habit of offering competitive prices to try and pique your interest. Mint Mobile is a good example of this, but there are a bunch of other MVNOs to choose from — some operated by the main carriers, and others than are independent.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Let's say you want a brand new phone, but there aren't any significant discounts to be had. That's a common occurrence for Apple's iPhones, and the discounts you do get often come from carriers that insist you sign up for an expensive monthly data plan. That is why it's important to check the cost of the associated plans before you buy.

Not all deals rely on expensive plans either. You could find yourself paying close to full price for a new phone, but in the process get access to a cheaper data plan. It's all about doing the math and working out what data and perks you actually need, and whether it makes financial sense to lock into a specific plan for however many years are necessary.

It's well known that trading in your old devices is a great way to save money on a new phone. But not all trade-in offers are created equally, and it literally pays to check the small print and see what the details of the deal actually are.

Typically trade-ins operate on a system of new phones being worth the most, and the better the condition, the more you get back. But there are instances where those rules don't apply. For example, T-Mobile currently has a deal that offers up to $1,200 off the cost of an iPhone 18 Pro Max with an any condition trade in.

This means it doesn't matter how battered your phone may be, if you have one of the eligible devices you will get the full $1,200 credited to your account each month. Though, the newer devices still earn you more credit compared to older ones.

So you find a deal, and you're wondering whether it's actually a good one. Prices fluctuate all the time, and just because a discount is on offer doesn't necessarily mean a better one isn't around the corner. But how can you tell? You can't predict the future, but you can look back at the price history and see how the current discount compares to what's been offered before.

If you can see that a specific phone was $100 less than the current deal price within the last few months (such as during Prime Day sales), then there's a good chance that the price might drop a little more as we get closer to Black Friday itself. Though, I will admit that the multitude of mid-year price hikes does complicate things — because the price you paid in July won't be the same as the price you pay between now and the end of the year.

As for which tools to use, we're big fans of CamelCamelCamel, which lets you check the price history of unlocked phones on Amazon — with a quick comparison against third party retailers. That gives you an idea of how much a particular phone could cost, when not purchased from a carrier. As for carrier-sold devices, things are a little more complicated, though the deals tend to be focused on trade-ins and data plans rather than the cost of the device itself.

Just because you see a deal on a phone you like doesn't mean you should buy it right away. If you think the price could drop even further, then you obviously want to wait it out and see what happens. You'll be kicking yourself if you buy a new phone, and two days after it arrives you see it drop even further.

But, at the same time, these discounts are always fleeting and temporary. Put off checking out for too long and you could be faced with the prospect of paying full price again. So if you see a deal that you are happy with, there's no harm in confirming your purchase.

Brand new phones are always the most expensive, but just because they're available and discounted doesn't mean you have to buy one. As we've seen with Walmart's ongoing Black Friday sale, there are also plenty of discounts on older devices and refurbished models that are looking for a second chance at life. These phones are older, but they're also a lot cheaper than the latest model.

These deals are, admittedly, not as plentiful because those phones are officially out of production — so there aren't as many devices to go around. Still, the thing you need to remember about modern smartphones is that the differences aren't that major year-on-year. So a Galaxy S25 isn't that much of a step down from the Galaxy S26, and thanks to Samsung's commitment to 7 years of software support, a year-old phone isn't going to be a security risk for some time.

#3477. 3 Best Prime Video Movies To Watch This Weekend (Nov 14-15)

November is already proving to be a popular month in theaters. As A24's viral documentary sensation, You Can See Everything, LAIKA's new animated masterpiece, Wildwood, and Olivia Colman's bonkers fantasy film Wicker continued to prove popular on the big screen last weekend, Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja's new Cat in the Hat movie and writer/director Takashi Yamazaki's Godzilla Minus Zero crashed onto the box office scene and stole the top two spots in the North American ranks. As another weekend approaches, you needn't get your movie fix with a trip to the theater. Here's a look at three Prime Video movies you should watch this weekend.

For more recommendations, check out our list of the best shows and movies on Prime Video.

Halloween might be over, but Stephen King's presence in your streaming rotation shouldn't be going anywhere. With that in mind, why not check out 2007's The Mist this weekend, based on King's 1980 novella, which was first included in the horror anthology Dark Forces. Set in the small town of Bridgton, Maine, the film follows a group of locals, including artist David Drayton (Thomas Jane), who become trapped when a sinister mist descends.

Written and directed by Frank Darabont and starring the likes of Marcia Gay Harden, Laurie Holden, Andre Braugher, and Toby Jones, this mid-noughties horror gem will chill you to your core as this politically relevant tale twists and turns towards a jaw-dropping finish. Featuring monsters designed by horror comics artist Bernie Wrightson and heaps of tension, you won't forget The Mist anytime soon.

For the perfect popcorn flick to add sparkle to your November weekend, look no further than one of the greatest adventure films of all time. Raiders of the Lost Ark, created by the winning combination of Steven Spielberg and George Lucas, stars Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones, who must race against both time and the Nazis to recover the biblical Ark of the Covenant.

Packed with typically Spielbergian ambition and heart, this iconic family favorite will never fail to brighten any weekend. One of Ford's most beloved performances features a smorgasbord of memorable moments, from the gun in a sword fight to the boulder chase. Raiders of the Lost Ark was the recipient of four Academy Awards, including Best Sound, Best Film Editing, and Best Visual Effects.

On weekends, we wear pink. This weekend, don't spend hours scrolling for what to watch when the most iconic chick flick of all time is ready and waiting for you on Prime Video. Mean Girls, written by Tina Fey and directed by Mark Waters, follows Lindsay Lohan’s Cady Heron as she joins a new school and immediately makes an impact with the A-list girl clique. However, when a mistake is made, all hell breaks loose.

Arguably one of the most quotable movies ever, Mean Girls is jam-packed with memorable moments that have been lovingly parodied countless times since. Rachel McAdams, Amanda Seyfried, Lacey Chabert, and more join Lohan in a perfectly assembled cast, as they combine to not just craft one of the best teen films of this century, but one that will forever define the genre.

#3476. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3475. These Bose QuietComfort Headphones Are $160 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones in Dewdrop Mint, Eucalyptus Green, and Hazelnut Taupe are down to $199 from $359 ahead of Black Friday, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly, making them comfortable to wear for extended periods. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case. The removable earpads are another welcome touch, since you can replace them as they wear down without having to retire the entire pair.

Comfort aside, noise cancellation is another area where these headphones deliver, doing a particularly good job of reducing lower-frequency rumble and background chatter, though some higher-pitched voices can still come through, notes this PCMag review. As for their sound profile, it leans warm and bass-forward, with deep lows that suit bass-heavy genres, while the companion app adds Bose Immersive Audio for spatial sound and lets you create customized listening profiles—the three-band EQ is fairly basic, though, so anyone who likes fine-tuning their sound may find the adjustment options limiting.

Connectivity, too, brings some useful upgrades over the previous generation, including Bluetooth 5.4, multipoint pairing for two devices, Google Fast Pair, and lossless audio over USB-C. That same USB-C port lets you charge the headphones while you listen, and the included USB-C-to-3.5mm cable covers standard headphone jacks, including the ones on in-flight entertainment systems. That said, battery life is less impressive, topping out at 24 hours with ANC enabled, although a 15-minute charge adds around 2.5 hours of playback. Wireless audio is also limited to the standard AAC and SBC codecs, with no support for the higher-quality aptX Adaptive—a feature available on Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra Headphones.

#3474. I tested the HP OmniBook 5 — and it’s a true MacBook Neo rival with an OLED display and nearly 20-hour battery life

The HP OmniBook 5 14 impresses thanks to its lovely design, sharp OLED panel, strong performance, and astonishing battery life. Though it lacks HDR and has a so-so webcam, it’s a worthy alternative to the MacBook Neo for Windows users.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The HP OmniBook 5 is the latest MacBook Neo rival on the market, and it makes a strong impression. Like Apple’s notebook, this budget laptop isn’t “cheap,” thanks to its striking color options and aluminum design. Along with its strong productivity performance and nearly 20-hour battery life, this also gives the equally wallet-friendly Dell XPS 13 reasons to sweat.

The compact, lightweight design is built for all-day travel, while the 14-inch display delivers strong colors and sharp 2K resolution. After class or work, you can unwind by watching your favorite videos.

Even though the display is more vivid than those on other budget Windows laptops, it doesn’t support HDR — which is odd for an OLED panel. Speaker quality is decent but rather thin, and the 1080p webcam can be a bit grainy even in well-lit rooms.

Despite some flaws, you’re getting your money’s worth with the HP OmniBook 5. Right now, it’s one of the best budget laptops and a worthy alternative to the MacBook Neo. Find out why in my full review!

1x HDMI, 2x USB-C, 1x 3.5mm headphone jack

1x HDMI, 2x USB-C, 1x 3.5mm headphone jack

Don't let the relatively low asking price fool you, as the HP OmniBook 5 is anything but cheap thanks to its eye-catching design, long-lasting battery life, and other excellent features.

Like the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13, the HP OmniBook 5 doesn’t look like a typical budget laptop. That's thanks to its thin, elegant all-aluminum design, which looks great and feels good to hold.

The lid flexes a bit when you press in on its center, but the laptop is otherwise very sturdy. At 12.3 x 8.62 x 0.46 inches and 2.5 pounds, this is a perfect laptop for all-day travel, since you’ll barely feel it in your backpack.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I’m a big fan of the keyboard deck, thanks to its relatively spacious size and thick keycaps that make typing a breeze. The backlit keys are nicely spaced and have excellent travel distance. The touchpad isn’t as large as I’ve seen on other laptops, but it's plenty responsive and never fails to register your gestures.

You can technically open the laptop with one hand, though the lid is a bit too sturdy to make that easy. Even though it’s easier to open the laptop with two hands, I appreciate that the lid doesn’t wobble when you’re walking around with the laptop open.

Port selection is fairly generous for a laptop this thin. The left side has an HDMI port and two USB-C ports, while the right side has a single 3.5mm headphone jack. The USB-C ports are USB3, whereas the MacBook Neo has one USB3 port and a slower USB2 port. That means you can charge the OmniBook 5 via either USB-C port.

Lastly, the OmniBook 5 comes in one of four colors: Peony Pink, Smoke Silver, Soft Honeydew, and Starlit Blue. Our review unit’s Soft Honeydew (green) color is quite nice and certainly more striking than the silver or black laptops I typically review.

The 14-inch 1920 x 1200 OLED panel on the HP OmniBook is pretty solid for a laptop in this price range. It delivers decent brightness and oversaturated colors, which helps colors pop. You can see this in the image above, where a video clip of a rabbit basking in the sun appears bright, colorful, and sharp.

Our display benchmark results corroborate my eyes-on experience. The display’s brightness averages 272 nits, which is just shy of the marketed 300 nits. This is as bright as it gets, since the display doesn’t support HDR. Color reproduction numbers for the sRGB and DCI-P3 color gamuts are well above 100%, which accounts for the oversaturated hues.

As you can see above, the displays on the Dell XPS 13 (2026) and MacBook Neo can get much brighter with SDR content, not to mention HDR. Color reproduction is also closer to 100%, so colors look more natural. Color accuracy (Delta-E) is also slightly lower (0 is best) on the HP laptop compared to its rivals.

The touchscreen is as responsive as you’d expect from a Windows 11 machine. It always registered all my taps and swipes accurately. Since the hinge can drop flat, you could theoretically draw on this display more easily. However, since it lacks stylus support, you’d have to draw with your finger, which likely won’t be comfortable or as precise.

The HP OmniBook 5 has modest specs fitting its price. The $649 starting configuration has an Intel Core 5 315 “Wildcat Lake” chip, 8GB of RAM, 256GB of SSD storage, and lacks a touchscreen. Our $749 review unit is a step up, packing an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a touch display.

This laptop is designed to handle the basics, such as web browsing, working in word processors, and streaming videos. I had no problem using HP’s notebook for my everyday work, which usually involves a dozen open Chrome tabs, light photo editing in GIMP, and the occasional YouTube video running in the background.

As you can see above, the HP OmniBook 5 fares well against similarly-priced budget laptops. In the Geekbench 6 CPU benchmark, its single- and multi-core scores are fairly close to the Dell XPS 13, which has the same Wildcat Lake processor and amount of memory. However, its SSD speeds (Blackmagic) and Handbrake (video transcoding) scores are noticeably lower.

Even though the MacBook Neo we reviewed has only 8GB of RAM, it still outperforms both of its Wildcat Lake-powered rivals by a large margin. The only area where Apple’s affordable MacBook lags is SSD speed. That says a lot about the rock-solid performance the Neo delivers.

Wildcat Lake is perfect for basic tasks, but it’s decidedly not built for graphically demanding gaming. In the 3DMark Wildlife Extreme test, which measures a machine’s graphical performance, the HP OmniBook 5 scored 2922 and averaged 18 frames per second.

That’s similar to the Dell XPS 13, though the MacBook Neo has an edge over both. Using its built-in benchmark tool, Borderlands 3 is unplayable at 10.5 fps at 1080p. The same is true for the Dell XPS 13 and MacBook Neo.

Even if the Dell XPS 13 and MacBook Neo have better displays and faster performance, HP’s OmniBook 5 smokes both in battery life.

In our battery life test, which involves continuous Wi-Fi web surfing with the display set to 150 nits of brightness, the OmniBook 5 ran for an astounding 19 hours and 52 minutes! As you can see below, its competitors don’t even come close. It's impressive that this humble laptop can last as long as a MacBook Pro.

There's a lot to like about the HP OmniBook 5, but its budget nature comes with some compromises.

If the HP OmniBook 5 were the only budget laptop like it, I’d likely overlook its lack of HDR support. However, given that the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13 do have HDR support, it’s something I can’t entirely ignore. That's why the display doesn’t get nearly as bright as those of its competitors.

In fairness to HP’s laptop, it does sport an OLED panel — something the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13 do not. As a result, this panel offers stronger contrast between dark and light elements than the Neo and XPS’ respective IPS panels. It also delivers bolder colors, which could be a plus for some folks.

The HP OmniBook 5 has a 1080p FHD IR camera. That’s certainly better than the 720p webcams that budget Windows laptops tend to pack. However, don’t expect the best picture or video quality here.

Even in my building’s well-lit lobby lounge, the picture I snapped is pretty grainy. Yes, you can still see me and the background clearly enough, but don’t expect to look your best.

The HP OmniBook 5 is yet another fantastic MacBook Neo rival for folks looking for a comparable budget Windows laptop. The sturdy design and long battery life are highlights, while the impressive OLED panel and strong everyday performance make for an all-around solid laptop that won’t break the bank.

The MacBook Neo still arguably has an edge thanks to its strong performance, brighter display, and seamless interoperability with Apple’s devices. But if you prefer Windows or want astounding battery life, the HP OmniBook 5 is a solid choice.

#3473. 30-Episode Netflix Action Thriller Series Cracked The Code For Book Adaptations

While Netflix’s action thriller series managed to pull off an incredible feat when it comes to page-to-screen adaptation, the streaming service doesn’t have a replacement for the show after its upcoming series finale. It is never easy to adapt a book to TV, whether creators are dealing with elaborate magic systems like SyFy’s The Magicians or complex in-universe worldbuilding, as was the case for Prime Video’s Lord of the Rings prequel The Rings of Power.

Even outside the lore-heavy worlds of fantasy and sci-fi, thriller novel adaptations can struggle just as much with their transition to the screen. Characters like Karin Slaughter’s Will Trent or Michael Connelly’s iconic detective Harry Bosch are lone wolves who don’t work well with others in their source novels, but the shows Will Trent and Bosch needed to alter this character detail so the strong, silent title characters would actually have some dialogue and character relationships.

However, the biggest challenge for screen adaptations of books always comes when shows run out of existing literary source material. Hulu’s dystopian show The Handmaid’s Tale faithfully adapted author Margaret Atwood’s novel in its first season, and spent the remaining five seasons telling an original story that expanded on the plot of the iconic book with new material. Similarly, Netflix’s The Night Agent lasted three successful seasons even after running out of source material.

Based on author Matthew Quirk’s 2019 novel of the same name, The Night Agent season 1 introduced Gabriel Basso’s conflicted FBI agent Peter Sutherland as he investigates a mole within the US government. The show’s first outing was a massive hit for Netflix, joining Prime Video’s The Terminal List, Hanna, Citadel, and Mr. & Mrs. Smith to become part of the streaming era’s spy show resurgence.

However, there was another series that The Night Agent garnered even more comparisons to. With its irredeemably evil villains, fast-paced action, and escapist feel, The Night Agent was frequently called a masterpiece of “Dad TV” alongside Prime Video’s iconic Reacher franchise. The big difference was that every season of Reacher adapted a different book from author Lee Child’s extensive, ongoing novel series of the same name, whereas The Night Agent ran out of source material at the end of season 1.

Fortunately, The Night Agent seasons 2 and 3 not only managed to overcome this, but even earned better reviews than their predecessor when the show moved on from its original inspiration. With a shared Rotten Tomatoes critical rating of 86% compared to season 1’s 75%, The Night Agent was a hit with viewers even though the show now had to come up with its own storylines on the fly.

Sadly, all good things must come to an end and, rather than trying to drag the show out for as long as possible, Netflix opted to cancel The Night Agent after its upcoming fourth and final season. Compared to the Reacher franchise’s recent expansion, this pragmatic but unfortunate choice makes sense, since The Night Agent is more likely to struggle without any source material after a full two seasons of original stories.

However, while Prime Video had Reacher in the proverbial chamber after the streaming service canceled their earlier Tom Clancy adaptation Jack Ryan, Netflix doesn’t have a similarly crowd-pleasing thriller franchise ready to replace The Night Agent. Although Netflix does have Black Doves, that darkly funny British spy series is closer in tone to Apple TV’s comparatively grounded Slow Horses than The Night Agent.

When it comes to purely fun, fast-paced action thrillers, Netflix risks lagging behind Prime Video thanks to Reacher’s popularity. Thus, the ending of The Night Agent is both well advised and, simultaneously, somewhat ill-time for the streaming service.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.
