There have been so many heist thrillers in movies and TV that it’s tough to find a fresh angle on the well-worn subgenre. The new Apple TV series “12 12 12” attempts to make its heist story stand out by dividing it among three timelines, inspired by a dubious-sounding FBI statistic quoted at the beginning of each episode: A high-level, professional heist requires 12 months of planning, 12 hours to execute, and if the robbers aren’t caught within 12 days, they never will be.

That gives creators Jim Keeble and Dudi Appleton a strict format to follow, but fracturing the narrative mostly serves as a distraction from the basic heist-thriller elements.

Just because it’s basic doesn’t mean that it’s bad, and as a connoisseur of this type of story, I still mostly had fun with “12 12 12.” Eight episodes is a long time to spend on a single crime, though, and the momentum flags as the season progresses, especially when the creators are simply filling in the gaps for events that viewers have already seen.

Jamie Dornan and Anthony Mackie are compelling as the central criminal and cop, respectively, and “12 12 12” is slick and propulsive enough to make for a mildly entertaining watch, even if it’s far from reinventing the heist thriller.

Although it could be confusing to follow three separate timelines of the same characters engaged in the same project, “12 12 12” makes it relatively simple, with onscreen graphics indicating exactly which part of which segment is taking place at any given time. The individual tracks (months, hours, days) unfold in a linear fashion, so that the first episode begins with the first month of planning, the first hour of the robbery, and the first day of the getaway. Each episode moves the story forward in all three time periods.

In that way, “12 12 12” is rarely disorienting, but the structure also robs the story of some potential suspense. Viewers already know that the planning stage will lead to an actual heist, and that the heist will succeed well enough for the perpetrators to get away. Even so, Keeble and Appleton are able to consistently deploy surprise twists, and they use the show’s structure for misdirection, when something that happens in one particular time period turns out not to be what it seems once information from later or earlier is revealed.

Laid out in a straightforward manner, the plot is pretty standard. Reformed robber Paul Galvin (Dornan) is drawn back into criminal activity by his screw-up older brother Bobby (Jack Kesy), who’s gotten himself in trouble with a powerful French mobster. That menacing crime boss threatens to kill Paul’s wife Severine (Agathe Rousselle) and his unborn child if he doesn’t take on the job of stealing nearly $1 billion in cash stored by the Russian mafia in a Swiss bank.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Meanwhile, FBI agent Jack Strickland (Mackie) has transferred to Europe so that he can track the Galvins after a failed takedown in Newark that left Jack’s partner dead.

To pull off the heist, Paul recruits an extensive crew that includes his drilling-expert father-in-law, the bank’s disgraced head of security, and a contortionist who can fit inside a safety deposit box, among others. Most of the characters get limited screen time, and even a recognizable star like Kali Reis of “True Detective” is little more than a cog in the heist plan, playing an expert in train engineering who plans the getaway. It’s a bit disappointing given the lengthy running time that there isn’t more room for character development beyond the combative relationship between the Galvin brothers.

That fraternal dynamic wears out quickly, but Jack has a more complex, rewarding arc, as he has to transcend his desire for revenge against the Galvins and find a way to move forward. The most compelling relationship in “12 12 12” is between Jack and Swiss police detective Lena (Sallie Harmsen), who goes from wary colleague to devoted ally to something more. Their scenes together have more emotional resonance than all of the Galvin brothers’ macho bluster.

Even if the characters never acquire that much depth, the plot moves so briskly that there’s rarely a chance to stop and wonder what makes these people tick. There are a couple of exciting car chases, especially one through the streets of Zurich in the first episode, plus plenty of nail-biting moments as the crew tries to solve various problems under the threat of imminent discovery or danger.

If nothing else, “12 12 12” puts its budget to great use, with action that spans multiple European countries and set pieces that include a giant avalanche and a narrowly avoided train collision. It’s not as lively or witty as the “Ocean’s” movies, and the rivalry between Paul and Jack has nothing on Robert De Niro and Al Pacino in “Heat.” But it holds the audience’s attention almost all the way to the end, until a final episode that has one or two superfluous conclusions.

The timeline trickery proves to be largely superfluous, too, but it keeps viewers on their toes and offers a few satisfying “aha” moments. That’s about all a heist thriller needs. If the formula works, there’s no reason to mess with it.

Josh Bell is a freelance writer and movie/TV critic based in Las Vegas. He's the former film editor of Las Vegas Weekly and has written about movies and TV for Vulture, Inverse, CBR, Crooked Marquee and more. With comedian Jason Harris, he co-hosts the podcast Awesome Movie Year.

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3447. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

Just like most other consumer electronics, the price of mid-range phones has increased substantially over the course of the last year. They’re still largely considered "budget," especially when many of the best phones and best foldables easily cost $1,299+.

Mid-range phones quite simply offer the right balance between features and performance. For my next face-off, I’m putting the iPhone 17e, Pixel 10a, and Galaxy A57 to the test to tell you exactly which one’s worth getting if you have $700 to spend.

I’ve personally tested all three of them over the last six months, so I’ll tell you how their cameras perform, how fast they charge, how their batteries hold up, and what software features they offer.

48MP (f/1.7) main, 13MP (f/2.2) ultrawide

50MP (f/1.8) main, 12MP (f/2.2) ultrawide, 5MP (f/2.4) Macro

Awesome Navy, Awesome Gray, Awesome Iceblue

As I said in my review, “the iPhone 17e feels more like what the iPhone 16e should’ve been from the start.” It’s also the most affordable option in Apple’s lineup if you’re looking to spend as little as possible, offering a well-rounded experience that gets the job done.

Just as before, though, Apple’s kept just a single camera on the back — which is unheard of in an era where practically everything has a dual-camera setup. But despite this shortcoming, the iPhone 17e’s 48MP main camera performs brilliantly across challenging lighting conditions. From the sharp details and definition it pulls out, to how it neutralizes hotspots in bright scenes, it doesn’t disappoint. It’s also a master of low light, proving to me it’s the best camera phone of the bunch in terms of raw performance.

Under the hood, it’s easily the powerhouse of this trio. Thanks to Apple’s A19 silicon, the iPhone 17e delivers superior CPU and GPU performance that keeps everyday multitasking snappy and handles demanding, graphically-intensive games far better than its Android counterparts. I appreciate that Apple also made a couple of smart hardware upgrades — like bumping starting storage to a generous 256GB and finally adding MagSafe support.

That said, the iPhone 17e isn’t without a few glaring compromises. Holding onto a 60Hz display feels increasingly dated when 120Hz panels have become standard across the rest of the mid-range market — and the lack of an ultrawide camera means it’s not as suitable for sprawling landscapes and group photos.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

And while iOS 27 brings some much-needed new features, like the ability to create custom passes and use generative AI with its Reframe tool to shift to a new perspective for photos, Siri AI remains functionally inferior compared to Gemini. While the assistant is more proactive with what I’m doing on the phone to offer actionable recommendations — like creating a reminder when someone texts me about an upcoming event — Siri AI lacks the deeper third-party app support that lets it work across more apps.

Worst of all, its recent price hike to $699 (up from its $599 launch price) makes those omissions much harder to overlook.

There’s good and bad with the Pixel 10a. Just like the iPhone 17e, the design makes it look like a generic slab — but at least Google’s made the camera housing completely flush and offers some fun color options. Despite these design tweaks, the phone is by and large similar to its predecessor, the Pixel 9a, including how it packs the same Tensor G4 chip as before.

Its 6.3-inch Actua display is surprisingly sharp and bright, besting its rivals with a peak brightness of 1,896 nits in our lab testing. Even better, it posted the longest battery life of the trio with an average of 15 hours and 16 minutes. Better yet, it also delivers the fastest wired charging times we’ve tested — reaching 64% in 30 minutes.

Where the Pixel 10a truly separates itself, though, is on the software front. Gemini remains leagues ahead of Siri AI and Bixby, especially in its ability to execute complex, multi-step actions across different apps. I’m not simply referring to asking it to check upcoming New York Knicks home games and add them to my calendar — I’m talking about everyday things like ordering Dunkin’ Donuts through DoorDash, all with a simple voice command.

If that’s not enough, the Pixel 10a really widens the software divide with how practically the Pixel desktop mode works when I connect it to an external monitor, turning the phone into a surprisingly capable workstation when I happen to leave my work laptop at home. Even on the photography side, new AI tools like Auto Best Take and Camera Coach help you nail group shots and framing without any heavy lifting.

However, Google’s decision to reuse the same Tensor G4 chip as its predecessor puts it at a major disadvantage in raw CPU and GPU benchmarking compared to the iPhone 17e. And in 2026, having a base storage of 128GB feels stingy. Even though the camera performance is better than most other mid-range phones, I’m disappointed that there's barely any improvement over its predecessor — a tougher pill to swallow now that its $100 price hike has pushed it to $599.

Out of the bunch, the Samsung Galaxy A57 has the most premium look and feel — rivaling its flagship sibling, the Galaxy S26. Not only does it combine the glass-meets-metal build Samsung’s known to give its top-tier models, but it also manages to have an IP68 rating.

If you prefer a phone with a larger screen to see more of what you’re doing or stream your favorite shows while on the go, the Galaxy A57’s massive 6.7-inch Super AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate doesn’t disappoint. It’s way bigger than the 6.1- and 6.3-inch screens of the iPhone 17e and Pixel 10a, respectively.

Another notable feature is how it’s the only phone in this trio to pack a triple-camera system on the back, pairing a 50MP main sensor with a 12MP ultrawide and a 5MP macro lens. While that dedicated macro shooter feels more like a forced addition just to give it the upper hand, having three distinct lenses nonetheless gives you extra shooting versatility that neither the iPhone 17e nor the Pixel 10a can match.

Throw in some S26-level Galaxy AI features — like access to object eraser and a voice transcription tool — and it has a robust toolset to help save you time. I also love how it caters to power users like myself, with the ability to run two apps side by side, which neither the iPhone 17e nor the Pixel 10a can do.

Where the Galaxy A57 stumbles, though, is under the hood. Powered by Samsung’s Exynos 1680 chip, it posted the lowest performance scores of the bunch in our testing, lagging behind both the Pixel 10a and especially the iPhone 17e. Worse yet, it doesn’t even have the luxury of wireless charging — a glaring omission, in my opinion, now that its $50 price hike has pushed the cost up to $599.

3DMark Wild Life Original Unlimited (score/fps)

If there’s one I’d buy with my own money, it has to be the Pixel 10a — with the iPhone 17e not too far behind it. That’s because Google’s mid-range phone checks off more of the boxes on my list than the other two.

All three phones got price hikes, but the Pixel 10a’s $599 price tag is easier to swallow than the iPhone 17e’s heftier $699 cost. And while the Galaxy A57 matches the Pixel’s price point, its weak processing performance combined with flat camera results aren’t enough to prove to me it offers better value at the same price.

Ultimately, the Google Pixel 10a is the mid-range phone I recommend. I can’t stress enough the value of its software package alone — and backed up by seven years’ worth of major Android and security updates, it’s undeniably the smartest long-term investment you can make in the mid-range market right now.

#3444. Ex-NFL Coach Rex Ryan's Alleged Hit-And-Run Victims Speak Out

One of Rex Ryan's alleged hit-and-run victims is speaking out ... claiming the former Jets coach "almost killed" him and his wife.

Attorney Michael Holland told the California Post that he and his wife were struck by the retired coach's pickup truck last week in Nashville.

Holland said ... "If we had been six inches further out, I’d be in a hospital right now and so would my wife."

Holland added that he and his wife were walking at the crosswalk when the ESPN analyst's "over-6,000-pound vehicle" struck them.

He added ... "He decided he wanted to turn and didn’t care and just ran over both of my feet, my wife’s foot and got her leg too."

According to Holland, Ryan went on his merry way before he caught up to the driver, pounding on his window.

After Ryan got out of his car, Holland claimed ... "He was told in no uncertain terms what he had done, and instead of staying at the scene or even saying, 'Sorry,' he just got back in his vehicle and took off."

We reported earlier ... Holland and his wife were the ones who were able to help catch Ryan after taking a photo of his license plate.

Cops were able to match the plate with Ryan's ID ... according to a warrant TMZ obtained.

Ryan later surrendered to the Nashville-Metropolitan Police Department this week.

#3442. The 10 Worst Albums From Usually Great Artists

If you put out enough stuff, regardless of the field you're in, it’s pretty much inevitable that you'll miss the mark on at least one occasion. You can see it with prolific authors, busy filmmakers, and then also with artists. If an artist or band hasn’t released anything bad as far as albums are concerned, then they're either a rare breed of artist/band, or they’ve not released a ton of albums.

These artists are all great, but each has put out at least one album of questionable quality, and said not-great albums are below. So, it’s a bit negative, critiquing those albums, but it’s also good to remember that an artist has to be pretty great to be included here, with the albums below standing out since they're generally surrounded by other compelling albums.

With a debut album in 1967 and a final release almost half a century later, it would've been truly surprising if David Bowie never misfired critically. As it stands, him only having a few misses is still remarkable, and then when you take into account just how high-quality most of his good albums were, it does make those less-than-great ones easier to forgive.

If you're not singling out his self-titled debut, you're probably going to turn to one of two 1980s albums by Bowie to mark as his weakest. At least 1984’s Tonight has “Loving the Alien,” while Never Let Me Down, which seemed like it was supposed to be a comeback after Tonight was largely critically dismissed, doesn’t really have any highlights. You're better off sticking with Scary Monsters (and Super Creeps) and Let's Dance if you want to hear some ‘80s Bowie, and then all his post-1980s stuff is more interesting than Never Let Me Down, too.

It feels a little hard to get too angry at Raditude, partly because it’s already been criticized to hell and back, and partly because that album cover is hilarious and it might feel nicer to pretend to be in on the joke. Because Raditude is almost definitely a joke. Also, it’s called “Raditude.” Weezer are a ridiculous band, but they do have ridiculous or somewhat eyebrow-raising albums that are of a higher quality than Raditude.

The opening track, “(If You're Wondering If I Want You To) I Want You To,” is kind of fun, but otherwise, you don’t have a lot here to really grab onto.

Even as far as funny album covers and titles go, Raditude can’t be the funniest combo, since Weezer also have an album named Hurley, and the cover is just a close-up of Jorge Garcia’s face (he played Hurley on Lost). How can you get too mad at a band that does that? It’s funny. That absurdity and willingness to be a meme can be appreciated, but if you're looking at Raditude specifically, and the music itself, uh, the opening track, “(If You're Wondering If I Want You To) I Want You To,” is kind of fun, but otherwise, you don’t have a lot here to really grab onto or remember.

While no one is going to mistake Weezer for Metallica, St. Anger does occupy a similar space critically to Raditude. All the bad things that could be said about an album have been said about these two, as notorious 2000s albums, yet with Metallica, it was a bit more of a downfall, since their heyday was in the 1980s, rather than the 1990s, like Weezer. Also, Weezer sort of bounced back in the 2010s, and the same can’t really be said about Metallica.

Sorry, it’s true. That doesn’t take away from that 1980s run, and then even in the 1990s, there was still some good stuff Metallica-wise. The good times can’t last forever, though. Eventually, there have to be sad times. Mad times. Angry times. St. Anger times. It gets worse for Metallica, though. Look a little further down, for another notorious album that came out eight years on from this one.

You can’t win here, because there will be people who don’t like the suggestion that Taylor Swift is a great artist, and there'll probably also be people who like everything she’s done and thereby won’t like The Life of a Showgirl being criticized. To the people in the first camp, she’s done some great stuff and is popular for good reason. To the people in the other camp, she is capable of so much more.

The Life of a Showgirl felt a little worse than being just Taylor Swift on autopilot. There are three somewhat solid songs at the start, and then the whole thing derails, with some truly questionable lyrics and a lot of repetition as far as the music itself goes (even for stuff belonging to the pop genre). It can only be up from here, for Swift. Well, at least it’s hard to imagine something missing the mark more than The Life of a Showgirl any time soon.

Calling a Michael Jackson album bad is about as risky as calling a Taylor Swift album bad, or maybe even a little more so, since he has dedicated fans as well, and saying Invincible (the album that ended up being his last) is bad probably constitutes a hot take. But Invincible is such a slog. It doesn’t have to be as good as Thriller, because not much is, but wow does that classic album move.

And it also feels coherent. There are other great Michael Jackson albums where you can also admire the consistency and flow. With his 1990s stuff, maybe a little less so, but at least there were more highlights. Invincible is trying to do too much and please too many people all at once, and the resulting album is one where you feel like you're fighting to stay focused throughout. The album should be focused, and you shouldn’t have to do all that work yourself. Invincible, honestly, is a chaotic mess of an album. Sorry.

There might be some more recent Kanye West albums that are worse than Jesus Is King, but this was his first real miss, rather than just putting out something divisive, and also, some of these recent albums just aren’t fun to engage with or even think about. You do have to acknowledge things have gotten worse on a quality front (2021’s Donda, though, was better than Jesus Is King), and also that Kanye West, as a figure, has continued escalating the questionable things he’s willing to do and say.

Knowledge of 2020s Kanye West makes Jesus Is King look even more absurd in hindsight. It was a weirdly clean-cut Christian hip-hop album that felt a bit rushed and bizarrely produced at the time, and now it just feels bizarre, clashing with the very unwholesome things West has returned to doing. It’s around this point where it really started feeling not worth keeping up, even if you'd weathered the storm(s) up until that point.

Since Lou Reed was credited alongside Metallica for Lulu, Metallica can sneak back on here for a second time, or more accurately, they're here 1.5 times. Lulu is more notorious than St. Anger, in any event, but neither Metallica nor Lou Reed were strangers to making divisive albums. The former had St. Anger, and the latter had Metal Machine Music, which is a wild one (research in your own time and at your own risk).

They collided to make Lulu, though, and the result was something people either gave up on long ago, or are still trying to make some kind of sense of a decade and a half later. If someone tells you they “get” Lulu, maybe they're geniuses. It’s possible. But if someone tells you they both get and genuinely enjoy Lulu, run away from them as fast as you possibly can.

The jokes write themselves. The Clash released an album called Cut the Crap and it was… yeah. It was the band’s final album and ended what had otherwise been a pretty great run on a real bummer, because the lead-up to making it and then the production was something that pushed the members of The Clash apart, and then its negative reception when it did finally see the light of day was a real nail in the coffin sort of thing.

Best to remember the good times. You know, London Calling, the self-titled album, maybe about half of Sandinista, and a fair few songs on Combat Rock, too. You can’t go too wrong with most of the other albums by The Clash, but you also can’t go right with anything on Cut the Crap. The legendary punk rock band was mortal/human after all.

There’s a great documentary called The Endless Summer. It isn't specifically related to The Beach Boys, but it did come out in 1966, when the band was at its peak (Pet Sounds!), and then The Endless Summer was about surfing, as were quite a few early songs by The Beach Boys. Anyway, if you wanted to argue there was some way to keep riding the high of the 1960s, continuing the summer with surfing and Beach Boys, maybe you could, at least until 1992.

Just over a quarter of a century on from all that optimism and literal sunshine came Summer in Paradise. Whether you even want to count it as a true Beach Boys album… definitely debatable. Brian Wilson wasn’t involved at all, and that’s otherwise unheard of for a Beach Boys album. And it’s been partially erased from history, in the sense that it’s out-of-print and hasn’t been reissued, and you can’t even find official uploads on the band’s channel on YouTube. They seem to want you to forget about it, and maybe you'll want to forget about it, too, should you be subjected to Summer in Paradise.

Hey, you’ve made it this far. And I’ve made it this far. Since we’ve made it this far, I’m going to get personal, and that’s where the “I’ve” and the “I’m” come in. And “I,” as in I really loved Arcade Fire. This band was everything for a while there, definitely before Everything Now, but even that album had its moments. The band’s first three albums were basically perfect. The follow-up to Everything Now, We, was a step in the right direction. And between the first three great albums and Everything Now, there was 2013’s Reflektor, which has always felt underappreciated and might well get the proper amount of love it deserves one day.

That’s all to say I either loved or felt okay with defending all of Arcade Fire’s first six albums. Then album #7 came out and I couldn’t finish it. Pink Elephant contained some of the dullest and most lifeless music I’d ever heard. I’ve listened to some albums by this band dozens, or possibly even hundreds, of times. I couldn’t get through the sonic sludge that was Pink Elephant a single time. What the actual hell happened here? Look how they massacred my boy…

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3441. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

The city I’ve inhabited since birth is known for so many things: the ease of public transportation, the strange smells, the bustling nightlife and the incredible food are chief among them.

On that last note, that sticks out to me as one of my favorite aspects of New York City. Everywhere I look, there’s your average hot dog vendor, a standout food truck, a NYC restaurant staple or a hidden gem that’s sure to blow up once it gets shared across IG. I’m prone to eating with my eyes and not thinking about how full I can get after just a few bites (especially since my metabolism isn’t what it once was).

Even so, I still love to go adventuring in my city with a friend in tow to enjoy all the good eats littered across every borough. Since I’m planning to enjoy that same activity this weekend with one of my closest (and always hungry!) buddies, I came to ChatGPT and Gemini with a simple request: find me the best and most affordable places I can eat at with a $100 budget in mind.

Here’s which chatbot gave me the best cheap eateries and the prompt you can put in place to try it out for yourself.

With this prompt, I requested ChatGPT’s help with locating a specific number of affordable spots to grab some grub at:

“Find me 7 of the best cheap restaurants in all five NYC boroughs for a total budget of $100, prioritizing filling meals. Include specific orders, current prices and a map.” Of course, you can change the number and location in that prompt to make it personalized to your preferences.

ChatGPT took note of my request and laid out a solid selection of dishes worth taking a couple of train transfers for: You'll get Chinese roast pork, Puerto Rican chicken and rice, Nepalese dumplings, Sri Lankan kottu roti, and more. After laying out a map of each location alongside its numbered review scores, the chatbot proceeded to detail its seven picks and an estimated price for each location’s best menu selection:

When it was Gemini’s turn, Google’s chatbot acknowledged my hunger for cheap, carb-heavy, protein-packed portions that my fellow culinary adventurer and I could enjoy.

And while it didn’t showcase a map as descriptive as ChatGPT’s, Gemini’s version still proved to be helpful since it laid out which trains and ferries I could take to get to each location.

Gemini produced its list of recommendations and delivered it in the form of an easy-to-read chart that highlighted the restaurant’s name, location, a specific order I should consider getting and its estimated price. A good example of that format is how Gemini listed an Italian restaurant located in Gravesend, Brooklyn that could fill me and my friend up with 2 Sicilian "Upside Down" Square Slices for a total of $9.

Underneath a section entitled “What Makes Each Spot Unbeatable & Filling,” Gemini went into further detail about the inexpensive eateries it chose for me:

Besides both chatbots generating the best and cheapest NYC food options I should consider, both ChatGPT and Gemini also gave me a budget breakdown of every meal.

ChatGPT also factored in the leftover money I’d have before public transportation fees, the taxes attached to each meal and any tips me & my hungry cohort may leave behind. Gemini’s aforementioned chart produced an estimated total for its recommended restaurants and meals, plus an approximate amount of money I’d have left over for sales tax, cash tips and subway swipes.

Overheating is a major barrier to good sleep. Elevated temperatures impact the smooth running of your body clock, whether from hormones, illness, environment or more. But I've been testing the Eight Sleep Pod 6, now up to $200 off at Eight Sleep, and this smart cooling mattress cover shows overheating the door.

Although, note I only said mattress cover. Head to our best mattress guide to find your new favorite bed to fit it onto.

I'm tracking all of this year's best Black Friday mattress deals and this early offer is one of the biggest discounts I've seen this year from Eight Sleep, making now a good time to buy. My full Eight Sleep review is coming soon, but for now, here's why this Pod 6 offer might be the deal of the season for hot sleepers and people who keeping waking up at night.

Eight Sleep Pod 6: From: $1,899 (was $1,999) US | $1,699 (was $1,799) UK at Eight SleepThe Pod 6 is the latest release from Eight Sleep, a smart mattress cover that delivers intuitive heating and cooling as you sleep. Eight Sleep never goes in for big sales so up to $200 / £200 off is an exciting discount but I'll be keeping an eye out for further price drops closer to Black Friday. A subscription is required, starting at $17/£17 per month.

When I spoke to Matteo Franceschetti, co-founder and CEO of Eight Sleep, he described overheating as the "biggest issue" affecting sleep. And temperature control is still at the heart of the Pod 6.

I could talk about active temperature control for ages but to keep things brief, I'll highlight the two things I'm loving about my Eight Sleep Pod 6 right now.

First, when I climb into bed, it's delightfully snug. Not too warm, which could disrupt my circadian rhythm, but not so cold I stay curled up in a tight ball until my body heat has taken the chill off the sheets.

Second, during the night the Eight Sleep gradually lowers the temperature. That means when my body starts naturally warming around 3 a.m., I don't wake up sweating on a too hot mattress cover. In fact, since testing the Eight Sleep I haven't woken up feeling stuffy at all.

Your daily sleep score is a great way of assessing 'why do I feel like this.' But it's a snapshot of your routine. To improve and strengthen your sleep hygiene, you have to look at the bigger picture.

This is what Eight Sleep's Autopilot app does so well. It places each night in the context of your overall sleep patterns. From this, you can identify the recurring issues and understand what works for your sleep.

And for anyone who gets easily overwhelmed by data first thing in the morning, Eight Sleep puts the info into easy-to-read graphics. A quick glimpse while still blurry-eyed and you can identify whether your sleep debt is in the red.

I previously tested the Orion, a more affordable cooling mattress cover. I had a lot of love for this design — you can read why in my Orion Sleep System review — but I can't deny that it's both noisy and bulky.

In comparison, the Eight Sleep is almost completely silent. While the Orion droned throughout the night, I have to strain my ears to even hear the Eight Sleep. For those very sensitive to noise overnight, I still suggest a pair of earplugs. But for most people, it shouldn't cause a disruption.

The central control hub of the Eight Sleep is also conveniently compact. I liked the look of the Orion but it took up a lot of bedroom real estate. The Eight Sleep fits more easily into limited floor space.

BedJet 3: From $437 (was $699) US | £399 (was £599) at BedJetWhile the Eight Sleep uses water to adjust the temperature of an attached cover, the BedJet blows hot or cold air gently over the surface of your mattress. It's not as high tech as the Eight Sleep but it will still help offset any night sweats and it's a cheaper option. A dual cover is also available, for bed sharers.

I've tested the Orion Sleep Sytem and its fast-response water-based cooling blew me away. It's cheaper than the Eight Sleep (especially in this massive sale) with a queen now down from $2,395 to $1,795. And there's no subscription required (although if sleep tracking is a deal breaker, you can add it for $250/year). Currently only available in the US, Orion hopes to add international shipping soon.

#3432. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

As it turn outs, 'pressure' is a good thing when it comes to sleeping through the night

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Picture the scene: you're mentally drained but can't fall asleep. Worse still, after you eventually do nod off, you find yourself wide awake at 3 a.m., staring at the ceiling, unable to go back to sleep.

That was my reality for months until a sleep doctor explained that the coping mechanisms I was using to get through my days were likely contributing to my 3 a.m. wake-ups.Here Dr. Ana Casas, a longevity and internal medicine specialist, and Dr. Shelby Harris, a Board-Certified Clinical Psychologist at Better Sleep, explain what sleep pressure is and why it's crucial for dropping off and sleeping through the night.

"Think of sleep pressure as your brain’s natural hunger for sleep," explains Dr. Casas, who co-authored the book Take Back Your Sleep: The Science-Based Strategy for Deep Sleep, Brain Longevity, and Peak Performance.

"Just as your body becomes hungrier the longer you go without food, your brain becomes hungrier for sleep the longer you stay awake."

"This is one of the two primary forces that regulate sleep, alongside our circadian rhythm, or internal body clock," adds Dr. Harris.

"When sleep pressure is sufficiently high and aligned with our natural circadian rhythm, we are more likely to fall asleep easily, move through the appropriate stages of sleep, and stay asleep throughout the night."

Healthy adults clocking up between seven and nine hours of overall sleep should be spending 45 to 90 minutes in deep sleep, experts recommend. Deep sleep is hugely important for our overall energy levels and stress management. Here are the common mistakes experts said were robbing me of sleep pressure and, as a result, the amount of time I was spending in deep sleep:

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

One of the mistakes I've made when it comes to building sleep pressure is using mental exhaustion as an excuse not to incorporate movement into my day. After all, I feel mentally drained — why do I still need to exercise? "A demanding workday can leave you feeling exhausted, but prolonged periods of sitting and limited physical activity may mean you haven't built as much sleep drive as you think," explains Dr. Harris, who notes that incorporating movement into the day supports healthy sleep patterns. "This doesn't mean you need an intense workout every day," says the sleep doctor. "Walking, taking movement breaks between meetings, getting outside in natural daylight, or doing some light exercise can all make a difference. The goal is to give your body enough activity and daytime stimulation to support restorative sleep at night."As well as helping build sleep pressure, a study by the University of Texas indicates that getting as little as 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day could help you get more deep sleep.

When you've had a rough night's sleep, you might mistake caffeine as your friend, helping you to power through the day. I know I have. However, caffeine has a half life. That means that half the amount of caffeine you have consumed will still be swirling around in your system between 3-7 hours later, depending on your tolerance to it.What does that have to do with sleep pressure? "Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors in the brain, temporarily masking our natural sleep pressure even though adenosine continues to build up," explains Dr. Casas.

Sleeping in on the weekend or going to bed early is a common go-to method of catching up on lost sleep. However, this can make it much harder to fall asleep later that night. "One of the biggest mistakes is spending too much time in bed, particularly when people try to compensate for a poor night's sleep by going to bed significantly earlier or sleeping in later," says Dr. Harris. "This can reduce the amount of time spent awake and prevent sufficient sleep pressure from building."Napping or falling asleep in front of the TV (guilty) has a similar effect. Sticking to a consistent sleep schedule is your best bet for allowing adequate sleep pressure to build. If you must nap, Dr. Harris recommends keeping them "relatively short and earlier in the day so they don't interfere with nighttime sleep pressure."

"Ultimately, healthy sleep isn't just about what you do at bedtime," concludes Dr. Harris. "It's about building the right conditions throughout the day so your body is naturally ready for sleep when night comes." These are her expert tips to increasing your sleep pressure so you can fall asleep quicker and stay asleep all night.

"If we haven't built up enough sleep pressure during the day, we may find it harder to fall asleep or experience more fragmented sleep," explains Dr. Harris, who notes that the first half of the night is when we tend to clock up the majority of our overall deep sleep. This is thanks to a healthy bank of sleep pressure that's been building throughout the day, lulling us into deeper, slow-wave sleep. When we're in a sleep pressure deficit, it takes us longer to fall asleep and can lead to waking up at night — specifically at 3 a.m.

"As the night progresses, that pressure naturally dissipates, and our sleep architecture shifts toward lighter stages of sleep and longer periods of REM sleep," explains Dr. Harris. "Around 3 a.m., depending on when someone goes to bed, they may be moving through these lighter sleep stages, making them more susceptible to waking from environmental disruptions, stress, or changes in body temperature," continues the sleep doctor. "If someone hasn't built up sufficient sleep pressure during the day, this transition can make it harder to maintain consolidated sleep," says Dr. Harris, who notes that insufficient sleep pressure isn't the only cause of waking up at night. "It's important to remember that 3 a.m. wake-ups aren't always caused by sleep pressure alone – circadian rhythm disruptions, alcohol, stress, and hormonal changes can also play a role."

#3423. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

Keeping your calf muscles strong can benefit your body in many ways

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I didn't know until quite recently that your calves are known as the "second heart" because they help pump deoxygenated blood back up the body. Not only that, but they also play a role in absorbing force during lower-body movement and provide stability to your lower limbs.

I'm not great at sitting still, so during my working days at my desk, I am known to have a quick wander to quell restless legs, and recently I learned about an exercise called a soleus push-up.

I've been performing maximum reps every hour while seated during my workday, and I've noticed a few things so far. Read on to find out more.

A soleus push-up (SPU) is a seated calf raise exercise that targets the deeper calf, or soleus muscles.

Collectively, the soleus and gastrocnemius muscles form your calves and are referred to as a secondary heart. These muscles help pump blood toward the heart, squeezing the veins with contractions so oxygen-depleted blood travels up the body rather than pooling in your lower limbs.

To keep circulation going, being as active as possible helps, including walking, running, or cycling. You may also find elevating your legs at times can be useful, especially after prolonged sitting. But if you don't fancy swinging your legs up onto your desk in the office, seated calf raises or soleus push-ups can help.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

But before we get into what happened when I tried it every hour, every day, for one week during work, there's a study I think you should know about. Published in the Journal of Biomechanics, the research found that people with chronic heart failure had smaller calf muscles (namely, the deeper soleus muscle that helps us walk and stand) than people deemed "healthy" with "functional hearts."

Performing these muscular contractions seated can be useful for people who have desk jobs or want to limit fatigue and blood pressure issues.

Here's what happened when I tried the exercise every day.

Research found that people with chronic heart failure had smaller calf muscles (namely, the powerful soleus muscle that helps us walk and stand) than people deemed "healthy" with "functional hearts."

I have very mobile, clicky joints, and my ankles get both noisy and stiff if I don't move often enough, so adding as many reps as I could for 60 seconds per hour during my workday really helped.

I set eight alarms, one for every hour, and timed myself for 60 seconds, performing reps at my desk while still working.

When I got up to move around, particularly later in the week, I found my ankles felt more mobile and warmed up, and my calves felt less stiff. I recommend learning how to do calf raises, as well as trying some ankle mobility exercises and lower-body stretches alongside this move to ramp things up further.

Because the movement is driven from the lower limbs while seated, it's extremely accessible and low-impact, meaning most people don't even need to stop working while performing the soleus push-up. That also means you can go for high rep ranges while sitting at a desk.

The soleus muscles thrive on sustained periods of movement, so this makes it an ideal exercise to repeat during the week while keeping those muscle contractions going during seated periods.

I added ankle weights to increase the intensity, and this is safe to do because there's no impact. I found it worked my muscles harder and, after stopping 60 seconds later, I felt like I'd been walking up a set of stairs. Add weights just above your knees for even more resistance.

Marc Hamilton pioneered the soleus push-up at the University of Houston and published findings in the journal iScience, saying the exercise provides "optimal activation" and "elevates muscle metabolism for hours, even while sitting."

He adds that the exercise helps sustain an "elevated local oxidative metabolism" which can improve blood glucose regulation by helping clear blood glucose from the bloodstream. Oxidative metabolism refers to a process where oxygen helps burn blood glucose or fats, depending on the energy needs of your working muscles.

“No one ever investigated how to use it to optimize our health, until now,” says Hamilton. “When activated correctly, the soleus muscle can raise local oxidative metabolism to high levels for hours, not just minutes, and does so by using a different fuel mixture.”

Of course, without a carefully controlled lab setting, I couldn't tell you if this made a difference for me or not.

I can be subject to swollen ankles and a little numbness in certain positions, a condition my musculoskeletal doctor hasn't been able to pinpoint just yet, so I was intrigued that soleus push-ups could boost circulation.

A week later, although not life-changing, I have noticed less swelling and numbness while sitting. This makes sense, as your soleus muscle helps pump blood toward the heart.

Plus, as we age, calf strength can decline, which can have a knock-on impact on gait and balance during movement. By maintaining strong, healthy calves, I know I'm reducing the workload on my joints, namely my ankles and knees, which should benefit me heading into my later years.

Keeping them strong can make everyday activities feel easier, too, while also improving balance, ankle stability and overall lower-limb function.

So, according to science, these muscles protect your heart, aid circulation, help produce movement, and impact gait and balance. What more reason do you need to give this exercise a try the next time you're seated?

#3420. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3419. FAA Rolled Out New A.I. Traffic Tool Days Before Nationwide Ground Stop

The Federal Aviation Administration began rolling out a massive new A.I.-powered air traffic system nationwide just days before Friday's shocking ground stop ... and the timing is raising some eyebrows.

On Tuesday, the agency announced it was expanding its $875 million A.I. system, called SMART, to all 22 air traffic control centers ... promising fewer delays, less fuel consumption and smoother travel.

But just three days later, the FAA ordered a rare nationwide ground stop ... throwing air travel into chaos.

As Gizmodo reported, the rollout had already sparked concerns ... with the National Air Traffic Controllers Association saying it wasn't involved in designing or testing the technology.

The FAA insists the A.I. only recommends flight routes, leaving final decisions to human controllers. Worth noting ... so far, there's no evidence linking SMART to the shutdown.

As TMZ previously reported ... the ground stop halted departures nationwide, sparking chaos at airports across the country as travelers were left stranded.

For now, the cause of the shutdown remains under investigation.

#3417. FAA Issues Rare Nationwide Ground Stop, Orders All Flights Halted

2:05 PM PT -- Markwayne Mullin, Homeland Security Secretary, states that they have not established a timeframe on getting flights back up.

1:51 PM PT -- Mary Schiavo, CNN's Aviation Analyst, states preliminary reports indicate this is not a result of a cyber attack ... and speculates this may be due to new software the FAA has begun to integrate.

1:36 PM PT -- Peter Muntean, an Aviation Correspondent for CNN, predicts that this issue may last for days, with one or two days being needed to diagnose the issue.

1:28 PM PT -- U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says the nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports follows a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. He says FAA technicians are investigating the issue.

Travelers across America are going nowhere fast ... the Federal Aviation Administration has ordered an extremely rare nationwide ground stop, bringing departing flights across the country to a screeching halt!

The Federal Aviation Administration issued the sweeping order Friday afternoon, citing "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety," according to U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

An air traffic control advisory states ... "All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice."

And even international flights are caught up in the chaos ... the FAA says incoming international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis.

The massive disruption comes as several major airports were already battling delays Friday, including Chicago's O'Hare and Midway airports, which were hit with ground stops tied to equipment outages.

Meanwhile, San Francisco International Airport reported average ground delays of more than two hours due to wind, while New York's LaGuardia Airport was also dealing with significant delays.

It's unclear exactly what prompted the nationwide order or how long planes will be forced to stay on the ground.
