The biggest movies in theaters this holiday season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The holiday movie season is almost here, and there’s plenty to look forward to if you’re planning a trip to the theater. November and December 2026 are bringing some huge releases to the big screen, including the return of the Avengers in “Doomsday,” another trip to Arrakis in “Dune” and a new chapter in the “Hunger Games” franchise.

There’s also a festive horror sequel, a new adventure that brings a beloved video game to life outside its console, and a chilling medieval werewolf horror from “The Witch” director Robert Eggers. Clearly, the coming weeks have plenty to offer. I’ve rounded up seven of the biggest movies hitting theaters this holiday season, so you can start planning your next cinema trip. Here’s what deserves a spot on your watchlist.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” is easily one of the biggest movie releases to look forward to this month, thanks to the franchise’s huge fanbase and enduring popularity. It marks the fifth film directed by Francis Lawrence in the dystopian series, bringing him back together with the creative team behind its distinctive cinematic style. Lionsgate moved quickly to bring Suzanne Collins’ latest novel to the big screen, announcing the film adaptation alongside the book in 2024. The novel went on to become a major bestseller.

Set 24 years before the events of the original film, “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” follows 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) as he prepares for the 50th annual Hunger Games. Living in District 12, Haymitch’s life changes when his name is selected during the Reaping, forcing him to leave behind his family and girlfriend, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak). This year’s competition, known as the Second Quarter Quell, doubles the number of tributes sent into the arena. Alongside fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), Haymitch must fight to survive.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" hits theaters on Nov. 20

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an intriguing follow-up for fans of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” with Quentin Tarantino returning to write the story and David Fincher taking over directing duties. This time, the setting shifts away from the sun-soaked nostalgia of 1960s Hollywood towards a much darker 1970s crime backdrop. Fincher’s visual style should give the film a distinctly different feel with a much grittier atmosphere. It’s also a notable release for Netflix, which is giving the movie an IMAX-first theatrical run before it arrives on the streaming service over the holidays.

Set eight years after the events of “Once Upon a Time “in Hollywood,” the film follows former stuntman Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt). Having stepped away from stunt work, Cliff now earns a living as a bartender, using his unconventional skills to handle problems for the entertainment industry’s biggest names. When talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) approaches him on behalf of television star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), Cliff becomes involved in a complicated situation involving Charlie’s wife Toni (Carla Gugino) and two mysterious gangster brothers causing trouble across the city.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" hits theaters on Nov. 25

For something with a much bloodier take on Christmas, “Violent Night 2” should be on your radar next month. David Harbour returns as the hard-hitting Santa Claus, with Kristen Bell joining the cast for a new round of festive action. The sequel comes from the production company behind “Nobody 2” and “The Fall Guy,” so there’s good reason to expect plenty of inventive stuntwork and over-the-top fight scenes. Its reported influences include classic Spaghetti Westerns and traditional holiday movies, which sounds like an entertaining combination.

Santa Claus (David Harbour) returns for another Christmas showdown when a ruthless gangster (Jared Harris) and his armed henchmen take over the Silver Bell Mall. Stranded away from the North Pole and stripped of his magical powers, Santa must find another way to protect the mall’s merchants and the surrounding community. With time running out and his usual abilities no longer available, he’ll need to rely on his fighting skills to take down the criminals. Fortunately, he won’t be tackling the job alone, as Mrs. Claus (Kristen Bell) arrives to help him fight back.

"Violent Night 2" hits theaters on Dec. 4

“Avengers: Doomsday” is undoubtedly one of the biggest and most anticipated movies of the year, and I’m very curious to see what Marvel has planned. The Russo brothers return to the MCU for the first time since “Endgame,” reuniting with longtime collaborator Stephen McFeely to direct this next chapter and its follow-up, “Secret Wars.” As the 39th film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, there’s a lot riding on this one, particularly with Doctor Doom stepping into the spotlight as a major threat. I’m incredibly excited to see how it all unfolds, but also a little nervous about just how brutal Doom could be.

The Avengers face their biggest challenge yet when a powerful new enemy threatens multiple universes. Led by Victor von Doom (Robert Downey Jr.), the looming crisis brings together heroes from across the Marvel universe, including the Avengers, Fantastic Four, X-Men and Wakandans. As their worlds are set on a collision course, the unlikely allies must confront a threat capable of changing the fate of the multiverse. With familiar faces including Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), Shuri (Letitia Wright) and Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal), the heroes must find a way to stop Doom before it’s too late.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters Dec. 18

Another huge film releasing next month and competing on the same day with “Doomsday” is “Dune 3.” Denis Villeneuve returns to direct what is expected to be the final chapter of his Arrakis saga, adapting Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel “Dune Messiah.” Rather than simply serving as a traditional trilogy finale, Villeneuve has described the film as more of an epilogue to Paul Atreides’ story, bringing his journey to a close while taking the franchise in a new direction. With the previous two movies proving such huge cinematic events, this is easily one of the biggest releases over the holiday season.

“Dune 3” continues the story of Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) following his rise to power on Arrakis. Set several years after the events of part 2, the film follows Paul as he rules as Emperor, while facing growing opposition to his reign and the consequences of the religious movement that has spread across the universe in his name. As rival factions secretly plot to overthrow him, Paul must contend with dangerous new enemies and a mysterious conspiracy involving the Bene Tleilax. Meanwhile, Chani (Zendaya) finds herself caught up in events that could change the future of House Atreides.

“Jumanji: Open World” brings the modern rebooted franchise to a close, reuniting audiences with its familiar mix of action, comedy and adventure. The latest instalment looks set to shake up the formula by bringing the game’s dangers into the real world, rather than transporting its characters into a virtual jungle. That means wild animals, chaotic stampedes and other game hazards spilling into everyday suburban and urban settings. It’s an interesting twist on the series’ familiar setup, and a promising way to wrap up this latest chapter of the “Jumanji” franchise.

The group are reunited for another adventure when the Jumanji video game unexpectedly escapes its console and spills into the real world. As wild animals and dangerous creatures wreak havoc, the game’s familiar avatars, Dr. Smolder Bravestone (Dwayne Johnson), Ruby Roundhouse (Karen Gillan), Mouse Finbar (Kevin Hart) and Professor Shelly Oberon (Jack Black), find themselves roaming the streets in demo mode. With the game threatening to turn everyday life upside down, the group must return to Jumanji and find a way to stop the chaos.

"Jumanji: Open World" hits theaters on Dec. 25

One of my most anticipated films of 2026 in general is “Werwulf,” the period gothic folk-horror feature directed by Robert Eggers. Following “Nosferatu,” the director is taking on another creature-focused story, this time set in a period setting with a folk-horror twist. It also reunites several familiar faces from his previous film, including Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp, Willem Dafoe and Ralph Ineson. Eggers is co-writing with Sjón, marking their second collaboration after “The Northman,” and has described the screenplay as the darkest he's written so far.

Set in 13th-century England, “Werwulf” follows a mute medieval farmer (Aaron Taylor-Johnson) who lives quietly with his family while hiding a terrifying secret: he transforms into a murderous werewolf whenever the full moon rises. When a hunting party arrives under the king’s orders to eliminate the wolves roaming the countryside, the farmer is forced to join them, putting his secret at risk. As the hunters search for the creature responsible for a series of attacks, he struggles to conceal his identity while protecting his wife and children from the growing danger.

Alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Advocacy groups want AI stopped and safeguards put in place

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The backlash against AI is getting harder for Silicon Valley to ignore. Just days after five people were arrested protesting Anthropic's planned IPO, a coalition of advocacy groups has filed a lawsuit seeking to stop some of the world's biggest AI companies from developing and releasing new models.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court, targets OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceXSI. The groups behind it argue that the companies are advancing technology that could cause catastrophic harm without adequate safeguards.

For consumers who use ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini every day, the case raises a question about the future of AI. Could the companies responsible for today's most popular chatbots eventually be forced to slow down?

The lawsuit comes from four nonprofit organizations: the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI.

According to The Associated Press, the complaint alleges that the companies have violated California's unfair competition law by endangering public health and interfering with people's use of property, including computer systems.

The groups point to reported incidents involving AI-assisted cyberattacks and warn that increasingly autonomous systems could eventually operate beyond human control.

They want a judge to prevent the five companies from developing or deploying new AI models.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

This represents an effort to use the courts to impose limits on an industry that has expanded rapidly over the past several years with very few safeguards.

The lawsuit follows another development involving Anthropic, the company behind Claude.

On Monday, November 9, protesters gathered outside Anthropic's Manhattan offices to oppose its planned initial public offering, which could value the company at approximately $1.4 trillion.

According to Democracy Now!, five protesters were arrested after blocking an employee security entrance.

The demonstration involved activists from Climate Defenders, New York Communities for Change and Planet Over Profit. Their concerns focused on the financial risks surrounding the AI industry, including the possibility that soaring valuations could contribute to a wider economic downturn.

According to a report shared with Tom's Guide, activist Jonathan Westin told Democracy Now! that he feared Anthropic and the wider AI industry could crash the global economy.

Unlike Thursday's lawsuit, which focuses on technological safety, the demonstration targeted the financial consequences of the AI boom.

These risks have been mentioned before. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has previously acknowledged the possibility of AI development going badly and called for the industry to slow the pace of progress so safety measures can catch up.

Yet Anthropic continues developing increasingly advanced AI systems while preparing for a potentially historic public offering.

That tension is becoming harder to ignore as the industry moves toward AI agents capable of performing complex tasks, interacting with computer systems and operating with less human supervision.

For now, nothing changes about how consumers can use these chatbots. The lawsuit is an attempt to prevent future AI development, not an order requiring companies to shut down existing products or suspend subscriptions.

But if the plaintiffs ultimately succeed in obtaining a broad court order, the consequences could extend well beyond Silicon Valley. New model launches, advanced AI features and the pace of competition between companies could all be affected.

#3408. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3407. Skydance confirms HBO Max and Paramount+ ‘value’ bundle plan

HBO Max and Paramount+ customers will soon be able to pay for one subscription that unlocks both services. That’s according to Skydance, the company that came out of Paramount’s Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition.

Skydance announced plans for the HBO Max plus Paramount+ bundle today, promising to deliver the package deal early next year.

Skydance doesn’t say how much the bundle will cost or if it will have ad-supported options. Both HBO Max and Paramount+ currently offer cheaper subscriptions with ads as well as premium ad-free options.

HBO Max can also be bundled with Disney+ and Hulu today, though this is a package offering that we can probably expect to go away in the future.

Ultimately, it would make sense for Skydance to package a unified service that includes all of the content from both services. For now, at least, it sounds like the short-term plan is to sell the two services separately with an option to bundle and save.

#3406. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3405. Today’s macOS updates fix security gap involving eMudhra certificates

Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Mozilla reported that private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra, an Indian digital certification company, had been compromised.

In essence, these certificates are used to establish trust in digital certificates that verify website identities and enable secure connections.

With access to the compromised private keys, bad actors could potentially create fraudulent certificates that appear legitimate, allowing them to impersonate websites and intercept sensitive user information.

In response to the compromise, Apple began automatically blocking the affected certificates on October 19, followed by additional protections on October 23.

These changes were delivered through automatic certificate configuration updates, meaning users didn’t need to install a macOS update to be protected.

While these measures protected Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple’s networking and security frameworks, they didn’t cover all of macOS, as certain command-line tools, including curl and git, could still accept the compromised certificates.

At the time, Apple published a support article with instructions for administrators to manually address this remaining security gap, while promising a fix in a future macOS update.

Today, Apple updated the document to confirm that the fix is now available.

As Apple explains, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, and macOS 15.8.3, released earlier today, prevent the affected command-line tools from accepting the compromised certificates, eliminating the need for administrators to manually address the issue.

The updates also remove five root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including three additional eMudhra certificates that weren’t part of Apple’s original manual workaround.

Still, for users who are unable to install the latest macOS updates, Apple continues to provide instructions for manually addressing the issue in its support document, along with the names and SHA-256 fingerprints of the 12 affected certificates and five root CA certificates removed by the updates.

Apple also notes that “some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don’t use Apple’s block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem,” and advises users to contact the developer of those apps and tools.

To read Apple’s full support document, follow this link.

#3403. Apple Intelligence completes regulatory registration for iPad and Mac in China

Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence’s expected launch in China this December. Here are the details.

In late October, Apple published a press release on its Chinese Newsroom website confirming its intention to launch Apple Intelligence in China this December, as part of iOS 27.3.

Apple went on to release the first iOS 27.3 developer beta a few days later, allowing users in China to test Apple Intelligence ahead of its public launch.

In its press release, however, Apple also noted that the initial rollout would be limited to iPhones, as support for other platforms was still pending regulatory approval.

Now, as spotted by Reuters, Apple Intelligence “has been ‌registered for use on tablets and laptops in China, Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator said on Monday.”

For context, generative AI services must complete a regulatory registration process before they can launch publicly in China.

Apple Intelligence, which, in China, relies on Alibaba’s Qwen model to power certain AI features, had already received regulatory approval for iPhones in July, following months of delays and negotiations with Chinese authorities.

With today’s registration, Apple has cleared another regulatory hurdle ahead of Apple Intelligence’s launch in China. However, the company has yet to confirm whether iPad and Mac support will also arrive in December.

#3402. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3401. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

‘Heartland’ shows the less glamorous side of fame

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A country music superstar, a missing rising star and the darker side of Nashville make for an intriguing setup, especially when you’ve got an Oscar-winning actress leading the investigation. That's the premise behind “Heartland,” Netflix's latest original thriller, starring Jessica Chastain as a retired country music legend. The film is written and directed by Shana Feste, who previously explored the country music scene in 2010's “Country Strong.” This time though, she's trading the musical drama for a mystery thriller.

In “Heartland,” Chastain plays Misty Jones, a former country music megastar who has spent 20 years away from Nashville and the spotlight. However, when her niece Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), an up-and-coming country singer, suddenly goes missing, Misty returns to her old hometown to find her. Her investigation quickly draws her into Nashville’s murkier corners, where she encounters a number of potential suspects: Charlie’s boyfriend Jace (Ross Lynch) and manager Roy Combs (Garrett Hedlund). Along the way, Misty also finds herself confronting some uncomfortable truths about her own past.

I’ve already watched “Heartland,” and while its premise certainly caught my attention, I’m not entirely convinced the finished movie delivers everything it promises. So, is this latest Netflix original worth adding to your watchlist, or are we looking at another forgettable thriller from the streamer? Here are my honest thoughts and whether I’d recommend giving it a watch this weekend.

I’m Alix, a lifelong horror nerd who loves watching, reviewing and writing about the latest movies and TV shows. When I’m not working through my ever-growing horror watchlist, I’m covering the biggest releases across streaming and film, including the latest DC movie "Clayface," "VisionQuest" on Disney+, and "The Institute" season 2 on MGM+.

“Heartland” gets off to a pretty jarring start, with Misty ending up in a heated disagreement with her neighbor over her dogs. I understand what the movie is going for here, using the confrontation to establish Misty’s closed-off nature and aggressive streak, but it’s an unusual way to introduce the character and didn’t immediately win me over. Still, like many of Netflix’s original movies, the first half is where “Heartland” is at its strongest.

We get straight into the mystery surrounding Charlie’s disappearance, with Misty’s brother pleading for her to return to Nashville after Charlie has missed several shows and concerts, leaving fans to drag her name through the mud online. Returning to her hometown also brings plenty of painful memories to the surface, with quick, scattered flashbacks offering glimpses into the trauma she’s spent years trying to bury. Chastain gives a strong enough performance, but I struggled to connect with Misty, which made it harder to invest in her personal journey. It was the mystery surrounding her niece that kept me interested.

Unfortunately, that mystery doesn’t have quite the staying power the movie needs. A major twist arrives around the halfway point, and rather than giving the story a much-needed boost, it pretty much sucks the intrigue out of the second half. Once the reveal comes into focus, there’s very little left to keep you guessing, particularly if you’ve been paying attention to how certain characters are introduced and positioned throughout the opening act. I had a pretty good idea of where things were heading from early on, so the eventual reveal didn’t carry much of a punch.

It’s a shame, because the first half does enough to make you curious about what’s really going on, but the film struggles to maintain that momentum once its biggest secret is out in the open. That said, “Heartland” does at least make good use of its country music roots, with plenty of on-stage performances and music woven into the story. There’s also an interesting look at the darker side of fame, particularly the pressure of staying relevant and the way public perception can turn against you.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Unfortunately, “Heartland” is another Netflix original that’s likely to be forgotten about before long. The biggest frustration is that it makes very little effort to deliver a genuinely compelling story, with weak reveals and predictable twists making the climax particularly dull. The atmosphere, music and locations feel deeply rooted in Nashville’s country music scene, which is arguably where the movie works best. However, those elements can only do so much when the mystery at the heart of the story is so underwhelming.

I’d say “Heartland” is worth a watch if you’re a fan of Jessica Chastain’s work or simply in the mood for some country music and a little Nashville drama. However, if you’re looking for a mystery thriller with clever twists, memorable characters and a satisfying payoff, this probably isn’t going to scratch that itch. For the most part, I’d recommend giving this one a miss and saving your Netflix evening for something better.

Alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

#3398. ‘Paper Tiger’ Is a Greek Tragedy With a Thick New York Accent

Cain had Abel, Biff Loman had Happy, and Michael Corleone had Fredo. For Irwin Pearl, the everyman hero of writer-director James Gray’s Paper Tiger, there is his older brother, Gary. Make no mistake: Irwin (Miles Teller) loves Gary (Adam Driver). You can tell by the way they tease each other, talk to one another, and trade inside jokes that the affection is mutual. And yet this solidly lower-middle-class engineer, who dreams of getting out of Queens and being somebody that his family can look up to, lives in the ever-looming shadow of his elder sibling.

Once upon a time — specifically, the 1970s and early 1980s — Gary was a New York City cop. He had connections, made moves, busted skulls, commanded respect. Then he quit the force, started and sold a business, made a fortune. Now Gary sports expensive Italian suits, drives a Mercedes and, per the words of Irwin’s wife, Hester (Scarlett Johansson), “has more money than God.” He’s the life of the party and the beloved cool uncle, happy to entertain his teenage nephews Scott (Gavin Goudey) and Benjamin (Roman Engel) by showing off the revolver in his ankle holster in between goofing around on the piano. If Gary’s going to show up at the last minute for dinner at Irwin’s place, he’s going to get Peter Luger’s steakhouse to cater it.

There’s a secondary agenda to the impromptu drop-in, however. The era of the Italian mafiosi keeping Brooklyn under its red-sauce–stained thumb are fading, and now the Russians are coming, the Russians are coming. The area around the Gowanus Canal had long been a no-man’s-land because of all of the pollution in the water. But the new mob in town want to develop the neighborhood. Gary smells opportunity. The man wears his streetwise bona fides like a badge of pride, so he’s going to broker deals between these immigrants with criminal-capitalistic aspirations and the bureaucratic powers that be. He wants Irwin to come on board as a “consultant” for cleaning up the area to code standards. Both of the Pearl brothers have dollar signs in their eyes. When it comes to this new breed of gangster, however, the old rules — the ones that Gary is fluent in, and takes for granted — no longer apply. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

James Gray has made movies set everywhere from the Amazon rain forests (The Lost City of Z) to outer space (Ad Astra), but it’s in the concrete jungles of New York that he tends to thrive, storytelling-wise. Crime and the city, along with family, are constants; so are compromised moralities and a throwback sense of New Hollywood grittiness. The Queens-bred writer-director specializes a sense of regional authenticity, and with this and his previous — and arguably best — film, Armageddon Time (2022), he’s added autobiographical strains of his own Gotham adolescence into the soup.

With this scuffed-up gem of a film, Gray mixes both his crime-thriller obsessions and his memories into one spiked brew, using a tale of two brothers caught up in the greed-is-good mentality of the go-go 1980s to fashion nothing less than a Greek tragedy with an outer-borough accent. The tension of his earlier work is there in abundance, especially when Irwin decides, in a misguided fit of pride, to take his sons to his new workplace in Carroll Gardens late one night. He wants to impress the boys: Dad may not have a Mercedes like Uncle Gary, but they’re all going to be on Easy Street soon enough! It turns out that his Eastern European clients aren’t keen on after-hours visits. Things go south. Gary’s got to clean up his brother’s mess with the new boss in town. Let’s just say that goes south pretty quickly as well.

You don’t need to know that Irwin and Hester are based on Gray’s parents, the encounter with thugs comes from a real-life incident, or that Gary is a composite of both the filmmaker’s uncle and a business partner of his dad’s. All you need to understand Paper Tiger — the title comes from Gary’s assumption that these Russian mobsters merely talk a big game, a call that will prove to have serious consequences — is that blood runs thicker than water. It also has a nasty tendency to get spilled when the talking stops and the guns are pulled. Or, in Gary’s case, the belt comes off; a scene in which the ex-cop whips the crap out of a trio of hoodlums with a clothing accessory reminds you that he’s not playing around, either. This veteran of the force thinks he’s untouchable. Spoiler: He isn’t. Related Content You Know Rosalind Eleazar From ‘Slow Horses.’ She’ll Blow You Away in ‘Misty Green’ Did ‘Misty Green’ Just Give Us Our Next Best Actress Winner? Adam Driver and Miles Teller Get Tangled Up With Russian Mob in ‘Paper Tiger’ Trailer Rosalind Eleazar Is a Hollywood Actress Fighting to Rebuild Her Life in Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’ Trailer

It’s worth noting that the movie’s ensemble is airtight, and gives you the sense that you’re witnessing an actual family dynamic at work, from hard-earned teenage eyerolls to Hester’s authoritative henpecking. Teller’s way of underplaying panic while still leaning into a sense of in-over-his-head helplessness suits Irwin. Johansson handles a third-act pivot to melodrama (this element is also pulled from the filmmaker’s direct experiences) with deftness, and anyone suggesting her New Yawk accent is better suited for selling chandeliers than channeling pathos has clearly never spent time in Flushing. Trending Stories Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage John Mulaney Has Many Thoughts on the 2026 Rock Hall Inductees — And Picks Next Year’s Class The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Dolly Parton Heals the Soul on Final Recording, ‘Torn,’ a Duet With Bono on U2’s New Album

It’s Driver, however, who gets the meatiest role, and he understands exactly where to pitch Gary’s combination of Teflon swagger and swinging-dick entitlement. Crown or no crown, he thinks of himself as a prince of the city, someone who still believes his mere presence is the equivalent of flashing a badge. There’s an early scene in which Gary takes his brother out for a meal at an Italian restaurant, “the last holdout of the Genovese family.” Despite the fact he was apparently one of the few non-corrupt cops on the force (something which never sat well with his fellow brothers in blue, and comes back to haunt him), Gary moves at ease in the environment. The Mafia is the devil he knows. His underestimating of the next generation of string-pullers is his fatal flaw. Driver lets you see the awe this character inspires in others, and the shock when he unexpectedly finds himself in a situation when he can’t charm or cold-cock his way out. That he also gets a standout shootout in the tall grass near LaGuardia airport is simply a bonus.

But the hulking actor also shows the love between this alpha and his beta brother that circumstances will rend asunder, and this is where the power of Paper Tiger really rests. Like we said, it’s a Greek tragedy that just happens to carbon-date to the Reagan era and feature kids playing a Ms. Pac-Man machine at Lum’s. But it’s also an American tragedy, one borne of the relentless drive and ambition and grass-is-always-greener greed that’s made this country and continually threatens to break it into tiny shards. Not even a loving family like the Pearls and their kin are immune to the fallout. Gray has said that he wanted to revisit this time in his life, when he felt like the American Dream was driving a wedge into his relations, because he wanted to say that a moral compass still matters in this world. He’s given us a movie brimming not only with sympathy but with the clarity that time allows. It’s not a look back in anger. Just a look back in sorrow.

#3397. Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over Google search deal

A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple over allegations that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. Here are the details.

In recent years, Apple’s deal with Alphabet to make Google the default search engine on Safari has drawn regulatory attention in the US, the UK, and Australia, while related search competition concerns have also come under scrutiny in the EU and Japan.

While the details of each investigation differ, they all raise concerns about the impact of Google’s dominance in search, as well as the extent to which its agreements with other companies might be limiting competition.

More recently, Apple’s agreement with Google received significant attention during the US Department of Justice’s antitrust case against the search giant, which included testimony from Apple executives Eddy Cue and John Giannandrea. The latter joined Apple from Google in 2018 and led its AI efforts until stepping down earlier this year.

As a result of the US case, a federal judge ruled in August 2024 that Google had illegally maintained its monopoly in online search through anticompetitive agreements, including its deal with Apple.

Now, evidence presented during that trial has become central to a class action against Apple in Canada, which a British Columbia Supreme Court judge recently certified.

The case was initially brought in 2021 by Spark Event Rentals Ltd., an event rental company based in British Columbia. The plaintiff alleged that Apple and Google conspired to limit competition in the search market, allowing Google to charge advertisers artificially inflated prices.

Apple, meanwhile, argued that its agreement with Google was a legitimate distribution arrangement rather than an unlawful conspiracy. The company also maintained that Google was the appropriate defendant, describing itself as an “innocent bystander.”

Interestingly, the lawsuit originally named both Apple and Google as defendants, but the plaintiff later dropped Google from the case following a dispute over an arbitration clause in its advertising contracts.

With Apple now the sole defendant, Justice Thomas has allowed the case to proceed as a class action, finding sufficient grounds to examine whether Google’s payments discouraged Apple from developing its own search engine.

The lawsuit seeks financial compensation for advertisers who allegedly overpaid for Google search ads, and the court has also allowed the question of punitive damages to proceed.

The class action covers Canadian residents who purchased search ads from Google since 2005, when Apple and Google first agreed to make Google the default search engine on Safari in exchange for a share of advertising revenue.

Importantly, the ruling does not establish that Apple engaged in anticompetitive conduct, but simply allows the allegations to proceed as a class action.

The central proposition raised by these pleadings is that Apple could have used its resources and distribution network to enter the search engine market, but chose not to because Google paid Apple billions of dollars in revenue-share payments to make Google the default search provider on Apple products. This arrangement gave Google market power, enabling it to charge supracompetitive advertising prices on search engines.

In my view, this pleads a common purpose to perform an act prohibited by s 45 of the Competition Act, such that it is not “clear and obvious” that the plaintiff has not pleaded an agreement between Google and Apple not to compete in the search engine market.

At one point in his decision, Justice Thomas cites Giannandrea’s testimony and directly quotes Cue’s from the US antitrust trial, before concluding that “this provides some basis in fact, supporting the inference that Apple did not compete with Google in the search engine market because of its Agreement with Google.”

Interestingly, the judge also acknowledges Apple’s objections to the evidence, agreeing that “the plaintiff has cherry-picked evidence to support his case,” but adding that, in his view, “it is appropriate to do so at this stage in the proceedings.”

With the class action greenlit, the case can now move forward toward trial, though no date has been announced yet.

#3396. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

How to clean a stainless steel sink and bring back its showroom shine using basic cupboard staples

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you are getting your home ready for festive hosting, do not overlook the sink. Even with pristine worktops and clean floors, cloudy stainless steel covered in chalky water rings instantly makes a kitchen feel tired.

Before the holiday cooking frenzy begins, you can revive a dull basin without scratching the metal or buying pricey specialty cleaners. This five-minute routine cuts through greasy buildup and seals in a bright, showroom shine just in time for visitors.

Rinse away loose food debris, then wash the entire basin thoroughly with hot water and dish soap. Using a soft microfiber cloth or non-scratch sponge, wipe in long, steady strokes that follow the faint brushed grain of the steel rather than scrubbing in circles.

This removes the surface grease film so your cleaning paste can make direct contact with the mineral spots underneath.

Sprinkle a light dusting of baking soda over the damp steel, concentrating on the drain and faucet base where hard water residue gathers. Using a damp cloth, work the powder into a paste along the metal's grain to lift dull water rings without scratching.

For stubborn hard-water marks, rinse the baking soda paste away thoroughly first, then apply a light spray of white vinegar directly to the mineral scale.

Letting the vinegar sit undiluted for a few minutes allows its mild acetic acid to chemically dissolve crusty calcium and magnesium deposits without being neutralized by the alkaline baking soda.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Avoid spraying vinegar onto specialized faucet finishes like matte black, brass, or oil-rubbed bronze, as the acid can strip or discolor the coating.

Once the mineral scale softens, use a soft-bristled brush or non-scratch sponge to gently agitate and lift any remaining gritty buildup from the metal’s surface texture.

Standing water left to evaporate is why cloudy spots return. Use a dry dish towel or microfiber cloth to wipe the entire basin, faucet, and drainboard until completely dry.

For an optional finishing shine, apply a single drop of mineral oil (like baby oil) or olive oil to a soft cloth and buff it into the steel, following the direction of the metal's grain. Buff vigorously with a clean, dry section of the towel until no residue remains.

This creates a light barrier that repels water beads and keeps the shine lasting longer, especially on faucets and handles.

#3388. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3386. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.
